docs.title: Chapter 2 · Bone and Muscle Capital: Two Accounts You Can Only Draw From, Never Pay Into
docs.text:
Last winter, your mother stumbled in the stairwell and only kept from falling by grabbing the handrail. She waved it off as nothing. But you noticed: she has got a little shorter over these past two years, and her hands aren't steady when she carries things.

You assume this is just "getting old". In fact there are two accounts she never paid into enough back then, and now she draws them down year by year.

This book keeps four accounts, and the first one is independence. Being able to walk on your own, get up on your own, carry things on your own — that rests on two accounts: bone and muscle. This chapter covers three things: how to tell how much you have left, where you can top up today, and when you should see a doctor instead of just pushing through on your own.

docs.title: 2.1 These two accounts are the exact opposite of a savings account
docs.text: Money can be saved late in life; bone and muscle can't. Both have a window, up to roughly age thirty: eat right and move enough before then, and the account grows year by year. Past that window, less and less goes in and more and more comes out. The question isn't "what do I do once I'm old" — it's "how much can I still put in now".

docs.title: 2.2 Bone capital: it tops out in your thirties, then only goes out
docs.text:
Bone grows your whole life, reaching its peak around age thirty — this is peak bone mass. After thirty to thirty-five it starts to decline (official wording Beijing Municipal Health Commission, "Strengthen Your Bones, Refuse 'Osteoporosis'" 2023; Chronic Disease Center of the Chinese CDC, 2025). The higher the peak and the later it comes, the more you can draw on for the rest of your life.

Why it declines: bone contains two sets of cells, one that tears down old bone and one that builds new bone. When you're young, building outruns tearing down; after thirty, tearing down overtakes it. The trabeculae — the spongy struts inside bone — thin out and grow sparse, and the bone turns brittle.

Women lose the most at menopause. Oestrogen normally holds the brake on the "bone-tearing" cells; after menopause it plunges, and bone is lost fastest in the first five to ten years after menopause, at 2 to 3 percent a year (official wording Clinical Diagnosis and Treatment Guidelines for Primary Osteoporosis (2022) (原发性骨质疏松症诊疗指南（2022）); third-party research Xinhua Net 2025). Men lose bone too, just more slowly and later: prevalence in men over 65 is 10.7 percent, with gonadal function declining after 70 (official wording Beijing Municipal Health Commission 2023).

The numbers for China: prevalence over age 50 is 19.2 percent (women 32.1, men 6.9); over age 65, 32 percent (women 51.6, men 10.7); and among people over 40, 40.9 percent already have low bone mass (official wording Beijing Municipal Health Commission 2023; Chronic Disease Center of the Chinese CDC, 2025).

One honest thing: half your foundation is genetic, and you can't change that; whether you lose bone fast or slow is half in your own hands.

docs.title: 2.3 Muscle capital: it peaks at thirty too, and falls faster after sixty
docs.text:
Muscle mass generally peaks around the thirties or forties, then declines year by year. How fast varies by source: one popular-science piece says it peaks at 30, then drops 1 to 2 percent a year, accelerating after 60 (third-party research China Food and Drug Network 2022); another article reviewed by the Chinese Medical Association says that after 50, leg muscle mass falls 1 to 2 percent a year and muscle strength 1.5 to 5 percent a year (third-party research Xinhua Net 2024). The two sources don't fully agree on the peak age or the rate, but they agree on the direction: past the peak it declines every year, and faster after 60. Drop far enough and it becomes a disease called sarcopenia; among community-dwelling older people in China prevalence runs 8.9 to 38.8 percent, reaching 67.1 percent over age 80 (third-party research Xinhua Net 2024).

Once the muscle on your legs thins you walk unsteadily, walking unsteadily makes you fall, and a fall puts you in bed for three months and costs you still more muscle — the same loop as the falls loop in Chapter 5. Be careful with the old saying "you can't buy leanness in old age": thin is not the goal, and being underweight is itself a risk factor (official wording Clinical Diagnosis and Treatment Guidelines for Primary Osteoporosis (2022) (原发性骨质疏松症诊疗指南（2022）)).

docs.title: 2.4 A rough self-test at home: grip strength, walking speed, calf circumference
docs.text:
• What it costs: basically nothing; a grip dynamometer is optional (Money: barely any money ｜ Time: ten minutes ｜ Effort: no strain ｜ Need to ask someone: no)
  • In short: these three numbers are the screening method set by the Asian Working Group for Sarcopenia — screen roughly at home first, and leave the formal judgment to a doctor.
  • What you can do: ① Grip strength: with your writing hand, squeeze the dynamometer with the arm hanging down; under 28 kg for men, under 18 kg for women counts as low. ② Walking speed: walk a straight 6-metre path; under 1 metre per second is slow. ③ Calf circumference: measure the thickest part while sitting; under 34 cm for men, under 33 cm for women suggests too little muscle. ④ The five-question SARC-F questionnaire: take a score of 4 seriously. Muscle mass itself requires DXA at a hospital; below 7 kg/m² for men, below 5.4 for women counts as low (all above third-party research: AWGS 2019).
  • Where this comes from: B ｜ the above are the standard criteria of the Asian Working Group for Sarcopenia (AWGS 2019) (diagnostic criteria). But the cut-offs come from multi-country Asian populations; finer China-specific lines are still being researched, so don't treat this as a diagnosis. Also note: a looser set of figures also circulates online — grip strength under 25 kg for men, walking speed under 0.8 m/s; those are an earlier line used for preliminary screening, and AWGS 2019 governs an actual diagnosis.
  • Who this is for: people who can stand and walk on their own. If you can't grip, get winded after a few steps, or have fallen in the past six months, don't test at home — go straight to the hospital.
  • What you get back: independence — no more fearing "I'm not sure whether I can still manage"
  • How this works in China: once you've measured, ask the contracted family doctor team at your community health centre whether it matters and whether you need a DXA scan.

docs.title: 2.5 Resistance training and weight-bearing activity: make your muscles work, put load on your bones
docs.text:
• What it costs: a resistance band costs a few dozen yuan; a pair of small dumbbells or two bottles of water will do (Money: barely any money ｜ Time: 20 minutes a session, two or three times a week ｜ Effort: somewhat tiring ｜ Need to ask someone: no)
  • In short: making your muscles work against a resistance (resistance training) and letting your body weight press down through your legs and spine (weight-bearing) are the two things that build muscle and bone — walking alone can't make up for it.
  • What you can do: ① Resistance: two to three times a week, working the same muscle again after a day's gap; 8 to 12 repetitions per set, two to three sets; start with legs and back — sit-to-stand, wall squats, band rows, biceps curls, and grip-squeezing all count. ② Weight-bearing: walk enough each day, totalling 150 minutes of moderate intensity a week; brisk walking, jogging, and stair-climbing (if your knees are okay) all load the bone, while swimming and cycling put little load on bone and can't replace them ([third-party research: West China Hospital reprint of the Chinese Expert Consensus on Prevention and Intervention of Physical Function Impairment in Older Adults (2022) (《老年人躯体功能受损防控干预中国专家共识（2022）》); official wording: Chronic Disease Center of the Chinese CDC, 2025]).
  • Where this comes from: B ｜ both kinds of training are unanimously recommended by Chinese geriatric-medicine consensus. But swimming and cycling have limited effect on raising bone density.
  • Who this is for: people who can stand steadily, sit and stand on their own, and walk without pain — start from a seated position and your own body weight. If you have heart problems, painful joints, uncontrolled blood pressure, or get winded after two steps, have a doctor look first before you start; while training you should still be able to talk normally.
  • What you get back: independence — no more fearing "my legs are getting weaker and can't hold me up"
  • How this works in China: communities and universities of the third age often run resistance and resistance-band classes and walking groups; ask the community health centre or the community eldercare service station.

docs.title: 2.6 Jumping movements: those with strong bones train with it, those with brittle bones avoid it
docs.text:
• What it costs: nothing (Money: nothing ｜ Time: a few minutes at a time ｜ Effort: quite tiring ｜ Need to ask someone: yes, easy)
  • In short: when you jump and land, the ground throws a jolt back up into your leg bones and spine; for bones that are still solid, that "shake" is a signal telling them to get harder.
  • What you can do: if your bones have been checked and are fine, you can start with very small hops in place, or hopping off a low step — keep the dose small and build up slowly. If your knees, ankles, or lower back are injured, switch to landing on the balls of your feet and walking briskly downhill instead.
  • Where this comes from: C ｜ the idea that "impact-type movement stimulates bone" has research support. But how much jumping actually helps bones get harder has no quantified domestic evidence; a 2025 consensus warns that people with exercise contraindications should avoid explosive and high-impact movements (official wording Shenyang Municipal Health Commission 2026, citing the Expert Consensus on Nutritional and Exercise Management of Primary Osteoporosis and Sarcopenia (2025) (《原发性骨质疏松症与肌少症的营养和运动管理专家共识（2025年）》)).
  • Who this is for: the "who this holds for" matters most with this one. People already diagnosed with low bone mass or osteoporosis, or who have had a fragility fracture, should not practise jumping on their own — the impact of landing can crush a bone outright; people with brittle bones should train weight-bearing, resistance, and balance, not jumping. Those who are overweight or have knee or ankle problems aren't suited to it either.
  • What you get back: independence — no more fearing "I can't tell whether bone gets harder or more brittle the more I use it"
  • How this works in China: this one is not something to practise, it's something to ask — take "can I jump, can I run?" to an orthopaedics or rehabilitation doctor.

docs.title: 2.7 Calcium and protein: get both from your plate, don't count on calcium tablets alone
docs.text:
• What it costs: a glass of milk, an egg, and a handful of soy products on the table every day — several dozen to one or two hundred yuan more a month (Money: some money ｜ Time: daily ｜ Effort: no strain ｜ Need to ask someone: no)
  • In short: calcium is the brick in bone, protein is the raw material for building muscle. Get enough of both from food first — a handful of calcium tablets alone won't rebuild muscle.
  • What you can do: ① Calcium: 300 to 500 mL of milk or yoghurt a day, plus tofu, dried tofu, and bean curd sticks; add rape greens, Chinese kale, and broccoli; small fish and shrimp eaten whole with the bones, and sesame paste, contribute a little too. Drink fewer carbonated drinks and less strong coffee, and use less salt. ② Protein: eggs, milk, fish and shrimp, lean meat, and soy products all count — put a little in every meal, don't pile it all into dinner; if chewing is a problem, use steamed egg, fish paste, or tofu instead. People with sarcopenia need more protein, and how much is calculated by body weight (official wording Chronic Disease Center of the Chinese CDC, 2025; Clinical Diagnosis and Treatment Guidelines for Primary Osteoporosis (2022) (原发性骨质疏松症诊疗指南（2022）); third-party research Xinhua Net 2024).
  • Where this comes from: A ｜ "eat more calcium-rich foods, use calcium supplements if intake is short, and get enough protein" is written into Chinese guidelines and the older-adult nutrition consensus. But how much to take daily, whether to use calcium tablets, and how many grams of protein all have to be decided by a doctor, taking diet, blood tests, and kidney function into account.
  • Who this is for: most people. People with kidney stones, poor kidney function, or high blood calcium are different: they must be especially cautious about calcium supplementation and can't eat a lot of protein either — ask a doctor first.
  • What you get back: independence — no more fearing "my bone is draining away and I don't know what to put in my mouth"
  • How this works in China: first go to a hospital for a bone-density scan and a kidney-function test, then decide what to eat and what to supplement. Where to ask: the community health centre, or the hospital's endocrinology or orthopaedics department; if there's a nutrition clinic, have the doctor calculate by body weight. Don't buy calcium tablets on your own from advertising.

docs.title: 2.8 Vitamin D: sun the right time of day, sun the right body parts
docs.text:
• What it costs: nothing (Money: nothing ｜ Time: a few times a week, ten-odd minutes each ｜ Effort: no strain ｜ Need to ask someone: yes, easy)
  • In short: for calcium to get into bone, vitamin D has to help carry it. It's made mainly by your own skin from sunlight, and there's almost none in food; if you get little sun, the calcium you eat won't stay either.
  • What you can do (per national guidelines): ① From early summer to late autumn, sunbathe between 10 a.m. and 3 p.m.; ② bare your arms and legs to the sun directly, don't sit behind glass, and don't apply thick sunscreen; ③ 15 to 30 minutes at a time, two to three times a week; ④ In northern winters, the plum-rain season, or for people indoors all day, sun exposure isn't enough and you have to supplement actively — the recommendation is 600 international units a day for people over 65 (600 IU, equal to 15 micrograms) ([official wording: Shenyang Municipal Health Commission 2026; Chronic Disease Center of the Chinese CDC, 2025; Chinese Nutrition Society, Dietary Reference Intakes for Chinese Residents (2023 edition) (《中国居民膳食营养素参考摄入量（2023版）》)]).
  • Where this comes from: A ｜ "get sun first, supplement if that's not enough" is written into China's dietary reference intakes; the time of day for sun comes from a domestic clinical expert consensus.
  • Who this is for: most people. People already taking a vitamin D supplement, or with high blood calcium, shouldn't stack supplements on top of each other — ask a doctor; and don't sunbathe until you peel.
  • What you get back: independence — no more fearing "I've supplemented for ages and don't know whether it stayed"
  • How this works in China: whether to test the vitamin D in your blood and how much to supplement — go to a hospital for a blood draw and ask a doctor; northern winters are all the more reason to ask.

docs.title: 2.9 Get a bone-density scan, and read the T-score properly
docs.text:
• What it costs: one clinic visit plus one scan, 100 to several hundred yuan, varying by place (Money: some money ｜ Time: half a day ｜ Effort: no strain ｜ Need to ask someone: yes, easy)
  • In short: bone density is the most direct test of how solid your bone is, and the internationally accepted diagnostic method is DXA (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry) — not the heel ultrasound at a check-up centre, and not the body-fat scale at home (official wording Healthy China, "Four Groups Advised to Have a Bone-Density Test" 2025).
  • What you can do: ① Who should be tested: anyone over 50 who has had a fracture; women over 65 and men over 70; postmenopausal women up to 65 and men 50 to 70 who have risk factors (such as lower-back pain after activity, being more than 3 cm shorter than in youth, or a stoop); and people taking bone-damaging drugs or with related diseases (official wording Healthy China 2025). ② Where to test: have the endocrinology, orthopaedics, or geriatrics department at a hospital order a DXA, scanning both the lumbar spine and the hip — testing only one site easily misses it. ③ T-score: not below −1.0 is normal; between −1.0 and −2.5 is low bone mass; −2.5 and below is osteoporosis (official wording Clinical Diagnosis and Treatment Guidelines for Primary Osteoporosis (2022) (原发性骨质疏松症诊疗指南（2022）)).
  • Where this comes from: A ｜ DXA diagnosis of osteoporosis is the international standard, and the T-score cut-offs are written into Chinese guidelines. But don't read the report yourself — a doctor has to judge it together with symptoms and medical history (third-party research Xinhua Net 2025).
  • Who this is for: the four groups above; those already diagnosed and on medication should be re-tested on the schedule the doctor sets — don't stop or adjust it yourself. A normal bone density doesn't mean you won't fracture, and the whole fall-prevention routine (Chapter 5) still applies.
  • What you get back: independence — no more fearing "I don't know whether my bones are up to it"
  • How this works in China: first get an order or referral from your contracted family doctor at the community health centre, then have the DXA done at a large hospital; in some cities a community check-up can do an ultrasound bone-density screen first, and those with a problem are referred for DXA (official wording Chronic Disease Center of the Chinese CDC, 2025); if you've signed up with a family doctor you can get regular follow-up and re-test reminders. Go by the latest local wording.

docs.title: 2.10 Smoking, drinking, and sitting still all draw down your bone capital early
docs.text:
• What it costs: nothing — it's about changing habits (Money: nothing ｜ Time: long-term ｜ Effort: no strain ｜ Need to ask someone: yes, easy)
  • In short: these two accounts — one is being paid into, the other can be drawn down by a few habits. Smoking, heavy drinking, and sitting from morning to night are three ways you draw down early.
  • What you can do: ① Smoking: what's in smoke damages bone cells and also worsens calcium absorption — quitting is the same act for your bones and your lungs. ② Alcohol: drinking too much damages bone and also makes you unsteady on your feet, more likely to fall. ③ Sitting: get up and move a few minutes every hour you sit.
  • Where this comes from: B ｜ "smoking, heavy drinking, and little physical activity" are listed in black and white as controllable risk factors in China's osteoporosis guideline (official wording Clinical Diagnosis and Treatment Guidelines for Primary Osteoporosis (2022) (原发性骨质疏松症诊疗指南（2022）)). But there's no precise figure for how much bone mass you can claw back by changing them.
  • Who this is for: it applies to anyone with these habits; when you can't change much, start with "stand up and walk for two minutes every hour you sit" — easier to keep than a grand "quit for good" goal.
  • What you get back: independence — no more fearing "I'm topping up and leaking at the same time, and I don't know it"
  • How this works in China: if you want to quit smoking, ask your community family doctor whether there's a cessation clinic or a referral.

docs.title: 2.11 If these things show up, see a doctor first — don't just train
docs.text:
• What it costs: one clinic visit (Money: the price of one registration ｜ Time: half a day ｜ Effort: no strain ｜ Need to ask someone: yes, easy)
  • In short: some signals mean the bone or muscle problem has moved past the "just train a bit and it'll be fine" stage — let a doctor sort it out first, then talk about how to move.
  • What you can do — go if you see these: ① Unexplained bone pain: pain at night, or pain whenever you exert yourself, especially lower-back pain. ② Weight loss: a clear, rapid drop in weight. ③ Fracture history: a fracture after age 50. ④ Losing more than 3 cm of height, or starting to stoop. When you go, say clearly where it hurts, for how long, whether you've fallen, and what medication you take, and ask the doctor to assess bone density, vitamin D, and kidney function.
  • Where this comes from: A ｜ these signals are written into China's osteoporosis guideline; treat them as a reason to "go get checked once", not as you diagnosing yourself.
  • Who this is for: anyone with any one of the above. Note: sudden severe bone pain, or being unable to move after a fall, doesn't fall under this — that's an emergency, call 120 (China's ambulance number) per Chapter 5.
  • What you get back: independence + money — no more fearing "a small problem dragging into a big one, and worrying about wasting money"
  • How this works in China: register at a hospital's orthopaedics, endocrinology, or geriatrics department; people over 65 get one free health-management check a year (National Basic Public Health Service), which includes a health-status assessment — ask the community health centre.

docs.title: 2.12 How this works in China: fold your bone density into the community's annual check-up
docs.text:
• What it costs: no extra cost (Money: nothing ｜ Time: once ｜ Effort: no strain ｜ Need to ask someone: no)
  • In short: the state has already folded these two accounts — bone and muscle — into community and annual check-ups, so you don't have to grope your own way in from a big hospital.
  • What you can do: ① Over 65: a free health-management check once a year — ask "bones, muscles, and whether I might fall" into it too (official wording National Basic Public Health Service Standards (3rd edition) (《国家基本公共卫生服务规范（第三版）》)). ② Some communities or check-up providers can do an ultrasound bone-density screen, forearm DXA, or quantitative CT first, and refer those with a problem to a hospital for DXA (official wording Chronic Disease Center of the Chinese CDC, 2025) — note that the standard items of the free check-up don't include bone density, and whether you can add it or be referred varies by place. ③ Contracted family doctor services are a scheme rolled out nationwide; once you sign up you get a fixed family doctor team that can follow up regularly, remind you about re-tests, and help refer you (official wording Guiding Opinions on Advancing Contracted Family Doctor Services (国医改办发〔2016〕1 号), 2016-06-06).
  • Where this comes from: B ｜ free check-ups and contracted family doctor services are basic services rolled out nationwide. But whether a community can do bone density and whether it can refer for DXA varies a lot by place.
  • Who this is for: people in cities and county towns near a community health centre; in rural areas, ask at the township health centre first.
  • What you get back: independence — no more fearing "I want to go get checked but don't know which door to walk through"
  • How this works in China: go to the community residents' committee or the community health centre and ask three questions: how do I book the free check-up, can you do bone density here, and is there a family doctor I can sign up with. Go by the latest local wording.

docs.title: 2.13 The one thing you can do today
docs.text:
Today, stand up from a chair without using your hands, then sit back down — two to three sets of 8 to 12 repetitions.

This move is both a test and a training: today it tells you how much capital is left in your legs, and from now on, twice a week, it's money you're paying into that account. From today, remember one number and compare it again on this day next year.

docs.title: 2.14 If you are reading this for a parent
docs.text:
How to say it out loud. Don't say "you have osteoporosis, your muscles are wasting away" — that's a verdict, and he'll go straight on the defensive. Say something specific that he can't argue with: "Mum, I measured it — you're a bit shorter than the year before last, and you walk more slowly than before. That's what worries me. I want to go with you for a bone-density scan, and a blood draw while we're there. We'll be back the same day." Put "I" into it and leave the judgment to him.

When he disagrees, what else you can do. Three things, none of which need his nod. First, change the table first: keep milk, eggs, and tofu in the house, a glass of milk and an egg a meal — don't say "calcium", just say "I feel like eating lighter lately". Second, measure without saying anything: while he stands up and walks, count in your head — can he get out of the chair, does he have time to cross the road — note it in your head, don't pass judgment to his face. Third, when you go with him to the clinic, ask the doctor three things on his behalf: whether he needs a bone-density scan, whether he needs a vitamin D and kidney-function test, and whether he can still jump and run. He may not admit it out loud, but his body gives an answer every day.

docs.title: 2.15 What I am not sure about in this chapter
docs.text:
• The specific effect of jumping and impact-type movement on bone density in middle-aged and older adults — I couldn't verify a quantified study in a Chinese population. The direction exists (weight-bearing and impact can stimulate bone), but there's no dose data for a Chinese population on "how much to jump, how long, to make bone harder", so this chapter treats it as "direction established, dose unknown". Next step: check the Expert Consensus on Nutritional and Exercise Management of Primary Osteoporosis and Sarcopenia (2025) (《原发性骨质疏松症与肌少症的营养和运动管理专家共识（2025年）》) and subsequent exercise-intervention studies in Chinese populations.
  • Whether a community can do a bone-density screen, whether it can refer for DXA, and whether the free check-up includes bone density all vary by place. Bone density is not among the standard check-up items of the national basic public health service "older-adult health management"; whether a community can add an ultrasound, forearm DXA, or quantitative CT screen, and whether it can refer for DXA, is up to local arrangements (the Chronic Disease Center of the Chinese CDC, 2025, notes that communities can do ultrasound screening first). Next step: check the free check-up items and referral paths of each province's health commission, province by province.

docs.title: 2.16 Sources for this chapter
docs.text:
• official wording Osteoporosis and Bone Mineral Disease Branch of the Chinese Medical Association, Clinical Diagnosis and Treatment Guidelines for Primary Osteoporosis (2022) (原发性骨质疏松症诊疗指南（2022）), Chinese General Practice (中国全科医学), 2023, Vol. 26, No. 14, pp. 1671-1691: peak bone mass, pathogenesis, controllable risk factors, T-score diagnostic cut-offs, calcium and vitamin D recommendations. https://www.chinagp.net/CN/rich_html/10.12114/j.issn.1007-9572.2023.0121 checked 2026-10-10
  • official wording Beijing Municipal Health Commission, "Strengthen Your Bones, Refuse 'Osteoporosis'" (强健骨骼，拒绝"疏松") (contributed by Beijing Chuiyangliu Hospital, 2023-10-20): peak bone mass age, osteoporosis prevalence over age 50 and over age 65 (by sex), calcium and protein recommendations. https://wjw.beijing.gov.cn/bmfw_20143/jkzs/jksh/202310/t20231020_3283828.html checked 2026-10-10
  • official wording Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention, "World Osteoporosis Day | Hold a Healthy Weight, Hold On to the Bone You're Losing" (世界骨质疏松日丨稳住健康体重，守住流失的骨量) (Chronic Disease Center, 2025-10-29): prevalence of low bone mass over age 40 and over age 60, community management of low bone mass, calcium and protein food lists, 150 minutes of activity a week, community ultrasound bone-density screening. https://www.chinacdc.cn/jkkp/mxfcrb/lnjk/202510/t20251029_313157.html checked 2026-10-10
  • official wording Shenyang Municipal Health Commission, "Does Your Vitamin D Level Need Routine Testing?" (维生素D水平需要日常检测吗？) (Shenyang Municipal Health Service Centre, 2026-08-31): time of day, duration, and body parts for sun exposure; the vitamin D recommendation for people over 65; the target serum 25(OH)D value; and the warning in the Expert Consensus on Nutritional and Exercise Management of Primary Osteoporosis and Sarcopenia (2025) (原发性骨质疏松症与肌少症的营养和运动管理专家共识（2025年）) to "avoid explosive force and high impact". https://wjw.shenyang.gov.cn/ztzl/xsxxjkdjt/202608/t20260831_5080580.html checked 2026-10-10
  • official wording Healthy China, "Four Groups Advised to Have a Bone-Density Test" (四类人建议做骨密度检查) (reprinted by Fujian Provincial Health Commission, 2025-10-22): who should be tested for bone density, DXA as the gold standard, the need to scan the lumbar spine and the hip, and why body-fat scales and ultrasound can't diagnose. https://wjw.fujian.gov.cn/ztzl/jkjy/jksh/202510/t20251023_7024376.htm checked 2026-10-10
  • third-party research Xinhua Net, "Bone-Density Testing: Two Groups Who Can Skip It" (骨密度检查，两类人群可以不做) (Popular Health magazine (大众健康), written by Wang Qin and reviewed by Ran Xingwu, West China Hospital of Sichuan University, 2025-11-16): 2 to 3 percent bone loss a year after menopause, rising risk in men after 70, and re-test intervals for glucocorticoid users. http://www.news.cn/20251116/24d1594293024875acb8783eecd9d75e/c.html checked 2026-10-10
  • third-party research Xinhua Net, "Past This Age, Muscle Wastes Away Fast..." (过了这个年纪，肌肉会快速流失……) (reviewed by experts of the Chinese Medical Association, 2024-11-05): the rate of muscle and muscle-strength loss after age 50, community sarcopenia prevalence, SARC-F, grip-strength and walking-speed screening, and protein recommendations. http://www.news.cn/science/20241105/88d6e3b8baa045bc93e3dde19a5a43d0/c.html checked 2026-10-10
  • third-party research Xinhua Net, "Double Ninth Festival | Fighting Frailty and Preventing Disability: Helping Older People Live Healthily, Starting with Exercise" (重阳节丨对抗衰弱、预防失能，助力老年人健康生活从锻炼开始) (jointly by the Science Popularisation Department of the China Association for Science and Technology and Xinhua Net, reviewed by Beijing Puren Hospital, 2023-10-23): sets, reps, and frequency of resistance training, balance exercise, aerobic volume, and what to watch for in heart rate and breathing during exercise. http://www.news.cn/science/20231023/e639a70cea4d4df0b78ea060ec5cd682/c.html checked 2026-10-10
  • third-party research China Food and Drug Network, "Don't Lose the 'Muscle', Once Lost It Won't Come Back" ("肌"不可失，失不再来) (2022-10-13): muscle mass peaks at about age 30, then falls 1%—2% a year, accelerating after 60; the article attributes community sarcopenia prevalence of 8.9%—38.8% and 67.1% over age 80 to the Chinese Expert Consensus on Diagnosis and Treatment of Sarcopenia in Older Adults (2021) (中国老年人肌少症诊疗专家共识（2021）), but "peaks at 30, 1%—2% a year" is that article's own wording and doesn't appear in the consensus text, so this chapter treats it as "the two sources disagree, give a range". https://www.cnpharm.com/c/2022-10-13/1001658.shtml checked 2026-10-10
  • third-party research West China Hospital of Sichuan University reprint of the Chinese Expert Consensus on Prevention and Intervention of Physical Function Impairment in Older Adults (2022) (老年人躯体功能受损防控干预中国专家共识（2022）) (Chinese Journal of Geriatrics (中华老年医学杂志), 2022, Vol. 41, No. 10): resistance training is the most direct category for improving muscle mass and strength, two to three times a week, 8 to 12 reps per set. https://www.wchscu.cn/public/department/nephrology/dynamics/70089.html checked 2026-10-10
  • third-party research Chen LK, et al. Asian Working Group for Sarcopenia: 2019 Consensus Update on Sarcopenia Diagnosis and Treatment. J Am Med Dir Assoc, 2020: grip strength, walking speed, 5-time chair stand, muscle-mass thresholds for DXA and BIA, calf circumference, SARC-F. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32033882/ checked 2026-10-10
  • official wording National Basic Public Health Service Standards (3rd edition) (国家基本公共卫生服务规范（第三版）), "Older-adult health management": a free health-management check once a year for people over 65, including a physical examination and a health-status assessment (the standard check-up items don't include bone density). https://www.nhc.gov.cn/ewebeditor/uploadfile/2017/04/20170417104506514.pdf checked 2026-10-10
  • official wording State Council Medical Reform Office et al., Guiding Opinions on Advancing Contracted Family Doctor Services (关于推进家庭医生签约服务的指导意见) (Guoyigai Banfa [2016] No. 1, 2016-06-06): implement contracted family doctor services, covering older people and other groups first. https://www.nhc.gov.cn/tigs/c100053/201606/a2f65c166d5b438f8abb684d3a8c13d0.shtml checked 2026-10-10
  • official wording Chinese Nutrition Society, Dietary Reference Intakes for Chinese Residents (2023 edition) (中国居民膳食营养素参考摄入量（2023版）): a daily vitamin D recommendation of 15 micrograms (600 IU) for people over 65. Quoted from the Shenyang Municipal Health Commission article of 2026-08-31 second-hand.
  • Note: all citations in this chapter are paraphrase and figures, not full translations of the originals; the grade is marked where a number first appears.

docs.title: Chapter 3 · Brain and Senses Capital
docs.text:
The TV volume goes up a notch every year. The family says it's too loud; to you it sounds just right. At the market the vendor has to say it twice before you catch it, and you wave your hand and say, "that's just what getting old is like."

This chapter covers five things: brain, ears, eyes, teeth, feet. They're like five switches in a row on the wall — when one comes loose, it's never only that one circuit that goes bad. If your ears can't hear clearly, you pull back from the dinner table, the card game, the people around you. If your teeth can't bite, you eat less meat and vegetables. If your feet hurt, you can't be bothered to go out the door.

docs.title: 3.1 What this chapter is for
docs.text:
As you age, the first thing to come loose is often not your legs — it's these five. They look as if each runs its own business, but in fact one leads into the next.

Being hard of hearing, blurry eyes, bad teeth, foot trouble — you tend to write these off as "normal for old age." Some of them can be stopped early; and some changes are your body telling you to go to the hospital that very day, not to wait until next month.

This chapter looks at three things: what can be fixed ahead of time, whether fixing it is worth it, and which kind of change cannot wait.

docs.title: 3.2 Hearing loss and dementia share a hard link
docs.text:
Research shows the link between hearing decline and dementia is solid; but how far hearing loss itself causes dementia is not fully settled.

The Lancet Commission on dementia prevention's 2024 report lists 14 modifiable risk factors for dementia, and hearing loss is one of them. The report models this with population-attributable fractions: push all these factors down, and in theory you could delay or stop nearly half of dementia — that's a modelled expectation, not an observed drop in incidence (third-party research Lancet Commission on dementia prevention, 2024 report). The World Health Organization also states that untreated hearing loss raises the risk of dementia and speeds cognitive decline (official wording WHO Deafness and hearing loss fact sheet). The number-one cause of hearing disability in China is age-related hearing loss, at 51.61% (third-party research China Hearing Health Report (2021) blue book, using data from the second national sampling survey of disabled persons in 2006).

One distinction to keep clear: correlation is not causation. People with poor hearing have more dementia — that is observed over and over; but the report itself writes that some of these associations "may only be partly causal."

So does managing it early lower the risk? The hardest evidence is the ACHIEVE trial (2023, The Lancet): 977 people aged 70 to 84 with untreated hearing loss, split into a group given hearing aids plus hearing rehabilitation and a group given only health education, followed for 3 years (third-party research Lin FR et al., Lancet 2023). Taken together, hearing aids did not clearly slow cognitive decline; among the subset at higher cognitive risk, decline was 48% slower.

One more point to flag: a few years ago an observational study said "hearing aids can lower dementia risk" and it was passed around everywhere; the paper was later retracted by The Lancet Public Health (third-party research retraction notice, 2023-12). Don't treat "hearing aids prevent dementia" as settled.

Are hearing aids worth it? The first thing they buy back is "being able to hear, to chat, not to be walled off from the sound of people talking" — that alone is worth it; and the dementia benefit, if any, most likely lands on people who already carry other risk factors (the group in ACHIEVE).

docs.title: 3.3 Get your hearing tested once first, and get hearing aids if you need them
docs.text:
• What it costs: a pure-tone audiometry test runs a few dozen to one or two hundred yuan (varies by place); a hearing aid runs several hundred to several thousand or over ten thousand yuan a pair (money: not cheap | effort: half a day for the test, fitting takes several trips | strength: not tiring | do you have to speak up?: the hardest step — this is where many people get stuck)
  • In short: hearing mostly declines slowly, hard to notice yourself, but the family notices first. Get tested once, get a chart, and then you have something to go on.
  • What you can do: ① register with otolaryngology (ENT) and say you "want to check your hearing," and get pure-tone audiometry; ② have the doctor sort out which type it is — some cases are not aging but middle-ear infection, earwax blockage, or sudden deafness, and need handling separately; ③ when it really reaches the point where you need one, get fitted at a proper hospital hearing centre or a fitting facility with the right qualifications — don't just buy one online; ④ after fitting you need to go back for adjustment and practise using it — discomfort in the first month is common.
  • Where this comes from: B | pure-tone audiometry with proper fitting is standard practice; but the evidence for "hearing aids prevent dementia" only goes as far as "people at higher risk may benefit" — don't treat it as insurance.
  • Who this is for: who it applies to: people who can hear but can't make out speech, and whose family keep saying you're hard of hearing. If your ear canal is draining pus, you have ear pain, or one side suddenly goes deaf, see 3.8 and go to hospital the same day.
  • What you get back: relationships + self-care — no more fearing "being walled off from the sound of people talking, until eventually nobody talks to me"
  • How this works in China: the free annual health management for people aged 65 and over includes a rough hearing check (official wording National Basic Public Health Service Standard, 3rd edition); for precise hearing testing and hearing-aid fitting, go to the ENT department of a tier-2 or higher hospital. Hearing aids mostly go through the Disabled Persons' Federation's assistive-device fitting subsidy — see 3.9.

docs.title: 3.4 Once cataract affects your daily life, stop putting it off
docs.text:
• What it costs: one outpatient visit plus one operation; the surgical fee is reimbursed against the local medical-insurance catalogue, and the out-of-pocket share varies by place (effort: mostly day surgery or outpatient surgery | strength: not tiring | do you have to speak up?: easy to ask)
  • In short: cataract is the world's number-one cause of blindness, and the most common cause of vision loss in older people. It can't be treated with pills or eye drops — the clouded lens has to be removed and replaced with an artificial lens.
  • When to do it: not when it "ripens." The National Health Commission's 2026 operational standard says: when the visual function lost to the lens no longer meets the needs of daily life and work, and surgery offers a chance of improvement, it can be done (official wording NHC Operational Standard for Adult Cataract Surgery (2026 edition)). Not being able to see the road and being afraid to step down a stair — you've reached that point.
  • What you can do: ① register with ophthalmology; check visual acuity, slit lamp and eye pressure, and check the fundus if needed; ② ask the doctor three questions: is it appropriate to do it now, which eye, and whether blood pressure and blood sugar need controlling first; ③ if you have high blood pressure or diabetes, get blood pressure and blood sugar steady before surgery, as the doctor says; ④ go back for follow-up after surgery as instructed.
  • Where this comes from: A | surgery is the only treatment for cataract; whether you've reached the point for it and how to do it are decided by the ophthalmologist together with your general condition.
  • Who this is for: who it applies to: people diagnosed with cataract whose vision is declining. A sudden change in vision, or severe eye pain with redness, may be a different emergency — see 3.8 first.
  • What you get back: self-care + dignity — no more fearing "not seeing the road clearly, afraid to go out, afraid of falling"
  • How this works in China: cataract surgery is a diagnosis-and-treatment item covered by medical insurance; how much is reimbursed, whether it can be done as an outpatient, and whether the artificial lens is chosen from inside or outside the catalogue all vary by place — go by the local medical-insurance scheme's latest wording. Where to ask: the hospital's medical-insurance office, or the local medical-insurance administration.

docs.title: 3.5 When your teeth can't bite, it runs all the way to nutrition and the dinner table
docs.text:
• What it costs: one dental check-up; fillings, dentures and implants differ widely in price, from a few hundred to over ten thousand (money: not cheap | effort: several trips | strength: not tiring | do you have to speak up?: easy to ask)
  • In short: once teeth are missing, you can't chew meat, vegetables or nuts, so you pick only soft things to eat, until your diet grows narrower and narrower. Worse, you start hiding from people when you smile and talk.
  • The current numbers: in the Fourth National Oral Health Epidemiological Survey, people aged 65 to 74 had on average only 22.5 teeth left, and 36.8% of those missing teeth had not been restored ([official wording: Fourth National Oral Health Epidemiological Survey, released by the National Health and Family Planning Commission on 2017-09-20; the figure of 22.5 retained teeth is on the release page, while the 36.8% missing-teeth-not-restored figure is survey detail, second-hand from China Population News, 2024-10-24 — see 3.13]).
  • What you can do: ① see a dentist every six months to a year, don't wait for pain; ② if you have calculus or bleeding gums, get periodontal treatment first, to save the teeth you still have; ③ restore missing teeth promptly: fix them in place if you can; if many are missing and your health is average, a removable denture is also a proper option, and a full denture needs time to adapt and several adjustments (official wording Chinese Stomatological Association, Guidelines for Oral Restoration in Elderly Patients T/CHSA 001-2021); ④ brush twice a day and use floss; take dentures out daily to clean them, and don't sleep with them in.
  • Where this comes from: B | timely restoration, periodontal maintenance and regular denture review are standard in oral-health guidelines; which type of restoration to choose is decided by the dentist together with your general condition and your wishes.
  • Who this is for: who it applies to: people starting to lose teeth, who can't chew, whose dentures are loose. If you've had a cardiac stent, take anticoagulants, have used bisphosphonate drugs, or have poorly controlled blood sugar, you must tell the dentist before extraction or an implant.
  • What you get back: self-care + relationships + dignity — no more fearing "not being able to eat, eating badly, and not daring to open my mouth to smile"
  • How this works in China: the medical-insurance rules for dentistry vary by place; generally extractions, fillings and periodontal treatment are partly reimbursed, while dentures and implants are mostly out-of-pocket — go by the local medical-insurance catalogue and the hospital you attend. Whom to see: the dental department of a general hospital, a dental hospital, or a prosthodontics department; if your community health centre has a dental department, ask there first. Where to ask about reimbursement: the hospital's medical-insurance office, or the local medical-insurance administration.

docs.title: 3.6 Not being able to cut your toenails is a different matter from diabetic foot
docs.text:
• What it costs: a suitable pair of nail clippers; or one foot-care session, a few dozen yuan (money: costs almost nothing | effort: low | strength: not tiring | do you have to speak up?: easy to ask)
  • In short: as you age, your eyes blur, your back can't bend, your hands can't reach your feet, and cutting your toenails gets hard. Cut into the flesh and it gets infected and fills with pus. If you have diabetes, that one cut can turn into big trouble.
  • If you cut them yourself: ① use large nail clippers with a straight blade; ② cut straight across, leave a little white edge, don't dig the corners in at the sides; ③ soak them soft first, use good light, sit steady, don't perch on one foot; ④ if you can't reach or your hands shake, switch to long-handled tools or have a family member cut them, and if it really comes to it, go to a foot-care clinic at a community or hospital service.
  • If you have diabetes, remember one more thing: your feet are not the same as other people's feet. The Chinese Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Diabetic Foot (2019 edition) state it clearly: diabetic foot is destruction of the skin and deep tissue below the ankle, often with infection and vascular disease; ingrown nails, blisters, bleeding and fungal infections are all its precursor lesions; trimming toenails, nail avulsion and ingrown-nail removal must all be done by trained medical staff, not at a bathhouse or a nail salon (official wording Chinese Diabetes Society, Chinese Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Diabetic Foot (2019 edition)). The same task that's a minor nuisance for an ordinary person can, for you, run all the way to ulceration and gangrene.
  • Shoes and socks: shoes should fit, support the foot and not squeeze at the front; don't go out in open-toed slippers; choose light-coloured cotton socks so a break shows up; check your feet once a day, including the soles and between the toes.
  • Where this comes from: A | the diabetic-foot guideline makes "check your feet daily" and "toenails and calluses handled by professionals" explicit recommendations; for ordinary people, cutting as above carries little risk, but there is no randomised trial specifically on "how to cut your toenails."
  • Who this is for: who it applies to: people who can't reach or cut them well; people with diabetes, lower-limb vascular problems, deformed feet or numb feet should not do it themselves — go to endocrinology or a foot clinic. If there's a break in the foot, blackening, redness, swelling, heat, pain, or fever, go to hospital the same day.
  • What you get back: self-care — no more fearing "a small wound on the foot that ends up costing me the leg"
  • How this works in China: high-risk diabetic feet need regular foot checks per the guideline, more often the more severe. Where to ask: a community health centre or a hospital endocrinology department.

docs.title: 3.7 Brain capital is saved day by day: move your body, use your mind, control blood pressure and blood sugar, sleep well, have people to talk to
docs.text:
• What it costs: ten-plus minutes of movement a day; the rest are mostly habits that cost nothing (money: costs almost nothing | effort: daily | strength: not too tiring | do you have to speak up?: no need to speak up)
  • In short: there's no drug that lets you deposit into this "brain capital" all at once — it comes from a string of ordinary things: move your body, use your mind, keep blood pressure and blood sugar under control, sleep well, have people to talk to, and don't leave your hearing and eyesight unattended.
  • How to do it (pick one you can start today):
  • Move your body: brisk walking, cycling, dancing, tai chi all work — accumulate enough each week, don't sit all day (see Chapter 13).
  • Use your mind: read books and papers, play chess, learn something new — this works better than repeating things you already know.
  • Control blood pressure, blood sugar and blood lipids: take your medicine and check your blood pressure as the doctor says, don't stop on your own. This is the most solid evidence, and high blood pressure is among those 14 factors.
  • Sleep well: keep a fixed wake-up time; if you snore loudly, feel sleepy all day, or wake up choking at night, get checked once for sleep apnoea. (Sleep is not among those 14 factors; the evidence is weaker.)
  • Have people to talk to: eat, chat and do things together with people often. Being all alone is also among those 14 factors.
  • Where this comes from: B | that managing several factors together can lower dementia risk is the core conclusion of this report; but which one helps you most, and by how much, can't be guaranteed.
  • Who this is for: who it applies to: people not yet diagnosed with dementia who want to push it off. If you're already clearly forgetting things, or suspect a brain problem, see a doctor first (Chapter 9).
  • What you get back: self-care + relationships — no more fearing "my mind running shorter every day, and in the end not knowing anyone"
  • How this works in China: communities, universities of the third age and senior activity centres often have ready-made classes and teams (tai chi, choir, walking groups). Where to ask: a community health centre, or a university of the third age.

docs.title: 3.8 These changes are signals to go to hospital the same day
docs.text:
• What it costs: one trip out, possibly to the emergency department (money: the cost of one registration | effort: same day | strength: not tiring | do you have to speak up?: easy to ask)
  • In short: some changes in hearing and eyesight are not "slow aging" but emergencies: sudden, one-sided, or with dizziness and unsteadiness. Wait a night, and you may lose something that could have been saved.
  • Go the same day:
  • One ear suddenly can't hear clearly, or suddenly goes deaf. This may be sudden deafness — sensorineural hearing loss coming on suddenly within 72 hours, an ENT emergency where the earlier the treatment the better (official wording Chinese Medical Association, Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Sudden Deafness (2015)).
  • One eye suddenly goes blind, or a black cloth seems to block your vision, or there's a sudden burst of flashes and a marked increase in floaters.
  • An eye suddenly becomes severely painful and red, with vision declining at the same time.
  • A change in hearing or vision together with dizziness, unsteady walking, slurred speech or weakness on one side of the body — treat it as a stroke and call 120 immediately (see Chapter 8 and Appendix D).
  • Where this comes from: A | the treatment window for sudden deafness and the emergency nature of sudden blindness in one eye are both written in the guidelines; remember "sudden, one-sided, with dizziness."
  • Who this is for: who it applies to: everyone. Don't put in a couple of eye drops or dig at your ear yourself and wait for tomorrow. Changes that come on slowly, over months — handle them per the sections above; the moment the word "sudden" appears, treat it as an emergency.
  • What you get back: self-care — no more fearing "something that could have been saved, and I dragged past it"
  • How this works in China: for sudden deafness, register with ENT — some hospitals can add you the same day; for eye emergencies, register with the ophthalmology emergency service; for slurred speech or weakness on one side, call 120. If you're not sure, go to the hospital's emergency-department triage first.

docs.title: 3.9 Where to get these things done in China
docs.text:
• Rough hearing and vision checks in the free health check-up: people aged 65 and over who have lived in the community for at least half a year get one check a year, done at a community health centre, a township health centre or a village clinic; the physical examination includes rough checks of mouth, vision and hearing (official wording National Basic Public Health Service Standard, 3rd edition, "Elderly Health Management"). This is a rough check, not a diagnosis; if problems are found, you're referred to a higher-level hospital to investigate.
  • Rehabilitation assistive-device fitting: basic assistive devices such as hearing aids and walking aids go through the Disabled Persons' Federation's "assistive-device fitting subsidy." All 31 provinces (autonomous regions and municipalities) and the Xinjiang Production and Construction Corps have issued policies (official wording China Disabled Persons' Federation / Xinhua News Agency, 2024-02). In most provinces the target group is local certificate-holding disabled persons and eligible disabled children. How much is subsidised, whether you need a disability certificate first, and where to apply all vary by place — go by the local latest wording. Where to ask: the Disabled Persons' Federation at the community (village) or township (sub-district) level, or the county (district) Disabled Persons' Federation.
  • Medical-insurance reimbursement: whether cataract surgery, dental treatment and diabetic-foot treatment are reimbursed, and how much, depends on the local catalogue and the hospital's tier. Where to ask: the hospital's medical-insurance office, or the local medical-insurance administration.

One honest word: of these five, some will keep getting worse all the way. Ears can be partly made up for with hearing aids, teeth can be partly made up for with restoration, and the brain and blood vessels can only be managed bit by bit, day by day. What this chapter can do is stop what can be stopped early, and get the same-day things done the same day.

docs.title: 3.10 The one thing you can do today
docs.text:
Remember roughly what notch the TV volume is on at home now, and look again next month. The volume creeping up one notch at a time is one of the easiest signals to miss after midlife.

Then, go for a pure-tone audiometry test.

docs.title: 3.11 If you are reading this for a parent
docs.text:
How to say it out loud: don't say "you should get a hearing aid" at the moment when he can't hear you and you've repeated the same sentence a third time — that's pointing it out to his face. Try another way, putting yourself into it: "My hearing's been off lately too — I'm going to get it checked, come with me?" After the test, mention his situation to the doctor in passing. Or leave the hearing aid alone for now and just say "the TV's too loud, the neighbours will complain soon" — giving him a way to save face about turning it down.

What you can still do when he disagrees: what usually trips older people up is "face" and "what's the use." There are three things you can do without his agreement. First, book the appointment and fix the time for him, turning "whether to go" into "which day to go." Second, help him find out how the local Disabled Persons' Federation's assistive-device subsidy works (see 3.9) — lower that money hurdle and the resistance drops too. Third, whether he's willing to wear it or not, start with the "being able to hear" situations: set him up with wireless headphones for the TV, put phone calls on speaker, seat him with his back to the wall at the dinner table and face him when you talk. Once he hears a little better, he'll know for himself that the thing is useful.

docs.title: 3.12 What I am not sure about in this chapter
docs.text:
The items in this chapter that were marked for verification have all been traced back to source where possible: the two oral-health figures go back to the survey release page and China Population News; the Lancet and hearing-aid passage goes back to the full report and the ACHIEVE paper; the Disabled Persons' Federation assistive-device subsidy goes back to the Xinhua piece on the Chinese government website. The remaining two are limits of the data itself, not things I failed to find, and I leave them as they are:

  • The randomised evidence on hearing aids and dementia is currently mainly just one trial, ACHIEVE, with 3-year follow-up; whether they can really delay dementia over the long term is still unanswered. The observational study a few years ago that said "hearing aids lower dementia risk" has been retracted by The Lancet Public Health and can no longer be used as a basis.
  • Among the causes of hearing disability in China, age-related deafness accounts for 51.61%, from the second national sampling survey of disabled persons in 2006; China Hearing Health Report (2021) was still using this older data when it was published in 2021, and there has been no new round of national sampling since, so this proportion is on the old side.

docs.text:

  • World Health Organization, Deafness and hearing loss fact sheet (over 25% of people aged over 60 have disabling hearing loss; untreated hearing loss raises dementia risk and speeds cognitive decline). https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/deafness-and-hearing-loss

  • National Basic Public Health Service Standard (3rd edition), "Elderly Health Management Service Standard" (国家基本公共卫生服务规范（第三版）"老年人健康管理服务规范"): once a year for people aged 65 and over; the physical examination includes rough checks of mouth, vision and hearing. https://www.jiangan.gov.cn/jaxxw/zfxxgk/fdzdgk/shgysy_41394/shjzhshfl/shfl/202011/P020201106429362006578.pdf
