docs.title: Chapter 7 · Warning Three: Can't Eat, Can't Swallow, Choking
docs.text: On the eating line there are three red lights. The first two come on slowly: can't eat, edging down over months; can't swallow, one meal choking worse than the last. The third is the fastest — that one minute of choking decides life or death.

docs.title: 7.1 What this chapter is for
docs.text:
Three things, with different time scales and different people to see.

  • Choking: a few minutes of first aid. It needs hands. You should know it now.
  • Can't swallow: a problem of swallowing function. Change how eating is done; see a rehabilitation department or a swallowing specialist.
  • Can't eat: a problem of appetite and nutrition. Find the cause (teeth, mood, chronic disease, medicines); see a nutrition clinic.

The three also join into one line: can't eat and can't swallow push a person toward malnutrition and muscle loss. That line closes in 7.5 and 7.6.

docs.title: 7.2 The minute of choking: first, look at whether he can still cough
docs.text: The only thing in this whole chapter that you should know "right now."

docs.title: Choking: first tell the two kinds apart
docs.text:
• What it costs: Nothing. The Red Cross public first-aid training is free.
  • In short: An airway block comes in two kinds. If he can still cough, still make a sound, the airway is not fully blocked — the most effective "tool" is his own cough. Don't slap him, don't thrust on him; the moment you act you may push the thing deeper.
  • What you can do:
  • Ask: "Are you choking?" If he can speak and cough strongly, stand beside him and watch, and encourage him to cough hard.
  • Can't speak, can't cough, can't breathe, both hands to the throat (the choking sign), face turning blue or purple — this is when you act.
  • Adults (over 1 year old): 5 back blows + 5 abdominal thrusts, alternating, until the object comes out or he becomes unresponsive. Stand behind him, slightly to one side, have him lean his upper body forward, and strike 5 times with the heel of your hand between the shoulder blades; if it doesn't come out, wrap both arms around his waist, make a fist with one hand above the navel and below the lower end of the sternum, cover it with the other hand, and thrust quickly inward and upward 5 times.
  • Once he loses consciousness, stop the thrusts, lay him flat, call 120, and start CPR.
  • Where this comes from: A | official wording: the first-aid guidelines updated in 2025 by the American Heart Association and the International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation set "back blows first, then abdominal thrusts" as the fixed sequence for those over 1 year old; Red Cross training in China has always taught it this way.
  • Who this is for: most adults of normal weight. Pregnant, or anyone you can't reach around the waist: switch to chest thrusts. Infants under 1 year: no abdominal thrusts; use "5 back blows + 5 chest compressions." Already unconscious: go straight to CPR. Don't fish for an object you can't see with your fingers — you'll only push it deeper.
  • What you get back: independence + relationships — no longer afraid of "watching him choke and not knowing what to do."
  • How this works in China: see 7.9.

docs.title: If you live alone, learn to save yourself first
docs.text:
• What it costs: A few minutes, learned once (money: nothing | effort: none | do you have to speak up: no)
  • What you can do: ① Make a fist yourself, thumb side against the spot above the navel, cover it with the other hand, and thrust quickly upward and inward; ② or press your upper belly against the back of a chair, the edge of a table, or a railing, and bend over, pushing inward and upward again and again; ③ at the same time, make a loud noise and call out.
  • Where this comes from: A | official wording: authoritative first-aid guidelines include self-rescue methods.
  • Who this is for: especially people who live alone and eat alone during the day. If family lives with him, the point is to teach the previous section to them.

docs.title: 7.3 Choking on water is not a small thing
One cough is aspiration; "no reaction" after the cough is worse
docs.text:
• What it costs: What it costs is effort: watching, recording, and maybe one extra clinic visit.
  • In short: Aspiration is food, water, saliva, or even stomach contents going into the windpipe. Overt aspiration you can hear: violent coughing, face turning purple, a wet voice after eating. Silent aspiration you cannot hear: something went into the windpipe, but his cough reflex is weak, so it can't come out and there's no commotion either. Quiet aspiration more easily drags on into pneumonia.
  • What you can do: Treat the following as "aspiration signals"; when one appears, pay attention: coughing or choking while eating or drinking; a "wet" or gurgling voice after eating; a feeling that "something is stuck in the throat"; unexplained low fever, duller spirits, slower reactions, smaller portions; repeated lung infections.
  • Where this comes from: A | third-party research: Beijing Tsinghua Changgung Hospital explains "silent aspiration" very clearly and cites a large Chinese study — from 2011 to 2017, in-hospital aspiration pneumonia was about 9.4 cases per 100,000 person-years.
  • Who this is for: advanced age; after stroke or traumatic brain injury; dementia; Parkinson's; COPD; after radiotherapy for head and neck tumours; and people taking sedatives or antipsychotics. China's Guidelines for the Rehabilitation Management of Dysphagia (2023 edition) note that about 42% of people have dysphagia in the acute phase of stroke, reaching 80% with brainstem lesions.

docs.title: A cup of warm water is enough to self-check
docs.text:
• What it costs: One cup of warm water, a few minutes (money: nothing)
  • In short: The most common bedside screen is the water-swallowing test (Kubota): drink about 30 millilitres of warm water and see whether it can be finished in one gulp within 5 seconds and whether he chokes. There is also a questionnaire, EAT-10. Doctors at Peking Union Medical College Hospital use the two together: a total score above 3 suggests possible dysphagia; above 4, see a specialist.
  • Where this comes from: B | third-party research: both tools are common in clinical use, but some doctors warn that the water-swallowing test may "underestimate" abnormality — testing fine at home does not mean there is no silent aspiration.
  • Who this is for: people who are awake and alert and can cooperate with drinking. If he already clearly chokes when swallowing, don't keep testing — go and see someone.

docs.title: "Repeated pneumonia" and "choking while eating" should be looked at together
docs.text:
• In short: If someone in the family has "pneumonia" several times within a year, each time after eating, don't just put it down to a "poor constitution." Dysphagia is the most common risk factor for aspiration pneumonia. A clinical report from the First Affiliated Hospital of Guangzhou Medical University notes that aspiration pneumonia makes up about 71% of community-acquired pneumonia in the elderly.
  • Where this comes from: B | second-hand: "about 71% of community-acquired pneumonia in the elderly" comes from Expert Recommendations on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Adult Aspiration Pneumonia (2022), cited by the clinical report from the First Affiliated Hospital of Guangzhou Medical University; the same recommendations also state that aspiration pneumonia is only about 5%–15% of all community-acquired pneumonia — the two figures differ by population. The direction "repeated pneumonia calls for a swallowing check" holds up.
  • Who this is for: older people with repeated lung infections.

docs.title: 7.4 The older people get, the less they want meat — it's not being fussy
docs.text:
It's several things stacked together.

  • What it costs: Nothing. Understand first, then talk about change.
  • In short:
  • Taste and smell fade: smelling and tasting get dull, with salt the least felt. The dish "has no taste" because he genuinely can't taste it.
  • Filling up fast: the stomach empties more slowly, so a little makes him feel full. A young person who gets hungry can make it up; an older person often can't.
  • Teeth: missing teeth, ill-fitting dentures — if he can't chew meat he simply stops touching it, and meat is the most direct source of protein.
  • Mood: older people eat more when they have someone to eat with; bereavement, loneliness, and no heart for cooking all pull the amount down.
  • Illness and medicine: depression, dementia; many chronic diseases and drugs suppress appetite.
  • Where this comes from: B | third-party research: each one has mechanistic studies ("anorexia of aging" already has reviews), but how much each weighs varies from person to person.
  • Who this is for: starting from "recently eating noticeably less," it holds for most families. If the amount drops suddenly over a short time and weight loss comes with it, it is more likely an illness — see a doctor first.
  • One admission: the food is all laid out and he hasn't said he won't eat — it's just that bite by bite he gets slower and slower.

docs.title: 7.5 Malnutrition and muscle loss twist into a circle of their own
docs.text:
• What it costs: Nothing (first, understand this circle)
  • In short: A circle that speeds itself up — eating too little, not enough protein → muscle drops (sarcopenia), less strength → moves less, wants to eat even less → immunity and cough strength also drop, more prone to infection and hospitalisation → hospital and infection push appetite down again, back to step one. It is slow, but it keeps turning.
  • Where this comes from: A | third-party research, figures checkable: muscle drops about 8% per decade from the thirties and forties, faster from 65 to 80; losing 5% to 10% of body weight in half a year is a main signal of malnutrition (official wording, NHS UK); a multicentre survey at Peking Union Medical College Hospital found the prevalence of sarcopenia in those over 80 is about 42% (third-party research, cited from Guidelines for Medical Nutrition Therapy for Elderly Patients in China (2026 edition)).
  • Who this is for: changes in weight and food intake hold for yourself and for your parents. Action: weigh him, write it down, look at the trend.
  • One admission: once the circle is turning, shouting "eat more" alone won't turn it back.
  • Breaking the circle: change eating and moving together. For eating see 7.6; for moving see Chapter 5.
  • What you get back: independence — no longer afraid that "once he gets thin he'll never get fat again."

docs.title: 7.6 When he can't swallow, how to change the three meals a day
docs.text: The principle in one sentence: change the food, change the posture, change the speed, and then learn the "see a specialist" signals by heart.

docs.title: Change the food: soft, slippery, not crumbly; not too thin, not too sticky
docs.text:
• In short: Food that swallows well has even density, doesn't fall apart, moves easily in the mouth, and doesn't stick to the mucosa. The opposite is what chokes most easily: thin liquids (plain water, clear soup), sticky things (rice cake, peanut butter), granular things (dry rice grains, nut fragments), dry and crumbly things (crackers, steamed cake), and things with bones or spines.
  • What you can do: ① Make dishes into purées, steamed egg custard, thick soups, jelly-like — easier to swallow than clear soup; ② water that is too thin will choke him — thicken it with a thickener to "like thin porridge" or "like pudding"; pharmacies and online stores sell it; ③ don't drink through a straw — it sends water too fast and is more dangerous; ④ when drinking from a cup, leave at least half a cup in it; with too little water he has to tilt his head back, and tilting back chokes most easily; ⑤ internationally there is a common graded framework (IDDSI), with drinks and foods graded in eight levels from 0 to 7. Just remember the direction: the thicker the liquid the safer; the softer the solid the safer.
  • Where this comes from: B | third-party research: texture modification and thickening are common practice (the popular-science pieces from Peking Union and the Affiliated Hospital of Jiangsu University, and the dysphagia diet consensus, all say so); which level fits him best needs a professional assessment.
  • Who this is for: people who have already choked. If he only chokes occasionally and hasn't been assessed, don't thicken everything to an extreme yourself — ask first.

docs.title: Change the posture: sit upright, chin down; don't lie down, don't tilt back
docs.text:
• What you can do: ① If he can sit, eat sitting, sitting upright, leaning forward about 20 degrees, neck slightly down; ② if he can only lie down, raise the head of the bed at least 30 degrees, flex the neck forward, and pad the shoulder on the paralysed side with a pillow; ③ the head can swallow with a slight chin-down, which narrows the entrance to the windpipe; ④ within half an hour after a meal, don't turn him, pat his back, or suction right away.
  • Where this comes from: B | third-party research: posture management is standard practice in swallowing rehabilitation.
  • Who this is for: people who have already choked. For those fully bedbound, the carer positions them according to the assessment.

docs.title: Change the speed: small bites, slow, swallow clean before the next bite
docs.text:
• What you can do: ① a small bite, starting from a very small spoon (a few millilitres) — too much leaks and chokes, too little doesn't trigger the swallow; ② swallow before the next bite, doing a few "dry swallows" after each; ③ alternate solids and liquids, swallowing a bite of solid then a small sip of water (also thickened); ④ don't talk, and don't watch a phone or TV, while eating.
  • Where this comes from: C | this book's own check (2026-10): feeding training is a common practice in rehabilitation; see the popular-science pieces from Peking Union and the Affiliated Hospital of Jiangsu University.

docs.title: When these signals appear, it's time to see a swallowing specialist
docs.text:
• In short: Repeated choking, a wet voice after eating, repeated lung infections, longer mealtimes, weight going down; an abnormal Kubota test or EAT-10 self-check; having already been hospitalised because of this. One is enough to go.
  • What you can do: Find a doctor who does swallowing assessment — rehabilitation department, geriatrics, otolaryngology (ENT), or neurology — and a speech-language therapist. The gold standard is the videofluoroscopic swallow study and the flexible endoscopic evaluation of swallowing.
  • Where this comes from: A | official wording: popular-science pieces from Peking Union, Beijing Tsinghua Changgung, and other hospitals all point to the path "assessment → specialist."
  • Who this is for: anyone with any of the signals above.

docs.title: 7.7 Dignity in this matter of eating
docs.text:
• What it costs: Nothing. What it takes is a few changed habits.
  • In short: Being fed, eating slowly, and food dribbling onto clothes are the three things many older people least want seen. What it hurts is not the body but dignity. Let one meal tell him "I'm useless" and he'll eat less, go out less, eat in front of others less — and get worse nourished.
  • What you can do: ① If he can eat by himself, let him eat by himself, even if it's slow, even if it's messy; ② don't rush him, don't stare, don't wipe his mouth in front of others; ③ put a suction pad under the bowl, cut food into small pieces, use less soup — reduce the "mess" at the source rather than scolding after; ④ let him decide what to eat and how much — "You can help me, but ask me." (Chapter 20)
  • Where this comes from: C | this book's own check (2026-10): caregiving experience; no trial can measure "how many points dignity is worth," but it belongs to the "dignity" of the four ledgers and can't be cut.
  • Who this is for: older people who can still express their wishes should be left to do it themselves as far as possible. For those fully fed, the dignity falls on the person feeding: steady hands, eyes not looking away, mouth not commenting.
  • What you get back: dignity — no longer afraid of "being coaxed like a child at the dinner table."

docs.title: 7.8 If you are reading this for a parent
docs.text:
First do three things that don't need his consent:

  1. Observe. At meals, watch whether he chokes, whether his voice changes after eating, how long he takes, whether he touches meat. Note it in your phone.
  2. Record weight. Weigh him once a month. If he loses 5% to 10% in half a year, take him to ask a doctor.
  3. Learn it yourself too. Learn the Heimlich manoeuvre in 7.2 — the person who knows it isn't necessarily your parents, but you may be the only one near them who does.

When he won't agree to change the food or refuses to see a doctor, it's still the three things from Chapter 20: build a file, ask the doctor on his behalf, find resources. Down at the level of eating, that means putting his choking, his weight changes, and his history of pneumonia onto one sheet of paper and handing it to the doctor at the next appointment.

docs.title: 7.9 How this works in China
First weigh him, then book a nutrition clinic or a sarcopenia clinic
docs.text:
• In short: In big hospitals, nutrition is handled by the clinical nutrition department, and the elderly by the geriatrics department. The 2024 Chinese Expert Consensus on the Outpatient Management Standards for Sarcopenia in the Elderly already recommends that hospitals at all levels open sarcopenia clinics, equipped with body-composition analysers and grip-strength meters; for a first screen a soft tape measure around the calf can be used.
  • What you can do: When booking, say three things clearly — how much weight he has lost in half a year, how long he has been eating less, and whether he has choked. After the doctor screens and assesses, they then decide whether to teach you to change his way of eating or to add oral nutritional supplements. Not every hospital has one; big-city tier-3 hospitals are easier to find.
  • Where this comes from: A | official wording: Chinese Expert Consensus on the Outpatient Management Standards for Sarcopenia in the Elderly (2024 edition), led by the Geriatrics Branch of the Chinese Medical Association (released by Peking Union Medical College Hospital, 2025-08).

docs.title: What's in the community canteens and elders' dining halls
docs.text:
• In short: Since 2023 the state has been promoting meal assistance for the elderly. With the approval of the State Council, the Ministry of Civil Affairs and 10 other departments issued the Action Plan for Actively Developing Meal Assistance Services for the Elderly; a sample survey showed 22.1% of older people have a need for meal assistance. The name differs from place to place: Shanghai calls them "community elders' canteens," Guangdong calls them "elders' dining halls," and there are also meal-assistance points and home delivery.
  • What you can eat and what it costs: a meal is put together like ordinary food, and many places have tiered subsidies for the very old, the disabled, and those living alone, cheaper than eating out. By the end of 2025 Shanghai had built 521 community elders' canteens and 1,977 meal-assistance points; by 2024 Guangdong had built more than 3,600 elders' dining halls.
  • One pitfall: many canteens are kept going by subsidies; once the subsidy shrinks they easily run at a loss and close.
  • What you can do: Ask the residents' committee or the sub-district eldercare service centre three questions — is there a meal-assistance point in this area, can someone in my situation get a subsidy, and can it be delivered to the home.
  • Where this comes from: A | official wording: the Action Plan for Actively Developing Meal Assistance Services for the Elderly by the Ministry of Civil Affairs and 10 other departments, and public data from the Shanghai Civil Affairs Bureau.

docs.title: For the teeth, see the dental department first
docs.text:
• In short: If he can't chew meat, fix the teeth first, not his willpower first. Fill the missing teeth and adjust the dentures, and the amount he eats often goes up with it.
  • What you can do: Go to the dental department of a general hospital, a dental hospital, or the prosthodontics department (the one that makes dentures); some places have a geriatric dental clinic.
  • What to know in advance: implants and dentures are mostly paid out of pocket, and medical insurance generally doesn't cover dentures. Ask the price and the plan first.
  • Where this comes from: C | this book's own check (2026-10): the care path is common sense; how much local medical insurance reimburses for dental care (especially dentures and implants) differs by place — go by the latest local rules.

docs.title: For swallowing rehabilitation, find the rehabilitation department and a speech-language therapist
docs.text: • In short: Swallowing rehabilitation is handled in the rehabilitation department, and the matching role is the speech-language therapist (sometimes called swallowing therapy). Not every hospital has one at present; big-city tier-3 hospitals are easier to find.

docs.title: 7.10 The one thing you can do today
docs.text: Search "your city + Red Cross + first-aid training" and sign up once. The Red Cross public first-aid training is free, and one class is enough to learn what to do in the minute of choking. Once you've learned it, teach it to one other person in the family — you may be the only one near them who knows it.

docs.title: 7.11 What I am not sure about in this chapter
docs.text:
• Online it circulates that "about 45% of people over 65 and about 75% of people over 80 have dysphagia," but only hospital popular-science pieces citing it could be found, and it couldn't be traced back to the original survey, so this chapter does not use those figures.
  • "Aspiration pneumonia makes up about 71% of community-acquired pneumonia in the elderly" is second-hand from Expert Recommendations on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Adult Aspiration Pneumonia (2022); its original study wasn't checked back. The same recommendations also give about 5%–15% of all community-acquired pneumonia; the two figures differ by population.
  • How much local medical insurance reimburses for dental care (especially dentures and implants) goes by the latest local document.
  • The subsidy standards and coverage of community canteens are local policy and change quickly; this chapter only writes "where to ask" and doesn't give specific amounts.

docs.title: 7.12 Sources for this chapter
docs.text:
First aid

  • Fuzhou Municipal Health Commission, "The Heimlich Manoeuvre Has Been Updated" (海姆立克急救法更新了) (2026-01-08): the 2025 AHA and ILCOR update — back blows first, then abdominal thrusts; no abdominal thrusts for infants. https://www.fuzhou.gov.cn/zgfzzt/swjw/fzwj/jkkp/202601/t20260108_5268351.htm
  • Xinhua Net, "Is the Heimlich Manoeuvre the Same as First Aid for an Airway Foreign Body?" (海姆立克急救法等同于气道异物急救法吗？) (2024-08): positioning for abdominal thrusts, the self-rescue method, abdominal thrusts possibly injuring internal organs, chest thrusts possibly causing rib fractures. http://www.xinhuanet.com/science/20240813/2f03f4831e3d467bb5c0f652825e6373/c.html
  • Beijing Ditan Hospital, Capital Medical University, "What Is the Heimlich Manoeuvre and How Do You Perform It?" (什么是海姆立克急救法及如何施救？): the Heimlich applies only to complete airway obstruction; someone who can cough should be encouraged to cough, not given thrusts. https://www.bjdth.com.cn/Html/News/Articles/7531.html
  • Midu County Red Cross, Yunnan Province, "What to Do About an Obstructed Airway" (气道异物梗阻怎么办): the V-shaped hand sign, encouraging coughing in mild cases, alternating back blows with abdominal thrusts, the self-rescue technique, and not blindly clearing with fingers. https://www.ynredcross.cn/mdx/article.jsp?id=22500&itemId=192
  • Shenyang Municipal People's Government, "Which First-Aid Knowledge and Skills Are Needed in Daily Life?" (日常需要掌握哪些急救知识技能？) (2025-08): key points for performing first aid on adults. https://www.shenyang.gov.cn/zwgk/zwdt/bxgz/202508/t20250815_4890516.html
  • Mayo Clinic, Choking: First aid (2025-08-25): back blows combined with abdominal thrusts, the self-rescue method, chest thrusts for pregnant people, and switching to CPR when the person is unconscious. https://www.mayoclinic.org/first-aid/first-aid-choking/basics/art-20056637

Aspiration and aspiration pneumonia

  • Beijing Tsinghua Changgung Hospital, "The Elderly Should Be Alert to Silent Aspiration" (老人警惕隐性误吸) (2024-06): the definition of silent aspiration, high-risk groups, and its signs; cites about 9.4 per 100,000 person-years of in-hospital aspiration pneumonia in China, 2011–2017. https://www.btch.edu.cn/ksdh/jzzb/zzyxk/jkjy_zzyxk/ccc73dffa5124f4ab33770a7d4a15416.htm checked 2026-10-10
  • Expert Recommendations on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Adult Aspiration Pneumonia (成人吸入性肺炎诊断和治疗专家建议), the Expert Group on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Adult Aspiration Pneumonia (She Jun, Ding Jianwen, Shen Jie, et al.): aspiration pneumonia makes up about 5%–15% of community-acquired pneumonia and about 71% of community-acquired pneumonia in the elderly; definitions of overt and silent aspiration, risk factors, and prevention. International Journal of Respiratory Medicine (《国际呼吸杂志》) 2022;42(2):86–96, DOI: 10.3760/cma.j.cn131368-20211209-00908. Full text (reprint): https://www.icu.cn/?p=3552 checked 2026-10-10
  • First Affiliated Hospital of Guangzhou Medical University, "A Case of Aspiration Pneumonia Treated Based on Respiratory Rehabilitation" (基于呼吸康复救治吸入性肺炎一例) (2022-12): cites the "about 71% of community-acquired pneumonia in the elderly" figure above. https://www.rccrc.cn/article/1405
  • Cleveland Clinic, Aspiration (2025-03-03): the definition and symptoms of aspiration. https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/aspiration

Dysphagia and texture modification

  • Peking Union Medical College Hospital, "Dysphagia in the Elderly: How to Cope?" (老年人吞咽功能障碍，怎么应对？): overt and silent aspiration, EAT-10 and the Kubota water-swallowing test, eating posture and food choices, bite size, and swallowing techniques. https://www.pumch.cn/detail/32830.html
  • Belafsky PC, et al. Validity and reliability of the Eating Assessment Tool (EAT-10). Ann Otol Rhinol Laryngol. 2008;117(12):919–924, DOI: 10.1177/000348940811701210 (PubMed 19140539): source of the EAT-10 scale, with a total score ≥3 as the abnormality cut-off.
  • China's Guidelines for the Rehabilitation Management of Dysphagia (2023 edition) (中国吞咽障碍康复管理指南（2023 版）), the Dysphagia Rehabilitation Committee of the Chinese Association of Rehabilitation Medicine: prevalence of dysphagia in people over 50 is 5.5%–8%, about 42% in the acute phase of stroke, reaching 80% with brainstem lesions. Chinese Journal of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation (《中华物理医学与康复杂志》) 2023;45(12):1057–1072, DOI: 10.3760/cma.j.issn.0254-1424.2023.12.001. https://cjpmr.tjh.com.cn/ch/reader/view_abstract.aspx?file_no=2301201057 checked 2026-10-10
  • Chinese Expert Consensus on the Rehabilitation of Senile Dysphagia (老年性吞咽障碍康复中国专家共识), the drafting group of the Chinese Expert Consensus on the Rehabilitation of Senile Dysphagia and the Dysphagia Rehabilitation Committee of the Chinese Association of Rehabilitation Medicine: 16 consensus statements covering screening, assessment, Chinese and Western rehabilitation, nutrition support, and nursing. Chinese Journal of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation (《中华物理医学与康复杂志》) 2025;47(12):1057–1065. https://cjpmr.tjh.com.cn/ch/reader/view_abstract.aspx?file_no=2501201057&flag=1 checked 2026-10-10
  • Affiliated Hospital of Jiangsu University, "A Few Simple Moves to Ease the Elderly's Difficult 'Swallow'" (化解老年人的难"咽"之隐，只需这几招) (2023-11): symptoms, the water self-test, using fewer thin liquids and sticky or granular foods, not using a straw, and keeping at least half a cup of water in the cup. https://www.jdfy.cn/changjianbingyufangyubaojian/10826.html
  • NHS, Dysphagia (2023-05): symptoms, when to seek care, referral to a speech-language therapist, thickening. https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/dysphagia/
  • Mayo Clinic, Dysphagia - Diagnosis and treatment: swallowing assessment and adjustments to diet and eating habits. https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/dysphagia/diagnosis-treatment/drc-20372033
  • IDDSI Framework (2019/2020): an 8-level grading framework for foods and drinks. https://iddsi.org/framework/
  • ENT Health, Aging and Swallowing (2018): age-related changes in swallowing and advice such as chewing thoroughly and taking small bites. https://www.enthealth.org/conditions/aging-and-swallowing/

Loss of appetite, malnutrition, and muscle loss

  • Cleveland Clinic, Sarcopenia: about 8% muscle loss per decade, acceleration from 65 to 80, and complications. https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/23167-sarcopenia
  • NHS, Malnutrition (2023-05): losing 5%–10% of body weight in half a year is a main signal of malnutrition, with those over 65 at high risk. https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/malnutrition/
  • Mechanisms of the anorexia of aging—a review (PMC5005824): decline in taste and smell, early satiety, slower gastric emptying, teeth and dentures, swallowing, depression and dementia, and social factors and bereavement. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5005824/
  • Guidelines for Medical Nutrition Therapy for Elderly Patients in China (2026 edition) (《中国老年患者医学营养治疗指南（2026 版）》) (Nutrition Support Committee of the Chinese Medical Association et al.): protein recommendations for sarcopenia in the elderly; cites the Peking Union multicentre survey, with a prevalence of sarcopenia in those over 80 of about 42%. https://www.nhc.gov.cn/sps/c100087/202604/a69d2fce21e040dc96cbc40b923a06d3.shtml
  • Peking Union Medical College Hospital, "The Chinese Expert Consensus on the Outpatient Management Standards for Sarcopenia in the Elderly Is Released" (《老年人肌少症门诊管理规范中国专家共识》发布) (2025-08-13): recommends that hospitals at all levels open sarcopenia clinics and use assessment tools. https://www.pumch.cn/detail/42665.html

Meal assistance for the elderly

  • Action Plan for Actively Developing Meal Assistance Services for the Elderly (《积极发展老年助餐服务行动方案》) (Minfa [2023] No. 58, the Ministry of Civil Affairs and 10 other departments). Xinhua Net report: http://www.news.cn/politics/2023-10/24/c_1129933524.htm ; full text at CCTV: https://news.cctv.com/2023/10/23/ARTI9Pyn8KMhwLtucWPgXBGa231023.shtml
  • "Policy Interpretation of the Action Plan for Actively Developing Meal Assistance Services for the Elderly" (《〈积极发展老年助餐服务行动方案〉政策解读》): 22.1% of older people have a need for meal assistance, and tiered subsidies for dining. http://www.nqbgx.gov.cn/nqbgx/zcjd/202405/eb7fe1b1321543019c1390933ad40069.shtml
  • Shanghai Civil Affairs Bureau, "Upgrading and Strengthening 50 Community Elders' Canteens" (为 50 家社区长者食堂提质增能): by the end of 2025, 521 community elders' canteens and 1,977 meal-assistance points had been built. https://mzj.sh.gov.cn/26shitang/index.html

Note: the key figures in this chapter all carry a tier (official wording / third-party research); there are no untiered figures. No dosages are given and no diagnoses are made. The links were checked and open as of 2026-10.

docs.title: Chapter 8 · Three red lines for going to hospital, and the first hour
docs.text:
Three in the morning: a heavy tightness in your chest wakes you up, and your back breaks out in a cold sweat. You lie there thinking: wait a bit longer, go to the hospital when it's light.

Eight in the morning: while brushing your teeth, one of your hands suddenly won't lift, and the cup drops into the sink.

The right thing to do is the same sentence both times: call 120 — China's ambulance number — right now.

docs.title: 8.1 What this chapter is for
docs.text:
This chapter is not about diseases, and not about how anything is treated. It settles one thing: in those few minutes when certain symptoms appear, should you call 120 — and what do you say on the phone.

You are better off never needing it in your life. Sometimes you call 120, get checked, and go home with nothing wrong — a wasted trip. That is better than "wait and see."

docs.title: 8.2 When you can't tell, calling 120 is not a mistake
docs.text:
• What it costs: one phone call, no money (do you have to talk? not necessarily)
  • In short: It doesn't matter if you can't remember the rest of this. One sentence is enough: when you can't tell whether it's an emergency, call 120 and let the professionals sort it out for you. The dispatcher asks a few questions, then either sends an ambulance or talks you through what to do.
  • What you can do: Put 120 on your phone's speed dial; tape the table in 8.10 next to the phone or on the fridge.
  • Where this comes from: A | The National Health Commission's emergency guidance is simply "if life is in danger, dial 120" — it does not ask you to judge accurately first.
  • Who this is for: It holds for everyone. Don't use 120 as a taxi (for an ordinary doctor visit, a non-emergency).
  • What you get back: Independence — no longer afraid of "running out of time."

docs.title: 8.3 Chest pain that won't ease after twenty minutes, with sweating and shortness of breath, means it is time to call 120
docs.text:
• What it costs: one phone call, no money
  • In short: The most typical heart-attack pain is a squeezing feeling in the centre of the chest or just left of it, radiating to the left shoulder, left arm, jaw or back, along with cold sweat, shortness of breath and nausea. The National Health Commission interview gives this dividing line: when this kind of chest tightness or chest pain won't ease after 20 to 30 minutes, you should strongly suspect a heart attack.
  • What you can do: ① Stop at once, sit down or half-recline where you are, and don't keep walking or climbing stairs; ② call 120 immediately, and if you are alone at home, tell your children or a neighbour as you do; ③ if you have a confirmed diagnosis of coronary heart disease and your doctor has prepared emergency medicine for you, take it as prescribed; ④ wait for the ambulance indoors — don't drive yourself.
  • Where this comes from: A | The "three dos and three don'ts" from a Fuwai Hospital specialist in the National Health Commission online interview (2026-09); that heart-attack symptoms in older people and in people with diabetes are often atypical and easily delayed is a point spelled out in the Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Acute ST-Segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction (2019) (see 8.14).
  • Who this is for: It is useful for people with typical symptoms. If you have diabetes or are very old, you may have little chest pain and instead show sudden shortness of breath, a whole-body cold sweat, nausea, or even fainting — for those cases, think emergency even more. Don't go looking for medicine to take to push the symptoms down — that masks the cause and makes the doctor judge wrong.
  • What you get back: Independence — no longer afraid that "toughing it out will make you too late."
  • How this works in China: When you call 120, say clearly "chest pain, how long it's lasted, whether you're sweating," and the dispatcher will send you to a nearby hospital with the capacity to treat chest pain.

docs.title: 8.4 Face drooping, one arm that won't stay level, unclear speech — any one of these, call 120
docs.text:
• What it costs: one phone call, no money
  • In short: Stroke (cerebral stroke) has a mnemonic ordinary people can remember, called "Stroke 120":
  • 1 — look at one face: ask him to smile, and see whether one side of the face droops while the other is level;
  • 2 — check two arms: ask him to hold both arms out level for ten seconds, and see whether one side drifts down;
  • 0 — a homophone for "listen": listen to speech — ask him to say one complete sentence, and see whether it's slurred or he can't get it out. Sudden numbness in the limbs on one side, severe headache, unsteady walking, or blurry vision may also be a stroke.
  • What you can do: ① If any of these appears, call 120 at once; ② write down the exact time the symptoms started — that time is the most useful thing of all; ③ lay him flat or on his side with the head turned to one side, and loosen the collar to stop vomit choking him; ④ don't give water or medicine, and don't move him back and forth.
  • Where this comes from: A | "Stroke 120" is endorsed by the National Health Commission online interview (2026-09) and the Stroke 120 project (The Lancet Neurology, 2016).
  • Who this is for: It holds for everyone, including people whose symptoms go away on their own after ten or fifteen minutes. That "getting better" is often a "mini-stroke" (transient ischaemic attack), a strong warning of a major stroke to follow — don't let it go just because the symptoms have passed.
  • What you get back: Independence — no longer afraid of "thinking it has passed and it's fine."
  • How this works in China: The sooner you reach a hospital able to give clot-dissolving treatment, the better. Intravenous thrombolysis has a time window: the standard window in current domestic guidelines is within 4.5 hours of onset; a proportion of patients screened by imaging can be extended to 4.5–9 hours after onset (see 8.14).

docs.title: 8.5 Won't wake up, answers beside the point, suddenly collapses unconscious — that is 120
docs.text:
• What it costs: one phone call, no money
  • In short: Shake his shoulder, shout at him, and see whether there is any response. No response means unconscious. Some people aren't unresponsive to being woken — they answer beside the point, and that counts as another red line.
  • What you can do: ① Call 120; ② see whether his chest rises and falls, and whether he is breathing. If he is not breathing, or takes only one or two sighing breaths (agonal breathing), start CPR at once: stack your hands and press on the midpoint of the line between the two nipples, at a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute and a depth of 5 to 6 cm, letting the chest fully recoil each time; ③ if you know how to give rescue breaths, do 30 compressions to 2 breaths; if you don't, just keep compressing without stopping until the ambulance arrives; ④ if there is an AED (automated external defibrillator), fetch it and use it to defibrillate.
  • Where this comes from: A | The CPR and call-for-help wording given in the National Health Commission online interview (2026-09).
  • Who this is for: It holds for unconsciousness that comes on suddenly. Don't take a coma for "asleep," don't pinch the philtrum, don't give water or medicine, don't wait for it to "pass" — none of that helps in an emergency, and all of it can cause choking.
  • What you get back: Independence — no longer afraid that "something happens to me alone at night and no one knows."

docs.title: 8.6 The first hour after a fall: rushing to pull him up often does harm
docs.text:
• What it costs: spend ten minutes observing first, then decide (money: nothing to pay)
  • In short: When an older person falls, the greatest fears are a broken bone and bleeding in the head. "Get him up quickly" is kindly meant, but it can turn an unbroken bone into a broken one and stir the bleeding worse. The original wording of the Technical Guidelines for Fall Intervention in Older Adults is: don't rush to lift him up; handle it according to the situation.
  • What you can do: First don't move him, and ask two questions: "Where does it hurt?" and "How did you fall just now — do you remember?" Then match against the list —
  • If any of the following appears, don't lift him yourself — call 120 at once:
    • won't wake up, dazed, answers off the point, can't remember how he fell;
    • face drooping, slurred speech, can't move the limbs on one side (possibly a stroke);
    • severe headache, severe pain in the neck or lower back, loss of bladder or bowel control, a leg out of shape or agonising pain on any movement (possibly a fracture or spinal injury);
    • if there is bleeding, press on it on the spot with a clean cloth; if he vomits, turn the head to one side and clear the mouth.
  • If he is conscious, can answer, and none of the above applies: you can help him sit up slowly and rest a while, watching him. But that same day someone must go with him to hospital to be seen once — the guidelines say "after any fall, someone should accompany the person to hospital for diagnosis and treatment" — because this fall is often a signal the body gave first (see Chapter 5).
  • Where this comes from: A | The Ministry of Health, Technical Guidelines for Fall Intervention in Older Adults (老年人跌倒干预技术指南) (2011-09-06); in 2026 the National Health Commission issued the further industry standard WS/T 887—2026, Technical Standard for Fall Prevention and Control among Older Adults in the Community (社区老年人跌倒预防控制技术标准).
  • Who this is for: It holds for older people who fall at home. Don't drag or heave him up alone; you should keep him lying as flat as possible and move him steadily; and don't think "it'll be fine after a rest." One more point: people taking anticoagulants or antiplatelet drugs should get to hospital soon even if they only knocked their head and were lucid at the time — this is one of the indications for a head CT (see 8.14).
  • What you get back: Independence — no longer afraid of "never getting up again after a fall."
  • How this works in China: Falls are the leading cause of injury-related death among older people in China; for what to change at home, see Chapter 5 and Appendix A.

docs.title: 8.7 In the minute someone is choking, letting them cough beats any manoeuvre
docs.text:
• What it costs: a few dozen seconds (money: nothing to pay)
  • In short: If he can cough and can make a sound, let him cough — don't touch him. Coughing works better than any manoeuvre. Someone who is completely choked is: unable to get air, unable to make a sound, both hands clutching the throat, face turning blue.
  • What you can do: ① For complete choking, lean his upper body forward and give 5 back blows with the heel of the hand between the two shoulder blades, one per second; ② if that doesn't work, do abdominal thrusts (the Heimlich manoeuvre): one hand in a fist, the other wrapping it, placed above the navel, and thrust quickly up and in 5 times; ③ alternate the two actions until the object comes out; ④ if he loses consciousness, lay him flat and start CPR while someone else calls 120.
  • For how to save yourself if you live alone, what to do for a pregnant woman or a child under one year old, and the full four-step write-up, see Chapter 7, 7.2 — that is the full text of this item, and its source is noted there.
  • Where this comes from: A | Same source as Chapter 7, 7.2: the first-aid algorithm updated in 2025 by the American Heart Association and the International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation (back blows first, then abdominal thrusts), which the Red Cross Society of China's training has taught this way all along.
  • Who this is for: It holds for older people choking on food or medicine just as much as for anyone else. Don't give water, and don't dig with a finger (something you can't see just gets pushed further in the more you dig).
  • What you get back: Independence — no longer afraid of "a mouthful of food killing someone."

docs.title: 8.8 Four of the most lethal thoughts — don't believe any of them
docs.text: What you will think Why it's dangerous What to do "Sleep it off / it'll pass with a rest" Stroke symptoms can go away on their own and it can still be a "mini-stroke"; a heart attack certainly won't improve with sleep Call 120 the moment the symptom appears "Wait and see" Treating a heart attack or stroke is counted in minutes; the time you spend waiting is heart muscle and brain that can't be saved Call now "Take some medicine first to push it down" Taking medicine at random masks the symptoms and makes the doctor judge wrong; chest pain may not be a heart attack either Take medicine only as your own doctor prescribed, and never as a substitute for 120 "Drive / cycle to the hospital myself" Your judgement and strength are both dropping, and if something happens on the way no one can help; 120 can take you to a nearby hospital with the capacity to treat you and starts care on the way Call 120 and let the professionals come

docs.title: 8.9 Say three things on the 120 call, then notify your children as well
docs.text:
• What it costs: one to two minutes (money: nothing to pay)
  • In short: The 120 dispatcher will ask several things, but wants three first: address, condition, phone number. Once these three are clear, the vehicle is sent out first, and the rest is filled in as it goes.
  • How to do it — say it like this:
  • Address: province, city and district + street and neighbourhood + building number + entrance + unit number. If the unit number is hard to find, give an obvious landmark. Then send someone to wait at the neighbourhood gate or the junction, and wave when they see the ambulance.
  • Condition: one sentence with age, sex, what the symptom is, and when it started — for example, "seventy years old, male, chest pain for half an hour, pouring cold sweat."
  • Phone number: leave a number that is on the scene, not just your mobile phone somewhere else. When calling 120 from outside the area, this is the easiest point to get wrong. Don't hang up in a hurry — wait until the dispatcher has confirmed, and keep the line open.
  • Whether to notify your children at the same time: yes. Calling 120 and calling your children don't conflict; it's one phone call done alongside. Your children can get there to meet the ambulance and bring the medical-insurance card (yibao card) and the medication record.
  • Who this is for: The order is call 120 first, then notify your children. Don't "wait for the children to arrive before deciding" — that's the slowest way to wait. If you are alone at home and already can't speak, use your phone's SOS if you can, or bang on the door, knock on the heating pipes, or phone a neighbour.
  • What you get back: Independence + relationships — no longer afraid of "not being able to explain when something happens, with no one to lend a hand."

docs.title: 8.10 Print this page out and tape it next to the phone
docs.text:
(This is the full-text version of Appendix D.)

What you see What it suggests What to do Squeezing chest pain radiating to the left shoulder, arm or jaw, with sweating and shortness of breath, not easing after 20–30 minutes Suspected heart attack Stop; sit or lie down; call 120; don't drive yourself One side of the face drooping / one arm drifting down when both are held out / unclear speech; or sudden numbness on one side, severe headache, unsteady walking Suspected stroke Note the time it started to the minute; call 120; lay him on his side to prevent choking; give no water and don't move him Won't wake up, answers beside the point, suddenly collapses Unconscious Check breathing; if not breathing, start CPR; call 120 After a fall: won't wake up / answers off the point / face drooping / severe headache / severe back pain / loss of bladder or bowel control / a leg out of shape and can't move Suspected fracture or problem inside the skull Don't lift, don't move; call 120; press on bleeding on the spot Can't speak, clutching the throat, face turning blue Complete choking 5 back blows ↔ 5 abdominal thrusts; if he loses consciousness, CPR + 120 Can't get air, extreme difficulty breathing A serious problem with breathing Call 120, don't wait Heavy bleeding, blood flowing out and won't stop Blood loss Call 120 Convulsions (seizures) that won't stop, or one after another Something acute happening in the brain Call 120 Took the wrong medicine, or an unknown substance Risk of poisoning Call 120, don't wait for it to pass Wetting yourself / forgetting to turn off the stove / a one-off headache / a one-off racing heart, while awake and fine soon after Not necessarily an emergency Write it down, see a doctor in good time; no need to call 120

The last four of these weren't listed as separate items above, and they are just as lethal: can't get air, extreme difficulty breathing — not enough air, and a few minutes' delay can be more than the person can take; heavy bleeding, blood flowing out and won't stop — the blood keeps draining and the person gives out fast; convulsions (seizures) that won't stop, or one after another — seizing without let-up means something acute is happening in the brain; took the wrong medicine, or an unknown substance — nobody knows what was swallowed, and waiting only makes it worse, so don't wait for the person to come round slowly. If you see any one of these, do one thing only: call 120, and say clearly "what the symptom is and when it started."

Two rules that don't fit in the table but matter more: ① If you can't tell, call 120. ② Call 120 first, then notify people.

Print it out, fill it in, and tape it next to the phone:

The chest-pain centre / stroke centre nearest my home: __________ Community or family-doctor phone: __________ Children's phones: __________ Neighbours' phones: __________

docs.title: 8.11 If you are reading this for a parent
docs.text: Print the table in 8.10 out larger and tape it next to the phone at your parents' home, with the address, community phone, and your and your siblings' numbers filled in. When you call 120 on a parent's behalf, the medication list, medical history and insurance type in your hands are the most useful things (Chapters 0 and 19).

docs.title: 8.12 The one thing you can do today
docs.text:
Take a photo of the top three rows of this chapter's decision table, save it to your phone's album and pin it; then add 120 to your phone's speed dial.

You don't have to remember all of it today. When the day really comes, the only things you need to recall are: call 120, don't drive yourself, and note down the time to the minute.

docs.title: 8.13 What I am not sure about in this chapter
docs.text:
• The thrombolysis time window updates with the method of treatment (there is now an extra tier of "extended time window after imaging screening"). This chapter follows the Chinese Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Acute Ischaemic Stroke 2023 in writing "within 4.5 hours of onset as the standard, extendable to 4.5–9 hours with imaging screening"; for exactly what to do, the guideline and protocol your hospital is following that day governs.
  • For how to assess people on anticoagulants or antiplatelet drugs after a fall, and when to do a CT, this chapter writes only "seek medical attention as soon as possible"; the specific handling is left to the emergency department and neurosurgery, and this text does not decide it on their behalf.

docs.title: Chapter 9 · Forgetting: how far from dementia
docs.text:
You are clutching your keys, hunting through every room for your keys. Then you find them — you had put them down in the wrong place. This happens to people of forty and to people of eighty.

It may have happened to your mother. What's different is that she burns the rice, leaves a sentence half said and hanging in the air, and can no longer think of something she set down a moment ago. The question in your mind you don't dare ask out loud: is this old age, or is this illness.

This chapter does not answer "is she demented." It answers one thing only: when should you go and get it checked.

docs.title: 9.1 What this chapter is for
docs.text:
Normal old age and dementia have a wide stretch of ground between them. Forgetting where you put the keys happens to nearly everyone; forgetting what keys are for, so that you can't open the door of your own home, is another matter.

At one end, carrying everything off as "he's old, it's normal" means missing the years when something could still be done. At the other end, two searches online turn you into a patient in your own mind. There is still no drug that turns this disease around, so this chapter gives you one thing only: a ruler.

docs.title: 9.2 Forgetting where the keys are and forgetting how keys work are two different things
docs.text:
• What it costs: nothing, just your eyes and your memory (money: nothing to pay | time: as you go about your day | effort: none | do you have to bring it up? easy)
  • In short: Memory and function are two different things. In normal aging, what is forgotten is "things": where the keys went, what you were about to say — a reminder brings it back. Dementia eats "function": you can't use a key to open a door, you can't make a phone call, you can't work out the change from the grocery shopping, and a reminder doesn't bring it back.
  • What you can do: Check him against these three; the more that match, the more it is worth getting checked. ① Things or function: is what's forgotten a "thing" (which can be filled back in), or "function" (something he could do and now can't)? This is the dividing line. ② Repetition: the same question asked several times, the same story told several times, insisting that things have been taken by someone. ③ The person has changed: someone who loved company stops going out, talks less and less, turns suspicious and quick to anger.
  • Where this comes from: B | The line between dementia and ordinary forgetfulness is "it affects daily life"; clinically, the criterion for mild cognitive impairment is that the more complicated everyday tasks (managing money, shopping, going out to run errands) go wrong, while eating, bathing and using the toilet can still be managed third-party research.
  • Who this is for: It holds for older people who can still get about on their own and are still living with family. For wheelchair users and people who have been bedbound for a long time, the "function" line is drawn differently and the focus of judgment has to change.
  • What you get back: Independence — no longer afraid of "I can still tell the difference, I just don't dare think the worst."
  • How this works in China: These three can be checked at home, with no equipment at all; if none of them match and you are still uneasy, book one outpatient visit as in 9.6.

docs.title: 9.3 The first to notice something is wrong is usually the family, not a scale
docs.text:
• What it costs: paying attention as you go about your day, plus one sheet of paper you can write on (money: nothing to pay | time: a few minutes each time | effort: none | do you have to bring it up? easy)
  • In short: Ask him to his face "is your memory getting worse" and you mostly won't get the truth. Either he won't admit it, or he can't explain it himself either. The first to see that something is wrong is the person who lives with him day after day.
  • What you can do: Don't write down one line, "bad memory." Write down three concrete things: ① things he used to be able to do and now can't (does he still remember to pay the bills, can he use the washing machine, can he make an appointment for himself); ② repetition (how many times the same question, how many times the same story); ③ the person has changed (someone who loved company no longer comes out, talks less and less). For each, write down: when it started, how often, who noticed. This sheet of paper is a clue for the doctor.
  • Where this comes from: B | The 2018 Chinese guideline put "report by the patient or by a knowledgeable informant" into the diagnostic criteria for mild cognitive impairment (grade A recommendation); the informant questionnaire (IQCODE) tells normal older people apart from mild cognitive impairment with an accuracy of about 79.9% third-party research.
  • Who this is for: It holds for older people and families who still live together. For someone living alone, the first to notice is often not family but a community follow-up visit, a neighbor, or an accident (a fall, wandering off).
  • What you get back: Independence — no longer afraid of "by the time I notice, it's already too late."
  • How this works in China: Write these three onto one page and hand it to the doctor at the next accompanied visit; it works better than saying on the spot "my mother's memory is bad."

docs.title: 9.4 "It's just old age, normal" may be blocking a batch of diseases that can be treated
docs.text:
• What it costs: one outpatient visit, plus a few tubes of blood (money: the price of one registration | time: half a day | effort: none | do you have to bring it up? easy)
  • In short: There is a batch of cases that look like dementia but come from other causes, and when the cause is removed the person may well recover. Treat it as "old age" and you never get the chance to check.
  • What you can do: Take this list along and ask the doctor, "have these been checked?"
  • Hypothyroidism: intolerant of cold, slow to react.
  • Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency: often with anemia, a sore tongue, numb hands and feet.
  • Abnormal blood sugar or electrolytes (sodium, calcium).
  • Depression: in someone whose mood is low, memory and reactions both slide; when the depression is treated, cognition often comes back with it.
  • Infection, abnormal liver or kidney function.
  • Drug side effects: sleeping pills, some antihistamines, antidepressants, antipsychotics.
  • Normal-pressure hydrocephalus, subdural hematoma: growing muddled slowly after a blow to the head — think of these two.
  • Where this comes from: B | Professional manuals and clinical guidelines all list these as potentially reversible causes of dementia-like symptoms, of which depression, thyroid, B12 deficiency and drugs can be treated or adjusted. But reversible does not mean it will necessarily reverse: a disease of brain degeneration does not turn around because one tablet was added. And "mild cognitive impairment" itself does not always lead on to dementia: in some studies about a quarter to 30% of people go back to normal cognition, though the studies differ widely third-party research.
  • Who this is for: It holds most of all for people who have only recently become muddled, whose change is fairly fast, or who have a clear trigger (a new drug, a blow to the head). People who have been sliding slowly for years with no trigger should not skip this step either.
  • What you get back: Independence — no longer afraid of "it could have been treated, and one word, 'old age,' cost us that."
  • How this works in China: When you register, say "his memory is getting worse and I want to rule out the treatable causes." The doctor will usually order a complete blood count, thyroid function, blood sugar, liver and kidney function, vitamin B12; most of it is covered by medical insurance (yibao).

docs.title: 9.5 Checking early does not buy you a cure, it buys you the extra years
docs.text:
• What it costs: the time for one assessment (money: registration plus tests | time: half a day | effort: none)
  • In short: The value of checking early is not in "curing" — it is in four concrete things, and all of them start with knowing early: getting onto medicine sooner, arranging care sooner, deciding the things that are yours to decide yourself.
  • What you can do: ① Medication: in the early stage (mild cognitive impairment, and mild to moderate dementia) some drugs help a little, slowing the drop in function; whether to take them and which one is for the memory clinic or the neurologist to judge. ② Non-drug measures: moving, keeping blood pressure and blood sugar under control, getting hearing and vision fitted, keeping up social contact and using your brain — these are written into standard dementia-prevention practice, mild in effect but real. ③ Care arrangements: while you are still clear-headed, you can decide for yourself whether to go into a facility, who lends a hand, how the work is divided at home. ④ Taking stock of money and authority: accounts, the flat, insurance, who manages the money — sort it out while you can still explain it.
  • Where this comes from: B | The World Health Organization's position is that dementia cannot be cured, but drug and non-drug interventions can help maintain life and function; doctors at public hospitals say the same, that intervening early at the mild cognitive impairment stage can delay the onset. But the drugs have only a limited effect on mild cognitive impairment itself.
  • Who this is for: It holds for people who can still decide things and speak for themselves. For someone who can no longer say what he wants, this step can only rest on documents prepared ahead of time (designated guardianship, an advance care plan — see Chapter 22).
  • What you get back: Dignity + money — no longer afraid of "in the end everyone else decides for me."
  • How this works in China: See 9.10; for how to write a designated guardianship and advance care instructions, see Chapter 22.

docs.title: 9.6 Go to a memory clinic, do the four kinds of test, and don't take a checkup package for a diagnosis
docs.text:
• What it costs: one to several outpatient visits (money: registration plus tests | time: half a day each | effort: none)
  • In short: Memory problems belong to the memory clinic, neurology, geriatrics, psychiatry (psychology). The doctor puts the history, the scales, the blood and the imaging together to judge — it is not one question on a test and then a verdict.
  • What you can do: Register with the right department, then match the kinds of test to it. ① History and scales: the doctor asks the person and also asks the family, uses a cognitive scale as a baseline, then tests again after a while to see the difference. ② Blood: the treatable causes in 9.4. ③ Imaging: usually one brain MRI, to look for atrophy, infarction, hydrocephalus, bleeding. ④ Added as needed: cerebrospinal fluid, brain PET, genetics — only when the doctor thinks it necessary and it would change the judgment.
  • Where this comes from: B | The 2018 Chinese guideline recommends a structural brain MRI for patients with mild cognitive impairment at their first visit (grade A recommendation), with blood tests as in 9.4; a brief scale alone is not sensitive enough, and the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) screens for mild cognitive impairment more accurately third-party research. Brain PET and cerebrospinal fluid are done only for people whose cause is unclear or whose plan needs adjusting.
  • Who this is for: It holds for people who can cooperate with a scale. For someone who can no longer cooperate, the tests have to be done another way and the focus moves to care. Don't conclude from one scale: the comparison between two of them matters more than a single score.
  • What you get back: Independence — no longer afraid of "not knowing where to start, being led along by a checkup package."
  • How this works in China: First ask whether there is a memory clinic near you (neurology or geriatrics at a tier-3 hospital, some psychiatric hospitals). When you register, ask directly for the "memory clinic" or the "cognitive disorders clinic." For the community route, see 9.10.

docs.title: 9.7 Don't buy these three yet: brain supplements, one drop of blood, whole-body PET-CT
docs.text:
• What it costs: a few hundred to tens of thousands (money: a lot | time: one go | effort: none)
  • In short: The moment word gets around that "it might be dementia," the most expensive things start arriving at the door. There are three where the price and the usefulness are furthest apart.
  • Brain supplements, memory supplements: no supplement has been shown to prevent dementia or to make memory better. What points the right way is moving, managing chronic disease, and seeing more of people. What you buy is reassurance, not effect.
  • "One drop of blood to test for dementia": blood markers for Alzheimer's disease really are moving forward, and in 2025 the US regulator approved the first blood test for use in supporting a diagnosis official wording; but its place is for people who already have memory symptoms, to help judge — not as a screening test for people with no symptoms. Someone without symptoms who spends this money may just buy himself a "positive" result and six months of fear.
  • Whole-body PET-CT: it is not a checkup item. Whole-body PET-CT in healthy people carries a large radiation dose, and its yield for early cancer is limited. The National Health Commission sets out the basic items of a health checkup as a short list, and whole-body PET-CT is not on it; the deeper tests are left to people at risk. In the cancer screening protocol, the official guidance is more direct: "it is not recommended to use chest X-ray, MRI, PET-CT or biomarker testing for lung cancer screening." The brain PET done when dementia is suspected is something the doctor orders to establish the cause, and it is a different thing from a "whole-body cancer-hunting package."
  • Where this comes from: C | These points are a sorting-out of "go by the evidence and the official wording, don't spend money at random"; they are not saying some test is useless. When there are symptoms, each test has its own place, and the doctor decides it.
  • Who this is for: It is most worth reading for families who want to "buy peace of mind with money." When symptoms really do appear, go through the memory clinic, not the checkup center and not a supplement livestream.
  • What you get back: Money — no longer afraid of "spending a great deal and buying back a false reassurance."
  • How this works in China: The words to refuse can be: "did a doctor order this test for me? If not, I'll leave it for now and go ask the memory clinic."

docs.title: 9.8 After a diagnosis, give the family a calendar for the first year
docs.text:
• What it costs: time, plus a checklist (money: depends | time: done bit by bit across the year | effort: a little tiring | do you have to bring it up? easy)
  • In short: The day of diagnosis is the most panicked, but the things that really have to be done can be put into an order. In the first three months, do three of them.
  • What you can do:
  • The first three months: ① Set up two files: a medical file (diagnosis, medication, scale results, the treating doctor's name and phone number, test sheets), and a family file (ID card, medical insurance, pension, insurance policies, bank cards, property deed). ② While he is still clear, settle two things: who speaks for you when you are not clear (designated guardianship, done at the notary office), and which resuscitations you do or don't want (an advance care plan, see Chapter 22). ③ Change four places at home: a lock or a tracker against wandering, a timer or an alarm on the gas stove, grab bars in the bathroom and beside the bed, and the dangerous things put away.
  • Over the first year, bit by bit: Care arrangements (who is in charge by day, who by night, whether you can use community day care or short-stay residential care to catch your breath); money (ask clearly whether long-term care insurance will pay, whether you can get a disability certificate and draw the two subsidies, see 9.10); support for the carer (the person doing the caring is the one more likely to break down; arrange shifts and respite); thinking ahead (driving, using fire, going out alone, large transfers).
  • Where this comes from: B | Care, guardianship, respite, long-term care insurance — all of these are written into the national action plan on dementia; exactly what you can get and how to apply differs from place to place.
  • Who this is for: It holds for people just diagnosed, still in the early or middle stage. For someone who can no longer manage at all, the focus moves from "arranging" to "hands-on care" (see Chapter 23).
  • What you get back: Dignity + relationships — no longer afraid that "one diagnosis and the whole family comes apart."
  • How this works in China: See 9.10.

docs.title: 9.9 This chapter is about when to get checked; Chapter 8 is about calling 120 now
docs.text:
• What it costs: the few seconds it takes to think it through (money: nothing to pay | time: a few minutes | effort: none)
  • In short: Memory getting worse, forgetting things slowly, is an outpatient matter. But a few things are urgent, and when they appear, don't wait for a clinic appointment: becoming muddled, not recognizing people, talking nonsense over a few hours to a day or two; suddenly unable to speak clearly, with weakness down one side of the body; muddled after a fever or after a blow to the head.
  • What you can do: One sentence to remember: confusion that comes on over hours or days is an emergency; forgetting that comes on slowly over months or years is an outpatient matter. If you can't tell, call 120.
  • Where this comes from: B | Sudden confusion is mostly caused by infection, lack of water, or muddled use of medicine, and people who already have dementia are more likely to have it.
  • Who this is for: It holds for all older people. For someone living alone nobody sees these things, which makes it all the more important to tape the table in 8.10 next to the phone.
  • What you get back: Independence — no longer afraid of "the ones who should have waited for a clinic went to the emergency room, and the ones who should have called 120 sat waiting for an appointment."

docs.title: 9.10 How this works in China: memory clinics, community screening, disability assessment
docs.text:
This section is about the mainland-China system. Where a term has a counterpart you may know from another country, the counterpart is named alongside it.

  • Memory clinics. The state is pushing memory clinics and specialist cognitive-disorder services (starting at county level and above in general hospitals), linking screening, diagnosis and treatment, rehabilitation and follow-up into a single line official wording (National Action Plan on Responding to Senile Dementia, 国卫老龄发〔2024〕42 号). By May 2024, 602 cognitive centers of various levels had been built nationwide, of which 298 were memory disorder prevention and treatment centers official wording. When you register, ask for the "memory clinic" or the "cognitive disorders clinic"; where there is no clinic under that name, register with neurology or geriatrics and say "my memory is getting worse and I would like a cognitive assessment."
  • The community gate. Everyone over 65 already has one free health-management check a year, and initial cognitive screening is being folded into it: the community screens first, and abnormal results are referred to a higher-level hospital for further assessment official wording (same plan). Go to the community health centre — the primary-care layer, the rough equivalent of a GP practice — and ask one question: "do you do the cognitive screening for older people, and how is it done?"
  • Disability assessment and subsidies. When dementia reaches the point of affecting daily life, you can apply for a disability certificate (intellectual disability or psychiatric disability category). China issues one national certificate for this; elsewhere the comparable step is registering for disability benefits, which comes with no card. Apply at the disabled persons' federation of the county or district, or the sub-district (township), where your household registration (hukou) is; collect the Disability Assessment Form; be assessed at the psychiatric (appraisal) department of the designated hospital; then the result is posted publicly and the certificate is made. A legal guardian generally handles it. Those who qualify can apply for the "two subsidies for disabled persons" (a living allowance for disabled people in hardship, and a nursing subsidy for people with severe disability); the severe-disability nursing subsidy generally does not look at household income, and some localities have brought grade 3 and grade 4 intellectual and psychiatric disability into it; it can be applied for online official wording (the "support for the vulnerable" section of the national government service platform).
  • Where to ask: the disabled persons' federation at the community or sub-district where you are registered, the district or county civil affairs bureau, the medical insurance bureau, plus the memory clinic at the hospital you usually go to. The specific standards are whatever the latest local wording says.

docs.title: 9.11 If you can only do one thing today
docs.text:
Run the person you are worried about through the line in 9.2: is what he forgets a "thing" or a "function"?

If you can't tell, or he has already fallen on the "function" side, do one thing: next time you register, don't book a checkup — book the memory clinic or neurology, walk in and say this sentence:

"His (my) memory has been getting worse lately, and I want to find out whether there is a treatable cause."

docs.title: 9.12 If you are reading this for your parents
docs.text:
How to say it out loud. Don't say "I suspect you have dementia" — say that and it turns into a fight. Put it on yourself instead: "my memory's been bad lately, I want to get it checked, come with me, we'll both do the test." Put him in the position of "coming with" and "both of us." Once it's booked, just go to the hospital; don't hold a debate at the dinner table first.

If he won't agree, what you can still do (without his nod). ① Start the files: one medical, one family, and keep a copy yourself. ② Keep an observation record as in 9.3 for three months, and next time say nothing else — hand the doctor that page first. ③ Talk to the doctor on your own once first, and ask clearly "if he comes, how would you check him." ④ At home, fix the dangerous spots first — the fire, the door, the floor.

What he wants is often not to stay away — it is the fear of being stamped "dementia." Keep that door open for the day he feels for himself that something is wrong.

docs.title: 9.13 What I am not sure about in this chapter
docs.text:
• How far Alzheimer's blood markers ("one drop of blood" tests) actually reach in Chinese outpatient clinics, whether they are self-paid, and what they cost have been changing fast in recent years; this chapter writes only the one piece of wording that has been checked — its place is for people with symptoms, to help judge, not as routine screening for people without symptoms. For how a particular hospital does it, ask the memory clinic.
  • The assessment process for disability certificates (intellectual and psychiatric) and the standards and scope of the two subsidies vary from place to place; this chapter gives the national-level wording, and what happens on the ground differs — ask the disabled persons' federation, civil affairs and medical insurance bureau where you are registered.
  • How far community health centres have actually got with initial cognitive screening varies in speed from place to place; the national action plan sets its target for 2030.
