docs.title: Chapter 10 · Urine, stool, and dignity
docs.text:
On the day you were going out, you counted it up in your head first: from home to the hospital, how many toilets along the way, and which ones you could get into.

When you had finished counting, you put the long trip off to next month. This chapter is written for that "putting off".

docs.title: 10.1 What this chapter is for
docs.text:
Two things — urine and stool — most people put up with in silence. Holding them in is where leaking, constipation, infection, and falls at night begin.

There is only one thing to say: most problems of this kind can be improved. Putting up with them is the only real defeat.

docs.title: 10.2 Leaking urine comes in four kinds, and each has a matching treatment
docs.text:
Leaking urine is not one disease; it is several problems sharing one name. Work out which kind it is first, and the treatment will match (official wording Department of Science Popularization, Chinese Medical Association, 2024).

  • Stress incontinence. It leaks when you cough, sneeze, laugh, run or jump, or lift something, and not at other times. The base of it is slack pelvic floor muscles and not enough support for the urethra; in women it is often related to childbirth, age, body weight, and pelvic organ prolapse (official wording health education prescription from Union Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology).
  • Urge incontinence. A sudden urgent need, and you can't hold it; often you leak before you reach the toilet. The bladder contracts before it is full — it is oversensitive (official wording Mayo Clinic).
  • Overflow incontinence. The bladder never empties properly, and urine seeps out a little at a time. Common causes are a blockage at the outlet (in men, usually an enlarged prostate), or a problem with the nerves or muscles of the bladder (official wording Mayo Clinic).
  • Mixed incontinence. Both of the above together. Which one predominates decides which end you treat first (official wording Department of Science Popularization, Chinese Medical Association, 2024).

There is another kind, called functional: there is nothing much wrong with the pelvic floor or the bladder; you simply don't get to the toilet in time, and it has to do with mobility and memory, so what you change is the route and the position (official wording Mayo Clinic). Among women patients, about 60% have stress incontinence, 10% urge, and 30% mixed (official wording Department of Science Popularization, Chinese Medical Association, 2024).

docs.title: 10.3 The pelvic floor is a muscle you can train, and both men and women have one
docs.text:
• What it costs: zero to a few hundred yuan (money: some | time: a few minutes a day | effort: none | do you have to speak up: easy — no one can tell)
  • In short: The pelvic floor is like a hammock holding up the bladder and the bowel. When it is slack, you leak as soon as you exert yourself; when it is strong, the gate stays shut. Like your arms and legs, it can be trained.
  • What you can do: ① Find it first. Pretend you are holding back urine and wind; the part that tightens is it. Don't actually practice by tightening and releasing while you are urinating — that leaves urine behind and invites infection (official wording Mayo Clinic; MSKCC in Chinese). ② Tighten and hold for five seconds, then relax for five seconds; once that is easy, work up to ten seconds. ③ Ten to a set, at least three sets a day — one lying down, one sitting, one standing. ④ Before you cough, sneeze, stand up or lift something, tighten first. ⑤ It usually takes weeks to months to show; once it works you have to keep at it, and it slips back if you stop (official wording Mayo Clinic).
  • Where this comes from: A | This is the first-line approach in Chinese guidelines and international practice alike: for stress incontinence, training it is the first choice, and it helps urge incontinence too (official wording Union Hospital health education prescription; Mayo Clinic).
  • Who this is for: People who can follow the movements. If it does nothing, or you can't find the muscle, it is usually that the method is wrong or you are training the wrong muscle — don't force it; have a pelvic floor rehabilitation clinic or a rehabilitation therapist take a look.
  • What you get back: Independence + dignity — no longer afraid that "one cough and I leak, and I can't trust myself to go out."
  • How this works in China: Many hospitals have opened a pelvic floor rehabilitation clinic or a pelvic floor dysfunction clinic, and you can register directly (official wording Beijing Ditan Hospital; Hangzhou First People's Hospital). Biofeedback and electrical stimulation are adjuncts; whether to use them is the doctor's call. Whether medical insurance (yibao — the mainland's public scheme, the counterpart of Medicare or the NHS) covers it, and how much it pays, differs from province to province: at the national level, rehabilitation items have been brought into medical insurance in two batches (9 items in 2010, 20 more in 2016), and "pelvic floor rehabilitation" is mostly added by the provinces themselves; ask the hospital's insurance office or the local medical insurance bureau before your appointment (see 10.14).

docs.title: 10.4 The more afraid of leaking you are, the less you drink — the most common thing to do, and the most damaging
docs.text:
• What it costs: one day of changing a habit (money: nothing | time: one day | effort: none | do you have to speak up: easy)
  • In short: Afraid of leaking, you drink less, so the urine gets concentrated; concentrated urine stings the bladder, the bladder grows more sensitive, you want to go more and more urgently, and so you get more afraid and drink even less. The circle tightens with every turn.
  • What you can do: Break the circle.
  • How much to drink: for most adults, roughly 1.5 to 2.0 liters of water a day (official wording Chinese expert consensus on chronic constipation, 2019). Spread it out, in small sips; don't down one big glass at a time.
  • When to drink: mostly in the daytime — don't cut out the day as well just to save yourself a trip to the toilet.
  • How to arrange it before bed: in the two to three hours before sleep, cut back on large amounts of fluid; go easy on coffee, strong tea, alcohol, fizzy drinks and very spicy food, which drive urination and irritate the bladder (official wording Tri-Service General Hospital; Mayo Clinic).
  • Train the bladder: when the urgency comes, don't panic — sit down firmly, breathe deeply, tighten the pelvic floor, and wait for the wave to pass before you walk; in ordinary times, try putting urination off a little at a time, starting with ten minutes (official wording Tri-Service General Hospital; Mayo Clinic).
  • Where this comes from: B | Adjusting what and how much you drink, and bladder training, are the basic measures every guideline recommends alike; but how much water is right varies from person to person, and anyone with heart failure or kidney disease must follow their own doctor on how much to drink.
  • Who this is for: People whose heart, lungs and kidneys work normally. If you have heart failure, kidney disease, or are on dialysis, ask your doctor how much to drink.
  • What you get back: Independence + dignity — no longer afraid that "I daren't go out, in case I can't find a toilet on the way."
  • How this works in China: Write down "what I drank and when I went" for three days and you have a voiding diary; take it to the clinic — it is more use than describing it from memory (official wording Department of Science Popularization, Chinese Medical Association, 2024).

docs.title: 10.5 Getting up to urinate three or more times a night — don't write it off as "that's what getting old is like"
docs.text:
• What it costs: one clinic visit (money: registration plus tests | time: half a day | effort: none | do you have to speak up: easy)
  • In short: Waking at night because you need to urinate, more than twice a night, already counts as nocturia (official wording Mayo Clinic). It is not an aging phenomenon you simply have to put up with; behind it there is often a cause that can be found and treated.
  • What you can do: Who to see, and what to ask.
  • Who to see: urology (men or women), or geriatrics; women can also go to a clinic in the urogynecology line.
  • What to ask the doctor to check: a urine test (for infection, and for blood); how much urine is left in the bladder after you have been; the three-day voiding diary you kept; blood sugar. If you snore loudly, are sleepy in the daytime, have swollen legs and feet, or pass a great deal of urine at night, tell the doctor that too (official wording Tri-Service General Hospital; Mayo Clinic).
  • Bring your medicines: many common medicines affect urination; write the list on a sheet of paper and have the doctor go through it.
  • Where this comes from: B | The list of causes of nocturia is the same everywhere, but what to check first, and in what order, is for the doctor to decide on your particulars.
  • Who this is for: People who sleep badly at night and have no energy in the day, and people who have already had a fall. Getting up half asleep at night is the time you are most likely to fall (see Chapter 5). If there is blood in your urine, it hurts to urinate, or you have a fever, don't wait — go as soon as you can.
  • What you get back: Independence + relationships — no longer afraid that "something will happen to me alone at home at night."
  • How this works in China: Register with urology or geriatrics; if you have a contracted family doctor, ask at your community health center first, then decide which tier of hospital to go to.

docs.title: 10.6 Constipation: say nothing, and you can hold it in until you are blocked
docs.text:
• What it costs: changing habits costs nothing; a visit is one clinic appointment (money: some | time: long term | effort: none | do you have to speak up: easy)
  • In short: Straining to pass stool is a dangerous move for anyone with heart disease or cerebrovascular disease; let it drag on and you can end up with fecal impaction or a bowel obstruction.
  • What you can do:
  • First see whether there is a cause you can change: eating refined food, too little fiber, too little water, too little movement all make it worse; many medicines cause constipation too, among them some antidepressants, anticholinergics, calcium channel blockers, and opioid painkillers (official wording Guidelines for the Primary Care Diagnosis and Treatment of Chronic Constipation, 2019).
  • Eating and drinking: eat more things with fiber — roughly 25 to 35 grams of fiber a day; 1.5 to 2.0 liters of water a day (official wording Guidelines for the Primary Care Diagnosis and Treatment of Chronic Constipation, 2019). Fiber needs enough water to go with it, or you end up more bloated than before.
  • The habit of going: the colon is most active when you wake in the morning and after a meal, so choose the morning or within two hours of a meal to sit down, and it comes more easily; concentrate while you are there, and don't stay more than ten minutes at a time (official wording Guidelines for the Primary Care Diagnosis and Treatment of Chronic Constipation, 2019). A squatting position empties more completely than a sitting one.
  • Where this comes from: A | Diet, fluid, exercise and the habit of going are the basic treatment every guideline agrees on, and they come before medicine (official wording Chinese expert consensus on chronic constipation, 2019).
  • Who this is for: Most people with functional constipation. If the signals below appear, this is no longer a matter of changing habits — get seen soon.
  • What you get back: Independence — no longer afraid that "straining will bring something on in the toilet."
  • How this works in China: If four to eight weeks of changed habits doesn't help, you can ask the doctor to consider medicine; which type, and for how long, is the doctor's decision — don't lean on stimulant laxatives yourself long term (official wording Guidelines for the Primary Care Diagnosis and Treatment of Chronic Constipation, 2019).

docs.title: 10.7 If constipation comes with these signals, don't put it off
docs.text:
• What it costs: one clinic visit, possibly a stool test or a colonoscopy (money: a fair amount | time: half a day | effort: some | do you have to speak up: easy)
  • In short: The great majority of constipation is functional, and changed habits plus medicine will ease it. But in a small share there is another disease behind it, and finding it early makes a large difference.
  • What you can do: If any one signal appears, go to gastroenterology or a general practitioner; don't add laxatives on your own.
  • blood in the stool, or a stool test positive for occult blood;
  • weight loss without trying, or anemia, or marked fatigue;
  • abdominal pain that keeps getting worse, or a lump you can feel in your abdomen;
  • can't pass anything, bloated and in pain, and vomiting (think bowel obstruction).
  • Where this comes from: A | These alarm signals, and "for a first visit over forty, assessment is recommended, with colonoscopy if needed", are the referral wording written into the Chinese guideline (official wording Guidelines for the Primary Care Diagnosis and Treatment of Chronic Constipation, 2019).
  • Who this is for: Anyone with any one of the above. If none of these signals is present and the history is long, you can be treated empirically first — not everyone needs a colonoscopy.
  • What you get back: Independence + dignity — no longer afraid that "I put up with everything in silence and let the time when it could be treated go by."
  • How this works in China: Register with gastroenterology; the doctor decides from the alarm signals whether to test the stool, take an image, or do a colonoscopy.

docs.title: 10.8 Change four things in the bathroom, and there is a rule for grab-bar height
docs.text:
• What it costs: grab bars and a commode chair run from a few dozen to a few hundred yuan, and fitting them needs a tradesman (money: some | time: a few days | effort: none | do you have to speak up: easy)
  • In short: Leaking, nocturia, constipation — in the end they all come down to "can you use the toilet safely, and with dignity". Chapter 5 covered the bathroom as the corner of the home where most falls happen; here are the few things that bear directly on elimination.
  • What you can do: ① Grab bars: on both sides of the toilet, fit a horizontal bar about 70 cm above the floor, and on the other side a vertical bar about 1.4 m high; bars 3 to 4 cm in diameter, with the inner side no less than 4 cm from the wall (official wording the national standard GB 50763-2012, Code for Accessibility Design). Those dimensions are the standard for public buildings (accessible toilets); at home, the closer fit is the Ministry of Civil Affairs industry standard MZ/T 218—2024, General Requirements for Age-Friendly Renovation of the Home Environment for Older Adults — grab bars should be provided beside the toilet and in the shower area, with the height set by the person's height and gait, and the gap between bar and wall no less than 40 mm. ② Raise the toilet, or add a commode chair: for someone who can't squat down, or can't get up, a commode chair is the answer. ③ Light the whole way when you get up at night: fit a run of motion-sensor night lights from the bed to the toilet, not just one; take up the mats along the route. ④ For functional incontinence, put a lidded commode by the bed, so that when there is no time to walk you can go right there (official wording Mayo Clinic).
  • Where this comes from: B | The grab-bar dimensions are the national standard wording, but that is a standard for public buildings; at home it has to be set to your height and your body — before it is fitted, have the workman hold the actual bar against you and check the height.
  • Who this is for: People who can still get to the toilet themselves, or half by themselves. Bars have to be anchored into the wall, so use a qualified contractor. Someone completely bedbound needs a different kind of care.
  • What you get back: Independence + dignity — no longer afraid of "falling on the way to the toilet in the middle of the night."
  • How this works in China: Some items in an age-friendly home renovation are subsidized by the government; go to the residents' committee or the sub-district eldercare service window and ask, "does a case like mine get the subsidy" (Minfa [2020] No. 86; see Chapter 5 for details).

docs.title: 10.9 Adult diapers and underpads: not a surrender, a purchase of dignity
docs.text:
• What it costs: depending on how much you use, a few dozen to a few hundred yuan a month (money: a fair amount | time: any time | effort: none | do you have to speak up: easy — used right, no one knows)
  • In short: Wearing one is so that you still dare to go out; it has nothing to do with winning or losing. It puts a lid on the "daren't sit, daren't go far, always worried my trousers are wet" for long enough that the days go on as usual.
  • What you can do:
  • How to choose: by how much leaks. If it is an occasional drip and you can still get to the toilet, use a thin underpad; if there is more, and it is at night, a thicker diaper.
  • How to change: change on a schedule; don't wait until it is soaked through. Sitting in wet makes the skin break down quickly (official wording Mayo Clinic).
  • How to protect the skin: change promptly when wet; warm water and a towel, wiping gently rather than scrubbing; let it dry before dressing; put on a layer of petroleum jelly or a similar barrier cream, to keep the skin and the urine apart; don't wash and irrigate repeatedly (official wording Mayo Clinic).
  • Where this comes from: C | This is standard nursing practice; there is no large trial behind the practice itself; but the moment the skin goes red or breaks, that is the moment to deal with it.
  • Who this is for: Everyone who needs one, and especially people who are bedbound, have dementia, or have thin skin. If the skin is already broken or infected, get a nurse or a doctor to deal with it.
  • What you get back: Dignity — no longer afraid that "I smell, and people keep away from me."
  • How this works in China: Nurses at a hospital nursing clinic or a community health center can teach you how to change and how to protect the skin. Long-term care insurance here is a social insurance scheme run by the state, not the private long-term care policies sold in some countries, and it mainly pays for "nursing services": the nationwide Catalogue of Long-Term Care Insurance Service Items (Trial) (《国家长期护理保险服务项目目录（试行）》) (Yibaofa [2025] No. 24) contains only 20 daily living care items and 16 medical nursing items, 36 in all; adult diapers and underpads, classed as "supportive assistive devices", are not in the national catalogue for now (the document says their inclusion will be "studied and explored" later). A few cities have a separate allowance for devices; whether you can claim, and how much, ask the local medical insurance bureau (official wording National Healthcare Security Administration; benefits differ from place to place, and the latest local wording governs).

docs.title: 10.10 Sex and intimacy: the thing that is assumed to have disappeared
docs.text:
• What it costs: one conversation, and possibly one clinic visit (money: the price of one registration | time: once | effort: none | do you have to speak up: hard — this is the one that takes the most courage)
  • In short: Many people assume that by this age there is no such thing any more, and so nobody mentions it. But people over fifty still think about it and still do it; the need does not vanish just because you are older (official wording Chinese Journal of Epidemiology, 2023).
  • What you can do:
  • How to start: you don't need to go round the houses. One sentence that works: "There is something I have been too embarrassed to bring up with you."
  • First work out what is in the way: it may be illness (diabetes, cardiovascular disease, stroke, a gynecological or prostate problem); it may be medicine (some blood-pressure drugs, antidepressants, and prostate drugs affect sexual function); it may be an operation you have had (prostate, gynecological); or it may simply be that mood and the relationship have changed (third-party research the UpToDate topic Sexual Dysfunction in Older Adults; a PMC review, 2024). A good many of these can be dealt with, but you have to say it first, and get it looked into first.
  • Who to talk to: geriatrics, urology or andrology, gynecology; for distress of mood and relationship, psychiatry or psychology. For problems such as dryness after menopause, gynecology has treatments that answer to it.
  • Where this comes from: C | "There is still sexual desire late in life, and the factors that shape it can be looked into and talked about" is a judgment with research behind it (third-party research, see sources); but how it can be handled for any one person has no single answer — you have to go through it point by point with a doctor.
  • Who this is for: People who want to talk about it, and are willing to see a doctor for it. Not wanting to talk about it is entirely all right too; not sorting this out does not stop you doing the other things well.
  • What you get back: Relationships + dignity — no longer afraid that "it is assumed I don't need it, and I am too embarrassed to say."
  • How this works in China: Register with geriatrics, urology, andrology or gynecology and say straight out, "I have a problem of this kind I would like you to look at"; if you can't get the words out, write it on a piece of paper and hand it over.

docs.title: 10.11 The one thing you can do today
docs.text:
Today, do one set of pelvic floor exercises.

First find the muscle: pretend to hold back urine, hold back wind — the part that tightens is it. Then tighten for five seconds, relax for five seconds, ten times in a row.

It costs nothing, no one can see, and you can start today. If you can't find the muscle, that is precisely the sign that this is worth one visit to a doctor.

docs.title: 10.12 If you are reading this for a parent
docs.text:
This whole chapter, there is almost nothing you can do by stepping in, because it is a matter of the body and a matter of face. There are two things you can do.

How to get the words out to him. Don't ask "do you leak?" — that is asking him to admit to something humiliating. Say it about yourself instead: "I've been getting up at night a lot lately, so I went and had it checked; the doctor says lots of people have this, and it can be treated." Lower yourself first, and he may pick up the thread. Or leave this chapter open on the table; that does more than ten sentences from you.

What you can still do when he won't agree. Three things that don't need his nod: ① start changing the bathroom — grab bars, night lights, take the mats up — and call it "steadier for me to use too"; ② buy a pack of underpads and put them in his room, saying they are "there just in case", and don't push him to use them; ③ when you go with him to an appointment, put the questions to the doctor for him — how many times he gets up at night, how his drinking is, what medicines he takes. He may not admit it out loud; his body will.

docs.title: 10.13 What I am not sure about in this chapter
docs.text:
• Pelvic floor rehabilitation items (biofeedback, electrical stimulation and the like): the range covered by medical insurance in each place, and the reimbursement rules, differ from province to province and city to city. At the national level only the framework for bringing rehabilitation items in by batch has been set; the specific additions are for each province to decide. This chapter has not verified them one by one — ask the hospital's insurance office or the local medical insurance bureau before the appointment.
  • Whether adult diapers and underpads are covered by long-term care insurance or by a local allowance differs from place to place. The nationwide Catalogue of Long-Term Care Insurance Service Items (Trial) does not yet include "supportive assistive devices" of this kind; a few cities have a separate allowance for devices, and you need to ask the local medical insurance bureau.
  • The grab-bar dimensions in GB 50763-2012, Code for Accessibility Design, are the standard for public buildings (accessible toilets); this chapter has added the civil affairs industry standard MZ/T 218—2024, which fits the home more closely, but the final height of a grab bar at home still has to be set to the person's height and body, and matched to the wording of the home age-friendly renovation program (Minfa [2020] No. 86).
  • The list of factors in the "sex and intimacy" section rests mainly on the outline of the UpToDate topic and one review; I have not checked each item back to the original study.
  • "About 60% stress / 10% urge / 30% mixed" for incontinence is the wording of the Chinese Medical Association's popular-science article (written by Lou Wenjia of Peking Union Medical College Hospital, reviewed by Zhu Lan); the original study based on a national survey gives different proportions among middle-aged and older women (see 10.14). Different populations and different years: the numbers cannot be carried straight across.

docs.title: 10.14 Sources for this chapter
docs.text:
• Department of Science Popularization, Chinese Medical Association, Incontinence: What Examinations Will the Doctor Do (《尿失禁，医生会做哪些检查》) (author: Lou Wenjia, Peking Union Medical College Hospital; reviewed by Zhu Lan), 2024-10-14: the three types of incontinence (stress, urge, mixed) and the roughly 60%/10%/30% split among women patients, and how to keep a voiding diary. https://www.cma.org.cn/art/2024/10/14/art_4584_59002.html checked 2026-10
  • Mayo Clinic, Urinary Incontinence — Diagnosis and Treatment: the types, what measuring post-void residual urine means, how to do pelvic floor exercises (hold 5 seconds up to 10, at least three sets a day), bladder training and timed voiding, environmental changes for functional incontinence, skin care (clean with a towel, air-dry, barrier cream, don't irrigate frequently). https://www.mayoclinic.org/zh-hans/diseases-conditions/urinary-incontinence/diagnosis-treatment/drc-20352814 [accessed 2026-10]
  • Mayo Clinic, Overactive Bladder — Symptoms and Causes: the definition of nocturia (waking to urinate more than twice a night), frequency (more than 8 times in 24 hours), the list of causes (neurological disease such as stroke, diabetes, enlarged prostate, constipation, menopausal hormonal change, and others). https://www.mayoclinic.org/zh-hans/diseases-conditions/overactive-bladder/symptoms-causes/syc-20355715 [accessed 2026-10]
  • Mayo Clinic, Kegel Exercises: A Guide for Women: how to find the muscle, tightening and holding, at least three sets of 10 to 15 a day, results in weeks to months, don't practice while urinating. https://www.mayoclinic.org/zh-hans/healthy-lifestyle/womens-health/in-depth/kegel-exercises/art-20045283
  • Mayo Clinic, Kegel Exercises for Men: Understanding the Benefits. https://www.mayoclinic.org/zh-hans/healthy-lifestyle/mens-health/in-depth/kegel-exercises-for-men/art-20045074
  • Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSKCC, in Chinese), Pelvic Floor Muscle (Kegel) Exercises for Men: finding the muscle, tighten 5 seconds and relax 5 seconds, repeat 10 times, at least 3 rounds a day, don't do it while a catheter is in place, helps with urine control and sexual health. https://www.mskcc.org/zh-hans/cancer-care/patient-education/pelvic-floor-muscle-kegel-exercises-males
  • Union Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Health Education Prescription for Stress Urinary Incontinence (《压力性尿失禁健康教育处方》): the definition of stress urinary incontinence; causes (childbirth, age, pelvic organ prolapse, obesity); the ICI and NICE recommendation to try non-surgical treatment first; pelvic floor muscle training (Kegel) as first choice. https://www.whuh.com/info/18711/57611.htm

(Clause as reproduced.) https://gf.cabr-fire.com/article-47428.htm

docs.title: Chapter 11 · Can't sleep, pain, no drive, loneliness
docs.text:
Three in the morning, you wake up and can't get back to sleep. There's a dull ache in your lower back, and turning over doesn't get you away from it. The room is very quiet. Someone asked you during the day how you were doing, and you said, "Pretty good."

These four things usually arrive together: sleeping badly, hurting, having no drive, and having no one to talk to. And they are the easiest things in the world to wave away with one sentence: put up with it, it'll pass.

docs.title: 11.1 What this chapter is for
docs.text:
Sleeping badly, hurting all the time, feeling empty inside, nobody to talk to — looked at one at a time, each of them seems like "normal for old age." Each of them can in fact be treated, and they tangle into each other: pain keeps you from sleeping, bad sleep pulls your mood lower, a low mood makes you less willing to go out, staying in makes you lonelier, and loneliness makes the pain and the sleeplessness worse again.

This chapter is not going to tell you to look on the bright side. It gives you a few things you can do today, and a few phone numbers you can call when something goes wrong. Of these four things, one cannot be endured and cannot wait — that is 11.8.

docs.title: 11.2 Can't sleep? Don't go looking for a sleeping pill yet
docs.text:
• What it costs: one outpatient visit; adjusting your daily rhythm takes a few weeks to show (money: the price of one registration | time: a few weeks | effort: none | asking anyone: easy)
  • In short: The older you get, the less deep sleep you have, the more often you wake at night, and the earlier you wake in the morning. That is normal; it is not an illness. What needs looking at is not "sleeping short" but whether your days are being dragged down: no energy, poor memory, mood falling apart.
  • What you can do: ① First separate "sleeping short" from "can't sleep" — it is worth investigating as a real problem only if it goes on for weeks, several nights a week, and affects your days; ② bring the "my medicines" sheet from Chapter 6 and ask the doctor whether anything you take is making you drowsy or foggy at night; ③ whether a sleeping pill can be used, which one, and for how long, the doctor decides. The general principle for medicines in older people is one less rather than one more, start at the smallest dose, don't take it long term.
  • Where this comes from: B | China's 2025 insomnia guideline from the Chinese Sleep Research Society recommends "non-drug therapy first for insomnia in older adults" official wording. A sleeping pill can get you to sleep faster, but in older people it costs you daytime drowsiness and falls when you get up at night, and there are also people who need one short term under a doctor's care.
  • Who this is for: who it holds for: people who wake often at night but still hold up during the day — don't treat it as an illness yet; people whose days have already collapsed, with their mood sliding down too, need to be seen.
  • What you get back: Independence — no longer afraid of "sleeping on pills, getting more muddled the more I sleep, falling more easily the more I sleep."
  • How this works in China: Register at a sleep clinic, or psychiatry and psychology, or neurology. To find out whether your area has a dedicated sleep clinic, call the hospital and ask.

docs.title: 11.3 Nail down your wake-up time, cut the nap to half an hour
docs.text:
• What it costs: nothing; what you change is your habits (money: nothing to pay | time: every day | effort: none | asking anyone: not needed)
  • In short: Sleepiness is built up by being awake during the day; once your daily rhythm is scrambled, you have no sleepiness left at night. Catching up on sleep during the day, and lying in bed scrolling on your phone, both take the night's sleep apart.
  • What you can do: ① Fix your wake-up time — however late you slept the night before, get up at the same time the next morning; this is the most important one; ② naps no longer than half an hour, and none after three in the afternoon; ③ go outside in the morning sun for twenty or thirty minutes, so your body knows it is daytime; ④ no strong tea or coffee after midday, and in the three hours before bed don't eat too much and don't drink alcohol; ⑤ the bed is for sleeping only — lie down, can't sleep, get up and sit for a while, and go back when you are sleepy.
  • Where this comes from: C | These items are the "sleep hygiene, stimulus control, sleep restriction" parts of cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), and they are also part of the first-line regimen recommended in China's 2025 edition of the insomnia guideline official wording. But done here and there they do little; done as a program, with a doctor or therapist guiding you, is what holds.
  • Who this is for: who it holds for: most people who sleep badly. People who get up several times a night, feel dizzy and weak in the legs during the day, or snore and stop breathing in their sleep should be checked for those first, and not just have their daily rhythm adjusted.
  • What you get back: Independence — no longer afraid of "lying there with my eyes open at night, and being foggy all day."
  • How this works in China: quite a few hospital sleep clinics and psychiatry and psychology departments can do CBT-I, and there are self-guided versions on your phone; ask your local hospital first whether it has one.

docs.title: 11.4 Pain is the kind he says "it's nothing" about
docs.text:
• What it costs: a pair of eyes, the ones you already have (money: nothing to pay | time: as usual | effort: none | asking anyone: easy)
  • In short: Older people mostly don't say they are in pain. He says "it's nothing," and you can see it anyway: he walks slower, holds the rail going up and down stairs, his face is set tight, he eats less, he doesn't want to go out, he turns over and over at night.
  • What you can do: Don't ask the vague "where does it hurt"; ask about specifics: what hurts first thing when you get up, which movement takes the most effort, are you walking slower than six months ago. Take a sheet of paper and write down when it hurts, how long it lasts, what movements make it worse. If he says "old problem, I'll tough it out," say this: tell me clearly where it hurts and when, and I'll go ask the doctor — you don't have to carry it yourself.
  • Where this comes from: B | The prevalence of chronic pain among Chinese adults aged 60 and over is 35.71% (based on the 2008–2015 CHARLS survey, 27 859 people), and the most common is low back pain, at 13.09% third-party research.
  • Who this is for: who it holds for: older people who can still speak. Pain that comes on suddenly, is very sharp, stays in one fixed place, or comes with weight loss or waking from pain at night — don't take it for an old problem, get it checked. Sudden chest pain, abdominal pain, or severe back pain: see Chapter 8 first.
  • What you get back: Independence + dignity — no longer afraid of "hiding the pain and pretending it's nothing, until I can't walk."
  • How this works in China: see the next item.

docs.title: 11.5 Chronic pain: don't buy painkillers and tough it out yourself
docs.text:
• What it costs: one outpatient visit (money: the price of one registration | time: half a day | effort: a bit tiring, you have to get to the hospital | asking anyone: easy)
  • In short: Pain that lasts more than three months is itself an illness that needs treating, not a fate you grit your teeth through. What is causing it, and how it can be handled, is something someone has to sort out for you.
  • What you can do: ① Write the place it hurts, the times it hurts, what movements make it worse, and what you have taken onto one page; ② where to register: geriatrics, the pain clinic, rehabilitation, or the specialty that matches the site (joints to orthopedics, nerve pain to neurology or the pain clinic); ③ take that page and ask the doctor three things: what is causing this pain, what options are there, when should I come back for review; ④ for painkillers you take long term, have the doctor look at them regularly, and don't raise the dose yourself.
  • Where this comes from: C | "Chronic pain needs its cause sorted out and needs handling on several fronts" is common practice. Which method to use, the doctor decides.
  • Who this is for: who it holds for: people who have hurt for more than three months and whose sleep and going out are already affected. Long-term painkillers need watching for stomach and kidney problems, and they are also no reason to skip going to a doctor (see Chapter 6).
  • What you get back: Independence + dignity — no longer afraid of "hurting too much to move, and going out less and less the more it hurts."
  • How this works in China: most hospitals at tier 2 and above have a pain clinic; some cities run pain care in the community. To find out which hospital you want and whether it has a pain clinic, call the hospital and ask.

docs.title: 11.6 Having no drive inside is an illness that can be treated
docs.text:
• What it costs: one outpatient visit plus a few follow-ups (money: registration plus medicine | time: a few weeks | effort: none | asking anyone: you have to, it is a little embarrassing, you have to be willing to admit that you feel bad)
  • In short: In old age, having no drive, not wanting to do anything, always saying you are useless — this often gets taken as "that is just what getting old is like." It is an illness, and it can be treated. Older people who have it often don't say they feel awful either; they say again and again that something in their body is wrong, and test after test finds nothing.
  • What you can do: Check yourself against these: more than two weeks with no drive, things you used to love doing left undone, sleeping badly and eating little, saying over and over "I'm useless," "I'm a burden on you," hurting here and there with no cause found. If you match several of them, go and register once at psychiatry and psychology. Don't hand someone "look on the bright side" as medicine, and don't block them with "it's not that bad."
  • Where this comes from: B | In 2023 about 14.75% of adults aged 70 and over had a mental disorder, most commonly anxiety or depression [official wording, WHO]; among Chinese middle-aged and older people aged 45 and over, the detection rate of depressive symptoms is 23.61% (2018 CFPS survey, CES-D scale, with the 80th percentile as the cut-off) third-party research. Depression in late life often has physical discomfort as its main complaint.
  • Who this is for: who it holds for: people who have been flat for two weeks and can't pull out of it. You have to tell the difference: low spirits after someone close has just died, or after a heavy blow, are normal and will ease slowly; sinking further and further and not being able to get up needs to be seen. If there is any thought of suicide, or a hint of one, don't wait any longer — go straight to 11.8.
  • What you get back: Relationships + independence — no longer afraid of "it isn't him making a fuss about it, he's ill and nobody is taking it seriously."
  • How this works in China: see 11.9 and 11.10.

docs.title: 11.7 Loneliness is itself a medical problem
docs.text:
• What it costs: time, and the bit of energy it takes to go out (money: not much money | time: every week | effort: none | asking anyone: easy)
  • In short: Loneliness is not just a mood; the harm it does the body is real: your chances of getting ill, of becoming confused, and of dying early all go up. Like smoking, it can be managed as a health risk.
  • What you can do: ① First admit that it is real; don't block it with "you've got plenty of people around, you just like to complain"; ② break "having someone with me" into something concrete: a fixed outing once a week (chess, a walk, doing the shopping with someone), one fixed person you can talk to; ③ use what is already there: community activities, the university of the third age, a choir, eating with others at the community canteen; ④ if you live alone, or your spouse has just died, set yourself one rule: every day somebody knows how I am today (one phone call, one knock on the door).
  • Where this comes from: B | The World Health Organization lists social isolation and loneliness as key risk factors for mental health problems in later life, affecting about one quarter of older people [official wording, WHO]; the WHO Commission on Social Connection's 2025 report estimates that loneliness is linked to about 871,000 deaths a year [official wording, WHO]. The US Surgeon General's 2023 advisory compared the mortality effect of social disconnection to smoking 15 cigarettes a day third-party research.
  • Who this is for: who it holds for: people who live alone, who have been widowed, who moved to a big city to follow their children (the parents who came to look after grandchildren), whose circle of friends broke up after retirement. Being on your own and being lonely are not the same thing: some people live quietly alone and do well, and some are surrounded by people and are still lonely.
  • What you get back: Relationships — no longer afraid of "nobody around, carrying it on my own."
  • How this works in China: community activities for older people, the university of the third age, community canteens; people who moved to a big city with their children have one more hurdle — medical insurance that doesn't travel, and fitting in (see Chapters 15 and 17).

docs.title: 11.8 "Living is pointless" has to be heard as meant
docs.text:
• What it costs: one serious answer, one phone call (money: nothing to pay | time: this moment | effort: none | asking anyone: easy, put down the taboo about "don't say unlucky things" first)
  • In short: When an older person says "living is pointless," "I'd be better off dead," "I'm a burden on you," many people let it go past them, taking it for grumbling, for fishing for attention. Those words usually are not fishing for attention. Once an older person has made up their mind, they are often very determined, and there is little room to turn back.
  • What you can do: ① Take it in, don't cut across it, don't say "you're overthinking it"; ② ask one question straight out, "Have you thought about not going on living" — asking does not plant the idea, it gives them a way out; ③ if the person is in front of you, don't leave, and put away anything around that could be used to hurt themselves; ④ get help at once: call a psychological assistance hotline, or take them straight to the nearest hospital emergency department or psychiatric department; ⑤ go with them once to be seen in psychiatry, and don't carry it alone.
  • Where this comes from: A | Depression is a risk factor for suicide in older people, and in older people with depression the suicidal thoughts are more stubborn, the plans more complete, and the success rate higher (Expert Consensus on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Depressive Disorders in Late Life (2025 Edition) (《老年期抑郁障碍诊疗专家共识（2025 版）》) official wording). In 2013 the suicide mortality rate in China's 80-and-over group was 73.39 per 100,000, far above the standardized rate for the whole population of 9.08 per 100,000 (Chinese Journal of Epidemiology 2017, based on Global Burden of Disease GBD2013 estimates) third-party research.
  • Who this is for: who it holds for: anything of this kind, from anyone, has to be taken seriously, and all the more for people who live alone, who have been widowed, who have just been diagnosed with a serious illness, or who have long-term pain. This section writes only recognition and where to get help; not one word about method or detail.
  • Hotlines (save them into your phone now): ① the national unified psychological assistance hotline 12356, set up by the National Health Commission; the official requirement is for a person to answer at least 18 hours a day, and many places run it round the clock official wording; ② the Hope 24 hotline 400-161-9995, 7×24-hour life-crisis intervention third-party research; ③ the Beijing psychological assistance hotline 010-82951332, answered by a person 24 hours third-party research. If someone is in danger right now, call 120 or 110.
  • What you get back: Relationships — no longer afraid of "missing that cry for help and regretting it for the rest of my life."
  • How this works in China: the hotlines can be called from anywhere in the country; for what other numbers exist locally, go and ask at the community health center or the mental health center.

docs.title: 11.9 Going to psychiatry: mostly outpatient; admission is about risk
docs.text:
• What it costs: one registration (money: the price of one registration | time: half a day | effort: none | asking anyone: you have to, it is a little embarrassing, you are afraid of being labeled)
  • In short: Going to psychiatry does not mean you are "crazy." Being seen for depression, anxiety and insomnia is like being seen for high blood pressure — you are going to get treated. When an older person goes, it is best if someone in the family goes along.
  • What you can do: ① Which department to register with: the psychiatry or psychology department of a general hospital (some are called clinical psychology, some psychosomatic medicine), and one with a geriatric psychiatry department is better; if there isn't one, register with geriatrics or neurology first and ask them to refer you; ② what the family can do: beforehand, write the symptoms, how long it has been going on, what medicines have been taken, and whether anything hopeless has been said lately onto one page and hand it to the doctor; during the consultation don't jump in to answer for the older person — let them speak, and when they can't go on, you fill in; ③ the difference between outpatient and inpatient: most mild and moderate cases are seen as outpatients with regular follow-up; where there is serious suicide risk, hallucinations or delusions, not eating or sleeping to the point of wasting away, or things getting worse despite outpatient care, the doctor will suggest admission — admission is to keep watch on the risk and adjust treatment in one concentrated stretch, and there is nothing shameful in it; ④ go to follow-ups on time, don't stop the medicine yourself, and give it a few weeks to work — it doesn't work after one day.
  • Where this comes from: C | "Mostly seen as outpatients, admitted only when severe" is common practice. Expert Consensus on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Depressive Disorders in Late Life puts psychotic symptoms — hallucinations, delusions, catatonia, stupor — among the indications for urgent psychiatric intervention, and notes that for patients with suicide risk, refusal to eat, or psychotic symptoms, doctors have more active treatment options; where things get worse on outpatient care and any of this appears, the doctor will suggest admission official wording. Who is admitted and who is seen as an outpatient is for the doctor to assess.
  • Who this is for: who it holds for: people with depression, anxiety, insomnia, heavy suspiciousness, or clearly worsening memory. When an older person has been through department after department and nothing is found, don't forget to think of psychiatry and psychology.
  • What you get back: Dignity + relationships — no longer afraid of "being taken for crazy, and dragging it out instead of going to be seen."
  • How this works in China: see 11.10.

docs.title: 11.10 How this works in China: care points, mental health prevention doctors, hotlines
docs.text:
• Elderly psychological care points: the National Health Commission ran the "Elderly Psychological Care Action" from 2022 to 2025; by the end of 2025, in principle every county (city, district) has at least one community or village with an elderly psychological care point, which does a mental health assessment for residents aged 65 and over, with priority for older people who are in financial difficulty, empty-nest (living alone), left behind, disabled (or with dementia), or in families under the family planning special-support scheme official wording. Go and ask at the community: do we have one of these here?
  • Community mental health prevention doctors: where a household has someone with a severe mental disorder (schizophrenia, for example), the community health center or township health center has a designated prevention doctor responsible for follow-up management; it is part of the national basic public health service, with at least 4 follow-up visits a year official wording. Go and ask at the community: who is the prevention doctor, and how do we get on the register?
  • Hotlines: see 11.8, and get them into your phone first.
  • These services are spread unevenly from place to place; asking once at the community is more accurate than guessing at home. What the local office says most recently governs. The arrangements above are the mainland-China ones — state-run community health centers, and a public health register kept by the local authorities. If you are reading this outside mainland China, the nearest counterpart is the community mental health team and your local crisis line; the structures differ, and this book does not judge which is better.

docs.title: 11.11 If you can only do one thing today
docs.text:
Save 12356 and 400-161-9995 into your phone and into your parents' phones. Then, at some quiet moment, ask your parents one question: "How have you been sleeping lately — is anything hurting?"

Ask first; don't wait for them to bring it up. Once that question is out, at least one of the four things stops being "put up with it" and becomes "somebody knows."

docs.title: 11.12 If you are reading this for a parent
docs.text:
How to say it to him: don't start with "are you depressed?" Start from something concrete: "I've noticed you haven't wanted to go downstairs these past few weeks," "you said you can't sleep — how long has that been going on?" Put the word "illness" later. About pain, don't ask "where does it hurt" either; say "let me take you to get it looked at."

What you can still do when he won't agree (no need for his nod): ① save 12356 and 400-161-9995 into his phone first, and into yours; ② quietly note what time he goes to bed, how many times he wakes at night, how much he eats, and whether he has said anything hopeless, make it into one page, and show it to a doctor when needed; ③ go to the community and ask whether there is an elderly psychological care point, and what the prevention doctor can help with; ④ the day he is willing to go to the hospital, go with him, write the symptoms on paper first and hand it to the doctor, and don't leave him alone to tell the doctor "I'm fine."

docs.title: 11.13 What I am not sure about in this chapter
docs.text:
• The nationwide figures on suicide in older people come from 2013 (based on Global Burden of Disease GBD2013 estimates), which is on the early side; for a more recent national picture, the latest mortality surveillance should govern.
  • How sleep clinics, pain clinics, geriatrics and psychiatry are set up and how you register differs from hospital to hospital; whether there is one locally and how to get in, the local situation governs.
  • The 23.61% comes from the 2018 China Family Panel Studies (CFPS), where the age cut-off is 45 and over and the scale is CES-D (with the 80th percentile as the cut-off); it, the WHO figure of "14.75% of those aged 70 and over with a mental disorder," and CHARLS-type surveys do not use the same sampling or the same scale, and cannot be compared with each other.

docs.title: Chapter 12 · What to Eat Every Day: Rebuilding the Table at Sixty and Seventy
docs.text:
The table of a person living alone shrinks quietly.

Same bowl, half the rice. The meat comes round and the chopsticks go around it. Vegetables go from three dishes to two, then to one. Nobody ever said "I'm not eating" — it's just that each meal is a little slower than the last.

What this chapter does is lay that table again. The core of it is one counter-intuitive thing: as you get older, your body's need for a few things does not go down. It goes up.

docs.title: 12.1 What this chapter solves
docs.text:
Lots of people hold to one belief: when you are old, eating less and eating plain — that is what looking after yourself means.

Half right. The portion can be smaller, and the direction is not wrong, but there are a few things you have to pay closer attention to than you did when you were young: protein, so the muscle doesn't quietly go; water; and the everyday business of salt, oil, alcohol and soup, community canteens, and supplements.

docs.title: 12.2 As you get older you need more protein, not less
docs.text:
• What it costs: No extra money. What changes is the combination (money: next to nothing | time: from this meal onward | effort: none | do you have to speak up: no)
  • In short: The Dietary Guidelines for Chinese Elderly (2022) (《中国老年人膳食指南（2022）》) has one sentence that matters: for older people, especially the very old, the need for energy falls, while the need for protein and calcium rises official wording. As you age your body gets worse at turning protein into muscle — the same chopstick-load of meat, you can't use half of it.
  • What you can do: Make "protein at every meal" the floor. Breakfast should not be only congee and pickles: add an egg and a glass of milk. Lunch and dinner each get one "solid dish" — meat, fish, shrimp, eggs, tofu, taking turns.
  • Where this comes from: A | the guidelines put that sentence into their core recommendations; the direction is clear.
  • Who this is for: sixty and up; it holds for most people. The exception is people already diagnosed with kidney disease who have to limit protein — how much they eat is up to the doctor.
  • What you get back: independence — no longer afraid of "can't eat, gets thin, never puts it back on"
  • How this works in China: see 12.12.

docs.title: 12.3 How to spread protein across three meals: an egg at breakfast, one solid dish at lunch and dinner
docs.text:
• What it costs: A few extra yuan a day (money: next to nothing | time: a few minutes per meal | effort: none | do you have to speak up: no)
  • In short: However much protein you eat at one sitting, there is only so much the body can take at a time to build muscle; spread across three meals it works better than one big load. The guidelines' combination: 1 egg and 1 glass of milk at breakfast, and at lunch and dinner a meat dish, vegetables, and one soy product official wording.
  • What you can do: In the morning, 1 egg and 1 glass of milk (or soy milk); at lunch and dinner a "palm-sized" piece of meat or fish, or a block of tofu; fish or seafood at least twice a week; if digestion is poor, mince the meat and steam it with egg, pick the fish bones out clean, stew the tofu soft.
  • Where this comes from: A | from the food-combination advice in The Dietary Guidelines for Chinese Elderly (2022).
  • Who this is for: people who can eat normally. People who can't swallow, or who choke, need a different way of doing it — see Chapter 7.
  • What you get back: independence — no longer afraid of "I'm not eating less, and the strength still drains away"
  • How this works in China: available in any food market or supermarket; when you can no longer cook, see 12.9 on community canteens.

docs.title: 12.4 If you want to cut down on salt: low-sodium salt works, but first see whether you are one of those people
docs.text:
• What it costs: One bag of low-sodium salt, a little dearer than ordinary salt (money: next to nothing | time: once | effort: none | do you have to speak up: no)
  • In short: The guideline's ceiling is less than 5 grams of salt a day official wording. Just adding less salt often doesn't help: the saltiness comes from sodium, and you can put the salt spoon away while the sodium in soy sauce and pickles stays. Low-sodium salt replaces part of the sodium chloride with potassium chloride — less sodium, the saltiness still there.
  • Evidence: a study called SSaSS, run in 600 villages in northern China with 20,000 people, swapped household salt for low-sodium salt and saw 14% fewer strokes, 13% fewer cardiovascular events, and 12% fewer premature deaths (third-party research: The George Institute for Global Health, 2021).
  • But low-sodium salt is not for everyone: the extra potassium has to be excreted by the kidneys. People already diagnosed with hyperkalemia must not use it — the guidelines give a "strong recommendation against"; people with impaired kidney function (eGFR<60 ml/min/1.73 m²) who want to use it must ask a specialist first — a "weak recommendation against" official wording Guidelines for the Promotion and Application of Low-Sodium Salt in China (《中国低钠盐推广应用指南》), Chinese Journal of Preventive Medicine, 2024. People taking potassium-sparing diuretics (such as spironolactone), ACE inhibitors, ARBs for blood pressure, or potassium supplements should also be careful: these drugs raise blood potassium on their own, so low-sodium salt is not advisable, or only under a doctor's guidance official wording Jilin Provincial Health Commission, 2021. If you are one of these, ask your doctor first: "With my kidneys and my blood potassium, can I use low-sodium salt?"
  • What you can do: Switch to low-sodium salt; go easy on cured and pickled things, pickles, cured pork; add the salt just before the dish comes off the heat, or lift the flavor with scallion, ginger, garlic, vinegar.
  • Where this comes from: B | that swapping salt lowers risk is backed by SSaSS; which people must not swap is checked against the list above — don't generalize.
  • Who this is for: with normal kidney function and no high blood potassium found, the swap is worth it. Bad kidneys, or on those drugs: don't swap; if you really want to, ask the doctor first.
  • What you get back: independence — no longer afraid of "a pinch of salt at every meal feeding the blood pressure"
  • How this works in China: low-sodium salt is in any supermarket; if you're unsure, bring it up at your next clinic visit.

docs.title: 12.5 The other three items on the table: oil, alcohol, soup
docs.text:
• What it costs: A graduated oil-control jug (money: next to nothing | time: once | effort: none | do you have to speak up: yes — and it's a bit awkward, refusing a drink costs face)
  • In short: The guidelines suggest no more than 25 to 30 grams of cooking oil a day; people with chronic disease should not drink, and if an adult does drink, no more than 15 grams of alcohol a day official wording. As for soup, stop believing "soup builds you up": however long you stew the meat, the protein barely dissolves into the soup — most of it stays in the meat (third-party research: The Paper, popular science).
  • What you can do:
  • Oil: switch to the measuring jug; steam, boil, stew and dress more, fry less; skim the oil off the top of soup; order less takeout and fewer oily ready-made dishes.
  • Alcohol: don't keep liquor in the house; pour the baijiu into a smaller cup, or simply drink tea instead; at the table, don't press drinks on others and don't accept them. If you are on medication, alcohol can clash with blood-pressure, blood-sugar, sleeping and pain medicines — best not to drink.
  • Soup: if you drink the soup, eat the meat even more, and make the soup thinner; people with gout or high uric acid should go easy on rich meat broth.
  • Where this comes from: B | less oil, limited alcohol, no faith in soup — the directions are all standard; there is no single trial showing "switch to an oil jug and you get fewer diseases."
  • Who this is for: most people. With gout or high uric acid, little or no rich meat broth; on the drugs above, if you can skip the alcohol, skip it.
  • What you get back: independence — no longer afraid of "putting away too much oil, salt and alcohol without noticing"
  • How this works in China: oil jugs and salt spoons are in supermarkets and online; whether you can drink at all — ask the family doctor at the community health centre.

docs.title: 12.6 When the teeth are bad or you can't swallow, soften the food first, then talk about eating enough
docs.text:
• What it costs: One dental visit, or a change in how you cook (money: one registration fee and up | time: once | effort: none | do you have to speak up: yes — and it's a bit awkward)
  • In short: People who can't chew meat often simply stop touching it, and the protein goes with it. But "can't chew" is mostly a matter of teeth, and has nothing to do with "should eat less meat." Fill the missing teeth, adjust the dentures, and the appetite often comes back.
  • What you can do: Deal with the teeth first — go to the dental department or the prosthodontics department; if it can't be solved for now, change how you cook: mince the meat and steam it with egg, pick the fish bones out clean, stew the tofu soft; if you choke or can't swallow, do texture modification and eating posture properly (details in Chapter 7).
  • Where this comes from: C | this book's own check (2026-10): fixing the teeth first and changing the cooking second is the common-sense care path; swallowing is handled in Chapter 7.
  • Who this is for: people with missing teeth, ill-fitting dentures, or a swallowing problem. With repeated choking, meals getting slower, weight going down — don't just change the cooking, see a swallowing specialist.
  • What you get back: independence + dignity — no longer afraid of "wanting to eat and not being able to chew"
  • How this works in China: the dental department of a general hospital, or a dental hospital; dentures and implants are mostly out of pocket — ask the price and the plan first.

docs.title: 12.7 Don't believe "thin in old age is worth more than gold": first work out whether you're losing muscle or fat
docs.text:
• What it costs: One bathroom scale, a few minutes (money: next to nothing | time: one minute | effort: none | do you have to speak up: no)
  • In short: "Thin in old age is worth more than gold" has done real harm. What you actually need to guard against as you get older is muscle quietly going. Losing weight is not necessarily good — what you lost may be muscle, which means throwing away your strength and your independence along with it.
  • What you can do: Same time, same scale, once a month; watch the trend, not the single number; a drop of more than 5% in half a year means ask a doctor official wording NHS UK lists losing 5% to 10% of body weight in half a year as a main sign of malnutrition; if the weight is falling but the waist hasn't changed much, or strength is clearly down (can't open a bottle cap, can't lift things), what you're losing is more likely muscle.
  • Where this comes from: B | weight trend, calf circumference and grip strength are the usual screening measures for sarcopenia; how to read the numbers is for a doctor to judge.
  • Who this is for: sixty and up, especially anyone who has visibly got thinner in the past half year without dieting. A sudden drop over a short period, with feeling unwell, is more likely an illness — see a doctor first. More in Chapter 2.
  • What you get back: independence — no longer afraid of the illusion that "thin is good"
  • How this works in China: weigh yourself at home and write it down; whether more tests are needed — ask the family doctor at the community health centre.
  • One admission: muscle loss never hurts, which is exactly why it gets taken for "just getting old."

docs.title: 12.8 How to make sure of your water for the day: not thirsty does not mean not short of water
docs.text:
• What it costs: A graduated water bottle (money: next to nothing | time: all day | effort: none | do you have to speak up: no)
  • In short: As you get older the thirst "reminder bell" gets dull; you may not feel thirsty while the body is already short of water. Clinical Hydration Practice Guidelines for Older Adults in China (2024 edition) (《中国老年人临床水化实践指南（2024版）》) lists older people as a high-risk group for dehydration, and notes that as many as 73.3% of older people in China don't reach the recommended daily water intake official wording.
  • How to do it (no fixed number of milliliters given): don't wait until you're thirsty — drink at fixed points: after getting up, after each meal, before bed; keep the bottle where you can see it and reach it; use urine colour as a ruler — dark means drink; the water in soup, congee, milk and fruit counts too; go easy on sweet drinks.
  • Where this comes from: C | this book's own check (2026-10): the hydration guidelines recommend keeping a "drinking diary," and list fixed times, watching urine colour, and choosing plain water or weak tea as the methods.
  • Who this is for: most people. The guideline's intake recommendation comes with a condition attached — "unless in special circumstances"; with heart failure, kidney failure, edema or hyponatremia, how much you drink is up to the doctor, and more is not better official wording that guideline.
  • What you get back: independence — no longer afraid of "that dizzy spell in summer was really dehydration and heat stroke"
  • How this works in China: a graduated cup is enough to start; with heart or kidney disease, take "how much should I drink a day" to the clinic and ask.

docs.title: 12.9 The community canteen: how to find one, what you eat there, and why some shut down
docs.text:
• What it costs: The price of a meal, usually cheaper than eating out (money: next to nothing | time: one meal | effort: none | do you have to speak up: easy to bring up)
  • In short: Cooking for one and eating alone is where people most easily make do, and after a while of making do the protein, the vegetables and the water all drop off with it. The community canteen solves exactly this: company, a hot meal, and a price someone keeps an eye on. A sample survey found that 22.1% of older people have a need for meal assistance official wording Ministry of Civil Affairs policy interpretation.
  • How to find one: ask at the residents' committee or the sub-district eldercare service centre: "Is there a meal-assistance point in this area?" Shanghai calls them "community elders' canteens," Guangdong calls them "elders' dining halls."
  • What you can eat: ordinary food with meat and vegetables; many places have tiered subsidies for the very old, the disabled and those living alone, cheaper than eating out official wording the policy interpretation above; by the end of 2025 Shanghai had built 521 community elders' canteens and 1977 meal-assistance points official wording Shanghai Civil Affairs Bureau.
  • Why some can't keep going: the policy interpretation itself points it out — everywhere reports that "meal-assistance services are hard to sustain": the margin on a meal is thin to begin with, it is held up by subsidy, and if the subsidy is small and not enough people come, it slides from thin profit into loss and shuts after a while. The funding formula is "individuals put in a little, enterprises give up a little, government subsidizes a little, collectives add a little, society donates a little," with the aim of being "profitable and sustainable" official wording.
  • What you can do: Ask three questions: is there a meal-assistance point, can I get a subsidy, and can it be delivered to my home when I can't walk.
  • Where this comes from: A | the policy and the local figures can both be checked; but subsidy standards and coverage differ by place and change fast.
  • Who this is for: people who get around easily and live near a canteen get the most out of it. Rural and remote areas are still poorly covered.
  • What you get back: relationships + independence — no longer afraid of "eating alone, and making do a little more each time"
  • How this works in China: ask at the residents' committee, the sub-district eldercare service centre, or the community eldercare service station; subsidies depend on the locality.

docs.title: 12.10 When the community canteen can't hold up, what you do yourself
docs.text:
• What it costs: An hour or two at the weekend (money: next to nothing | time: once a week | effort: a bit tiring | do you have to speak up: easy to bring up)
  • In short: Not everyone has a canteen nearby, and not every canteen survives. Rather than waiting for a table, build one yourself.
  • What you can do: Batch cooking — cook once at the weekend, portion and freeze, three days' worth; ready-made components — washed vegetables, frozen dumplings, ready-to-eat chicken breast, unsweetened yogurt, throw together a meal with protein in it; cook with neighbors — two or three households take turns cooking and share; home delivery — ask the community whether there is any.
  • Where this comes from: C | this book's own check (2026-10): this is caregiving and living experience, with no trial to measure it; but it holds up the very solid problem of "not eating enough."
  • Who this is for: people living alone, and people for whom cooking is a strain. If family can lend a hand, the point is to share the cooking out, not to carry it alone.
  • What you get back: independence + relationships — no longer afraid of "from the day I can't cook, I start eating too little"
  • How this works in China: first ask the community about meal delivery, then talk to neighbors you know about cooking together.

docs.title: 12.11 Supplements and "nutrition products": when you really need them, and when you're buying peace of mind
docs.text:
• What it costs: Don't rush to spend (money: can be high or low | time: one consultation | effort: none | do you have to speak up: easy to bring up)
  • In short: If you can eat, and eat enough, protein powder, calcium tablets and vitamins are mostly unnecessary — the money buys peace of mind. The people who genuinely need supplements are, first, those who don't eat enough (illness, recovery, poor appetite), and second, those a doctor has found to be deficient; in that case they can be used under a doctor's or dietitian's guidance official wording.
  • One iron rule: health foods are not medicine. The State Administration for Market Regulation requires the packaging to carry the line "health food is not medicine and cannot replace medicine in the treatment of disease" official wording Guidelines on Warning Wording on Health Food Labels (《保健食品标注警示用语指南》), in force since 2020.
  • What you can do: Before buying, ask three questions: am I actually short of this, has a doctor said so, and could it stand in for my medicine; keep a list of the supplements you take and hand it to the doctor along with your medicines at the next visit, to see whether they collide (Chapter 6); when it's a sales lecture, or someone calling it a "sure cure," walk out.
  • Where this comes from: B | "food first, supplements under a doctor's or dietitian's guidance" is the standard line in both the guidelines and market regulation.
  • Who this is for: if you can eat, spend the money on food first. If you genuinely don't eat enough, or you're recovering, supplements may help; which one and for how long — ask a doctor.
  • What you get back: money + dignity — no longer afraid of "being talked into buying a cupboard full of useless things by a lecture and an acquaintance"
  • How this works in China: for medicines look for "Guoyao Zhunzi" (the national drug approval number), for health foods look for the "blue hat" logo — only the former is medicine; if you're unsure, take it to a doctor.

docs.title: 12.12 How this works in China
docs.text:
Everything in this section is the mainland-China system: the people you ask are the residents' committee, the sub-district office and the civil affairs department — roughly the counterpart of a local senior-services or eldercare office in the US or UK, with the names differing from city to city.

  • Nutrition clinic: In big hospitals nutrition is handled by the clinical nutrition department, and older people by the geriatrics department; the 2024 Chinese Expert Consensus on the Outpatient Management Standards for Sarcopenia in the Elderly (《老年人肌少症门诊管理规范中国专家共识》) already recommends that hospitals at all levels open sarcopenia clinics. When you register, say three things clearly: how much weight has gone in half a year, how long you have been eating less, and whether you choke.
  • Community canteens and meal subsidies: Ask at the residents' committee, the sub-district eldercare service centre or the community eldercare service station whether there is a meal-assistance point in this area, whether you can get a subsidy, and whether it can be delivered to your home. Standards differ by place; go by the latest local wording.

docs.title: 12.13 If you can only do one thing today
docs.text:
Go and weigh yourself once now, and put it in the notes app on your phone. Then at tonight's dinner, add one "solid dish" to the table — an egg, a glass of milk, a palm of meat or fish, or a block of tofu, just one, set it in the middle.

Weighing yourself gives you a baseline; every weigh-in after that is compared against it. Adding one solid dish gives your body that bit of protein we just talked about. Neither takes more than a few minutes.

docs.title: 12.14 If you are reading this for your parents
docs.text:
How to say it out loud. Don't say "you eat too little, too plainly" — in his ears that means "you're old, you're finished." Put it another way, and put yourself in it too: "I've been learning a new way of eating — an egg at breakfast, a bit of meat or tofu at lunch and dinner. Shall we try it together?" Or come at it from the cooking end: you cook, put the steamed minced meat with egg and the soft-stewed tofu on the table, don't comment, and he'll pick up his chopsticks himself.

What you can still do when he disagrees. Three things that don't need his agreement: every time you visit, bring a meat dish he can chew, or cook one in front of him; keep a record in your phone of his weight each time, how much he eats, and whether he chokes, and hand it to the doctor at the next appointment; go to the community once and ask about meal assistance — is there a canteen in this area, can it be delivered to the home, is there a subsidy for someone in his situation. The more concrete your preparation, the less you have to rely on persuading him.

docs.title: 12.15 What I am not sure about in this chapter
docs.text:
• The names and addresses of each city's "elders' canteen map" and "meal-assistance point finder" differ a lot, and I have not checked them one by one; asking at the residents' committee or the sub-district eldercare service centre is more reliable than hunting for a web portal.
  • Subsidy standards and coverage for community canteens and elderly meal assistance are local policy and change fast; this chapter only writes "where to ask," not specific amounts.
  • For The Dietary Guidelines for Chinese Elderly (2022) this chapter quotes the "Core Recommendations" and the "Illustrated Explanation of the Balanced Diet Pagoda" published on the Chinese Nutrition Society website; I have not checked each point against the page numbers of the printed book.
  • This chapter gives no doses and makes no diagnoses. Whether to switch to low-sodium salt, how much water to drink, whether to take supplements — all of it depends on your own illnesses and medicines. Ask a doctor or dietitian.

docs.title: 12.16 Sources for this chapter
docs.text:
Checked 2026-10-10.

  • The Dietary Guidelines for Chinese Elderly (2022) (《中国老年人膳食指南（2022）》) (Chinese Nutrition Society): higher protein needs, 1 egg and 1 glass of milk at breakfast, 1 meat dish and 1 soy product at lunch and dinner, fish or seafood at least twice a week, one portion of milk a day, and other food combinations. On the Chinese Nutrition Society's dietary guidelines site, "Core Recommendations of The Dietary Guidelines for Chinese Elderly (2022)" (《〈中国老年人膳食指南（2022）〉核心推荐》) (2022-11-22): http://dg.cnsoc.org/article/04/op9MZtpBQHehHCo0SSqsmw.html ; "Illustrated Explanation of the Balanced Diet Pagoda for Older People in China" (《中国老年人平衡膳食宝塔图示解析》) (2024-05-16): http://dg.cnsoc.org/article/04/VQocp-iITrutzK4FILTdTw.html ; Chongqing Center for Disease Control and Prevention, "The Dietary Guidelines for Chinese Elderly (2022), Please Read" (《〈中国老年人膳食指南（2022）〉，请查收》) (2023-05-15): https://www.cqcdc.org/index.php?a=shows&catid=252&id=2651
  • Dietary Guidelines for Chinese Residents (2022) (《中国居民膳食指南（2022）》), guideline 5, "less salt, less oil, control sugar, limit alcohol" (salt <5 g, cooking oil 25–30 g, people with chronic disease should not drink, adults who drink ≤15 g of alcohol a day): Chinese Nutrition Society. http://dg.cnsoc.org/article/04/ApX3_ozGTmSoqQaFFh5z_Q.html
  • Low-sodium salt and stroke: the SSaSS study (14% fewer strokes, 13% fewer cardiovascular events, 12% fewer premature deaths), The George Institute for Global Health fact sheet The China Salt Substitute and Stroke Study (SSaSS) (2021): https://www.georgeinstitute.org/sites/default/files/documents/factsheet_the-china-salt-substitute-stroke-study-ssass-august-final.pdf ; the paper itself: Neal B, et al. Effect of Salt Substitution on Cardiovascular Events and Death. NEJM, 2021 (rate ratios: stroke 0.86, major cardiovascular events 0.87, all-cause death 0.88): https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2105675
  • Who low-sodium salt is for and who must not use it: Guidelines for the Promotion and Application of Low-Sodium Salt in China (《中国低钠盐推广应用指南》) (Health Risk Assessment and Control Society of the Chinese Preventive Medicine Association, Chinese Nutrition Society, Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention, et al.; Chinese Journal of Preventive Medicine 2024,25(8):957-973) — "strong recommendation" for people with hypertension, people at high cardiovascular risk, and middle-aged and older people; "strong recommendation against" for people with hyperkalemia; "weak recommendation against" for impaired kidney function (eGFR<60 ml/min/1.73 m²), who must follow the specialist's advice. The original is in Chinese Journal of Preventive Medicine 2024, vol. 25, no. 8, pp. 957–973 (the guidelines' own site serves the PDF unreliably to outside networks, so what is given here is a directly openable explainer, from the nutrition department of Guangdong Provincial People's Hospital): https://www.thepaper.cn/newsDetail_forward_29932346
  • People who should not use low-sodium salt, and the related drugs (potassium-sparing diuretics such as spironolactone, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, potassium supplements): Jilin Provincial Health Commission, "Is Low-Sodium Salt Good? Is It for Everyone?" (《低钠盐好不好 是不是人人适用？》) (2021-12-23): https://wsjkw.jl.gov.cn/zdzt/jkkp/202112/t20211223_8338994.html checked 2026-10-10
  • The nutrition in soup is mostly in the meat, and rich broth is high in purines: The Paper, "When You Stew Soup, Is the Nutrition in the Meat or in the Soup?" (《炖汤的时候，营养到底在肉里还是汤里？》): https://www.thepaper.cn/newsDetail_forward_3482987
