  • Drinking water and dehydration in older people: Clinical Hydration Practice Guidelines for Older Adults in China (2024 edition) (《中国老年人临床水化实践指南（2024版）》) (Geriatrics Branch of the Chinese Medical Association, Geriatric Medicine Physicians Branch of the Chinese Medical Doctor Association; Chinese Journal of Geriatrics 2024, 43(8):954-969): older people are a high-risk group for dehydration; as many as 73.3% of older people in China do not reach the adequate daily water intake; recommends keeping a "drinking diary" and drinking mainly plain water or weak tea; the intake recommendation carries the condition "unless in special circumstances (heart or kidney failure, edema, hyponatremia)." Full text (Chinese Medical Association, directly openable): https://medphy.yiigle.com/uploads/guide_html/6731.html checked 2026-10-10
  • Policy on meal assistance for the elderly: Action Plan for Actively Developing Meal Assistance Services for the Elderly (《积极发展老年助餐服务行动方案》) (Minfa [2023] No. 58, the Ministry of Civil Affairs and 10 other departments, 2023-10) and the Policy Interpretation by the Eldercare Services Department of the Ministry of Civil Affairs (22.1% of older people have a need for meal assistance; tiered subsidies; "individuals put in a little, enterprises give up a little, government subsidizes a little, collectives add a little, society donates a little"; "meal-assistance services are hard to sustain"). Full text of the plan (the Chinese government portal, directly openable): https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/zhengceku/202310/content_6911233.htm ; policy interpretation (China National Committee on Aging, directly openable): https://www.cncaprc.gov.cn/xxzcfg/10030934.jhtml checked 2026-10-10
  • Shanghai community elders' canteen figures: Shanghai Civil Affairs Bureau, "Upgrading and Strengthening 50 Community Elders' Canteens" (《为 50 家社区长者食堂提质增能》): by the end of 2025, 521 community elders' canteens and 1977 meal-assistance points for the elderly had been built: https://mzj.sh.gov.cn/26shitang/index.html
  • Warning wording on health foods: Guidelines on Warning Wording on Health Food Labels (《保健食品标注警示用语指南》) (State Administration for Market Regulation announcement No. 29 of 2019, in force from 2020-01-01), packaging must carry "health food is not medicine and cannot replace medicine in the treatment of disease": https://www.samr.gov.cn/zt/ndzt/2019n/bjspjsqjxcjwljxyjsckpxc/zcfg/art/2023/art_fdb7d9ff30a7467eab4a2da27e697cf6.html
  • Weight-loss signal (losing 5%–10% in half a year is a main sign of malnutrition): NHS UK, Malnutrition (2023-05), second-hand, see the sources for Chapter 7.

Note: the key figures in this chapter all carry a tier (official wording / third-party research / this book's own check); there are no untiered figures. No dosages are given and no diagnoses are made. The links were checked and open as of 2026-10.

docs.title: Chapter 13 · How to Move Every Day
docs.text:
After dinner you go downstairs and walk two laps around the compound. Ten minutes in, your knees ache, and you remember the line you hear all the time — "you're old now, don't push yourself" — so you turn around and go home. The next day, two laps again. The third day it rains, you don't go. A month later, the two laps are gone too.

Nobody stopped you. You stopped yourself. This chapter is for starting again, and it's also for you if you're the one trying to get your parents moving.

docs.title: 13.1 What this chapter solves
docs.text:
Of the four accounts, movement is the cheapest one, and the only one that improves several at once: whether you can still dress yourself and get out of bed (independence), your mood, your blood sugar and blood pressure, whether you can sleep at night. Most pills fix one thing. Move once, and several things move together.

Two sentences stop most people: "to exercise you have to run, and work up a sweat," and "you're old, don't go messing about with exercise." Both are wrong, and wrong in different ways. Below I take the two sentences apart, then give you numbers you can measure, movements you can do sitting down, and where it's worth doing them.

docs.title: 13.2 Move once, and four accounts get paid down together
docs.text:
• In short: in the World Health Organization's guidelines, regular physical activity lowers the risk of all-cause death, death from cardiovascular disease, high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes and falls in older adults, and improves anxiety and depression, cognition and sleep (official wording). No drug covers that many at once.
  • Where this comes from: A | this is the direction written into both the WHO guidelines and China's guidelines.
  • Who this is for: people who can still walk a few steps on their own. If you're already bedbound and can't get up, the way you move is completely different and a rehabilitation therapist has to set it (see 13.12).
  • What you get back: independence — you stop fearing "every day I can do a little less"
  • How this works in China: it costs nothing. Whether you need tests, and how to train, ask the contracted family doctor at your community health centre (see 13.12).

docs.title: 13.3 What stops you isn't your body, it's two sentences
docs.text:
The first sentence: "to exercise you have to run, and work up a sweat." A lot of people hear "exercise" and think of running, and decide "I can't run, so never mind." The aerobic activity in the guidelines means endurance activity — walking, cycling, swimming, dancing — and brisk walking counts (official wording). Running is only one of them, not the entry threshold.

The second sentence: "you're old, don't go messing about with exercise." It sounds like concern. It does the most damage. You're afraid of falling, so you stop moving; the less you move, the weaker your legs and the worse your balance, and the more likely you are to fall. The Chinese CDC's core messages on preventing falls list "being so afraid of falling that you just stop moving" as something to avoid (official wording).

Put the two sentences together and you're wedged between them: the big movements aren't allowed, and the small ones don't count.

  • In short: it isn't that you don't want to move; it's that you haven't found the movement that is "small enough, and not embarrassing". 13.6 is for that.
  • Where this comes from: A | the World Health Organization and the Chinese CDC say the same thing (official wording).
  • Who this is for: people who are afraid of falling, afraid of looking foolish, afraid they can't do it.
  • What you get back: dignity — you stop fearing "I want to move, and I feel it's too late, that I can't"
  • How this works in China: "don't stop moving because you're afraid of falling" sits inside the Chinese CDC's twelve-character fall-prevention slogan — "exercise, accept that you're older, make your home age-friendly, treat early" (see Chapter 5).

docs.title: 13.4 Four kinds of movement, each with its own job
docs.text:
Kind What it covers Examples Aerobic heart and lungs, blood pressure and blood sugar, mood, sleep brisk walking, cycling, swimming, square dancing Resistance (strength) strength in your legs, enough to stand up and hold yourself sit-to-stand, heel raises, resistance bands, water bottles Balance catches you when your body can't adjust in time standing on one leg, heel-to-toe walking, tai chi Flexibility joints that can reach, and reach far shoulder rolls, calf stretch
  • In short: aerobic keeps the "engine" running; resistance keeps the "frame" standing. The falls in Chapter 5 are mainly covered by resistance and balance; this chapter only fills in the amounts.
  • Where this comes from: A | the four-way split is the framework both the WHO and China's guidelines use (official wording).
  • Who this is for: everyone. Walking without any strength work is the most common imbalance in older people.
  • What you get back: independence — you stop fearing "I've been at this for ages and I don't know which thing I'm training"
  • How this works in China: tai chi classes and fitness groups in the community, in parks, at the university of the third age bring aerobic and balance together.

docs.title: 13.5 Working out the weekly amount
docs.text:
This is the one set of numbers to remember from this chapter.

  • Aerobic: 150 to 300 minutes a week at moderate intensity, or 75 to 150 minutes at vigorous intensity, and a mix of the two counts as well (official wording World Health Organization, 2020; Physical Activity Guidelines for the Chinese Population (2021) (《中国人群身体活动指南（2021）》)).
  • Resistance: at least 2 days a week, working the main muscle groups (official wording same as above). The British Journal of Sports Medicine pooled 16 studies: 30 to 60 minutes of strength training a week goes with about 10% to 20% lower risk of all-cause death (third-party research Momma et al., 2022).
  • Balance plus strength (multicomponent): at least 3 days a week (official wording World Health Organization, 2020).
  • Broken down to a day: 150 minutes divided by 5 is 30 minutes a day, 5 days a week (official wording Healthy China Initiative, National Fitness Action).
  • What counts as moderate: score it by feel, 5 to 6 out of 0 to 10 — you can talk, but you can't sing (official wording). The Healthy China Initiative gives another way to work it out: a heart rate of 64% to 76% of your maximum, where maximum heart rate is 220 minus your age (official wording).

  • How older people adjust: the adult recommendation applies to older adults too; if your body won't allow 150 minutes of moderate intensity a week, move as much as you can (official wording Physical Activity Guidelines for the Chinese Population (2021) (《中国人群身体活动指南（2021）》)).

  • Where this comes from: A | on amount, intensity and frequency, the international and the Chinese guidelines line up.

  • Who this is for: people who can stand and walk. If you can barely move at all, or a certain movement hurts as soon as you try it, put the numbers down and go ask a doctor (see 13.7, 13.12).
  • What you get back: independence — you stop fearing "I don't know how much counts as enough, so I just don't move"
  • How this works in China: this set of numbers is in the Physical Activity Guidelines for the Chinese Population (2021) (《中国人群身体活动指南（2021）》); whether you're getting enough, ask the contracted family doctor at your community health centre.

docs.title: 13.6 Do it sitting down, do it holding the chair back, do it while the TV is on
docs.text:
One rule first: if any of the feelings in 13.7 shows up afterwards, stop.

Sitting down (after a meal, in front of the TV, anytime):

  • Seated leg raise: sit up straight, slowly lift one leg until it's level, hold 3 seconds, put it down. 8 to 12 times per leg, 2 sets.
  • Ankle pumps (flex and point): heel on the floor, toes up, then press down. 20 times. If you sit a lot, this helps the blood in your calves flow back.
  • Seated desk push: both hands on the edge of the table, push slowly for 5 seconds, then relax. 5 times.
  • When to stop: sharp pain inside the knee, numbness in the leg, a racing heart.

Holding the back of a chair (closer to daily life):

  • Chair-supported heel raise: hold the chair back firmly, slowly rise onto your toes and come down. 10 to 15 times, 2 sets.
  • Chair-supported single-leg stand (balance): hold the chair back firmly, lift one foot and stand for 10 to 30 seconds, 3 times per leg; once you're steady, slowly take away the support of your hands.
  • Chair-supported sit-to-stand: stand up from the chair and sit down again (see 5.8), 8 to 12 times, 2 sets, using your hands as little as possible.
  • When to stop: unsteady on your feet, dizzy, tightness in the chest.

While the TV is on:

  • When the ads come on, get up — march in place or go and pour a glass of water. Two minutes.
  • Wall sit: back against the wall, feet moved half a foot forward, slide down to a height that doesn't hurt, hold 10 to 30 seconds.
  • Use a resistance band or a bottle of water for curls and shoulder presses, while you watch. 2 sets.
  • When to stop: heat or pain at the front of the knee, your lower back can't hold it.

Flexibility (save it for the end): shoulder rolls, calf stretch, seated arm raises. Slow; stop when it feels "a bit tight"; don't bounce.

  • Where this comes from: C | the movement categories are taken from the few the WHO and the Chinese CDC mention (heel raises, sit-to-stand, standing on one leg and so on); the repetitions and sets follow common practice, and no study has specifically tested "how many sets you should do while watching TV".
  • Who this is for: people who can sit unaided and stand holding something. If you use a walker, have had a joint replaced, or have severe osteoporosis, have a rehabilitation therapist run through the movements once first.
  • What you get back: independence — you stop fearing "I want to move and I don't know which movement to start with"
  • How this works in China: you can do these at home. If you want someone watching you do them, ask at the community activity room or the community health centre whether they have fitness instruction.

docs.title: 13.7 If any of this shows up, stop and ask a doctor first
docs.text:
During exercise, if any one of these shows up, stop at once — don't push through: tightness, pressure or pain in the chest, or pain that runs up into the shoulder, arm or jaw; dizziness, black spots before your eyes, feeling sick; breathlessness so bad you can't speak, a racing or irregular heartbeat; breaking out in cold sweat.

Beijing's 120 service warns that chest tightness during exercise needs to be taken seriously, and that you should call 120 promptly (official wording Beijing Municipal Health Commission, 2022). If speech goes slurred, or one side of your body goes weak, call 120 straight away.

In these situations you have to ask a doctor before you move: a heart attack or stroke recently, or just out of hospital; blood pressure or blood sugar badly out of control; cancer that has spread to bone (bone metastases), or a fracture recently; fever, infection, or an acute illness that isn't over yet. For people with chronic disease, China's guideline states plainly that you should consult a doctor before exercising and exercise under professional guidance (official wording Physical Activity Guidelines for the Chinese Population (2021) (《中国人群身体活动指南（2021）》)).

If you're a cancer patient, a Chinese expert consensus draws this line more finely: with bone metastases, or a pathological fracture or spinal cord compression already present, exercise is not suitable; with bone metastases, or known or suspected osteoporosis, don't do routine muscle strength and muscular endurance testing; with an acute systemic illness, fever, or the acute phase of a cerebral hemorrhage or cerebral thrombosis, don't move yet (third-party research Chinese Expert Consensus on Exercise Therapy for Patients with Malignant Tumors (2022 edition) (《中国恶性肿瘤患者运动治疗专家共识（2022 年版）》)).

  • Where this comes from: B | "chest tightness or a racing heart means stop at once and get medical care" is written repeatedly in official material; the bone-metastasis and acute-fever lines are set out item by item in a Chinese expert consensus (see sources); "a fracture recently" is standard orthopaedic rehabilitation practice, and I found no specific guideline line for it.
  • Who this is for: everyone; if you have a history of heart disease, diabetes, osteoporosis or cancer, the line has to be drawn tighter.
  • What you get back: independence and money — you stop fearing "I'm afraid something will happen while I'm exercising, and I don't know where the red line is"
  • How this works in China: for an emergency, call 120; read these lines out to your contracted family doctor at the community health centre and ask them to draw the line for you once.

docs.title: 13.8 "Stop when it hurts" is wrong, but you have to tell which pain
docs.text:
"Don't move if it hurts" and "train through the pain" are equally bad. The thing to separate is two kinds of pain.

  • Soreness from doing it right: the soreness sits in the muscle, arrives a day or two after, and eases when you move a little or rest. It's usually the response to a new movement or a heavier load.
  • Pain that means stop: the pain sits in a joint (knee, shoulder), shows up during the movement, catches or feels like a needle when you move in a certain direction, or gets worse the more you train and swells. This is your body calling stop.

  • How to use it: if it's muscle soreness, you can carry on at low intensity; if it's sharp joint pain, catching or swelling, stop and go to orthopaedics or rehabilitation.

  • Where this comes from: C | "separate muscle soreness from joint-injury pain, and the latter needs medical care" is standard sports-medicine practice; hospitals' patient-education material says the same, and there is no graded guideline.

  • Who this is for: people who can tell "sore" from "pain" and can still move normally. If you wake at night with the pain, if it's bad enough to disturb sleep, or if there's fever with it, see a doctor soon.
  • What you get back: independence — you stop fearing "it hurts when I move, and I don't know whether I should tough it out"
  • How this works in China: register at an orthopaedics or rehabilitation medicine outpatient clinic; the contracted family doctor at the community health centre can also make a first judgment and refer you upward.

docs.title: 13.9 Sitting too long is the most underrated item
docs.text:
Sitting too long is harmful in itself, and whether you also go and exercise is a separate account. In 2020 the WHO put "sit less" into its guidelines as its own item for the first time: sit less, and replace sitting with activity of any intensity — even light intensity counts (official wording).

  • What you can do: cards, TV, the car, the phone — set an alarm, get up for two minutes every hour: pour a glass of water, walk a lap, do a few heel raises.
  • A small randomized crossover trial gives a finer version: 11 people each sat for a full 8 hours under several "break up the sitting" schedules, and only the "get up and walk for 5 minutes every 30 minutes" arm had a clearly smaller rise in blood sugar after meals; for blood pressure a smaller dose was enough, and getting up to walk for 1 minute every 60 minutes lowered it the most (third-party research Duran et al., 2023).
  • Where this comes from: B | "less sitting is better" is the line both international and Chinese guidelines agree on; the "5 minutes every 30" comes from a small randomized crossover trial of only 11 people, looking at that day's blood sugar and blood pressure response, and the long-term outcome isn't settled (see 13.15).
  • Who this is for: everyone who sits a lot. But for people who can't stand at all (wheelchair, bedbound), the substitute is different — ask a rehabilitation therapist.
  • What you get back: independence and money — you stop fearing "a day of sitting, and by evening my legs are swollen and my blood sugar is up"
  • How this works in China: no equipment at all; an alarm on your phone is enough.

docs.title: 13.10 Only a few things are worth buying, and only a few places are worth going
docs.text:
• Small money worth spending: a pair of well-fitting shoes with a treaded sole that isn't too soft (how to choose, see 5.6); a resistance band (a few dozen yuan); an empty water bottle filled with water as a dumbbell.
  • What can wait: big items like a treadmill or a spin bike. Before you buy, ask yourself: the last time you stuck with exercise, how many weeks did it last?
  • Don't spend extra on these: fat-shaking machines, "qi and blood circulation" machines, "unblocking" massagers. Claims like these are the manufacturer's, not evidence ([manufacturer's claim]).

  • Where to go: if you only want to walk, the compound, the park, the walking trails — free is best; if you want balance and strength work and you're afraid of falling, go where there are people — the community activity room, a fitness group; if you have heart disease or diabetes, or have had surgery, one session of an "exercise prescription" or at a rehabilitation clinic is worth the money (see 13.12).

  • Where this comes from: C | "put your money into a good pair of shoes and a resistance band" is standard advice, with no controlled study behind it.

  • Who this is for: people on a limited budget who are just thinking of starting. If you already train regularly at a gym, you don't need to change where you go to save money.
  • What you get back: money — you stop fearing "I buy a pile of equipment and it all ends up gathering dust"
  • How this works in China: the free equipment points in parks and communities and the classes at the university of the third age are the cheapest tier; ask the residents' committee where the nearest ones are.

docs.title: 13.11 Stick with it through a partner and a record
docs.text:
Getting moving isn't hard. What's hard is going on the third day, when it rains.

  • Hang it on a habit you already have: tie movement to something you do every day and can't forget. "After dinner I go downstairs." "After the news, one set of sit-to-stands."
  • Find a partner: fix on one person, and whoever doesn't show owes the other one. Square-dance teams, walking groups, tai chi groups are all partners.
  • Keep a record: tick a calendar, count steps on your phone. It doesn't have to be exact; a tick is enough.

  • Start small: the WHO's advice is to do a little first, then slowly add amount and time (official wording). 5 minutes today is more likely to survive than a plan to "start Monday, 30 minutes a day".

  • Where this comes from: C | these behavioral methods are standard practice; which one works best differs from person to person.

  • Who this is for: everyone. If you've been diagnosed with depression, or the pain keeps you from getting downstairs, deal with that first (see Chapter 11, 13.12).
  • What you get back: relationships — you stop fearing "on my own, I move twice and then stop"
  • How this works in China: find a partner in a community fitness group or a square-dance team; ask the residents' committee or the community eldercare service station how to join.

docs.title: 13.12 How this works in China
docs.text:
• The equipment in housing compounds and parks is mostly free. The state is pushing a "15-minute fitness circle" in urban communities, meaning a place to exercise within 15 minutes' walk or cycle; a 2025 survey by the General Administration of Sport found that 90.4% of residents aged 19 and over can reach one within 15 minutes (official wording). Ask the property office or the residents' committee where the nearest equipment point and the bigger parks are.
  • If you want people to move with: community aerobics groups, square-dance teams, tai chi groups, walking groups — mostly in parks, on squares, in community activity rooms. Where to ask: the residents' committee, the community eldercare service station, the university of the third age.
  • If you want to know whether you're moving enough: communities and physical fitness monitoring stations run the national physical fitness test, which measures balance, strength and flexibility, using the National Physical Fitness Test Standards (2023 revision) issued by the General Administration of Sport (official wording). Where to ask: the community health centre, the district physical fitness monitoring station.
  • If you have a chronic disease, have had surgery, or are afraid of falling: register at a rehabilitation medicine or geriatrics department and have a doctor set out an "exercise prescription" once — they cover everything from cardiac rehabilitation to fall-prevention training. Where to ask: the rehabilitation medicine clinic at a tier-3 hospital, or your contracted family doctor.
  • If you're not sure how to apply locally or what it costs: ask the community health centre and the residents' committee. Specific programs and subsidies differ from place to place; go by the latest local wording.

docs.title: 13.13 If you can only do one thing today
docs.text:
Set an alarm on your phone for "get up for two minutes every hour", starting this afternoon.

No changing shoes, no going out. When the alarm goes, stand up and walk about, pour a glass of water, do a few heel raises. Sitting too long is the cheapest thing in this chapter to change, and the one fewest people change.

docs.title: 13.14 If you're reading this for your parents
docs.text:
The most useless sentence in trying to get your parents moving is "you need to exercise more". What he hears is "you're finished".

Say it differently, start with "I": "My back can't take sitting all day lately. Let's walk for half an hour together after dinner — come with me." You're not sending him off to exercise; you need him to keep you company. Older people are more willing to go out for "being needed".

When he won't agree, the things you can do that don't need his agreement: change the environment first — walk the route from his building to the park with him, find the nearest free equipment point and the easiest flat path; find him a partner, don't be his supervisor — help him connect with a group, with someone he knows; whoever can get him out the door does more than a hundred things you say; hang it on his old habits — whatever he does every single day, put the walk right after it; see the doctor when it's a doctor matter — chest tightness, dizziness, bone pain, go with him to register once, and read the lines in 13.7 out to the doctor.

He may not admit it out loud. His body will.

docs.title: 13.15 What I'm not sure about in this chapter
docs.text:
• The "get up and walk for 5 minutes every 30 minutes" arm comes from a small randomized crossover trial of only 11 people, looking at the acute response of blood sugar after meals and blood pressure that same day; whether it translates into fewer illnesses and fewer hospital stays over the long run is not settled, and there is no local research on the equivalent dose for Chinese people. This chapter treats it as a direction, not a precise prescription.
  • The square-dancing randomized controlled trial had a sample that was mostly women (about 78%); the intervention group trained 3 times a week, while the control group had only 3 health-education classes in 12 weeks, so the two groups' contact time was not equal; the authors' own conclusion is "associated", not "causal", and you should be careful about generalizing to men, or about treating it as "square dancing definitely does this".

docs.title: 13.16 Where this chapter's numbers come from
docs.text:
• World Health Organization, WHO guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour (2020-11-25): for older adults, 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity or 75–150 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic activity a week, muscle strength on at least 2 days a week, multicomponent (balance plus strength) training on at least 3 days a week, less sedentary time, and 5–6 on a 0–10 scale as moderate intensity. https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240015128 ; Chinese fact sheet https://www.who.int/zh/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/physical-activity checked 2026-10
  • Physical Activity Guidelines for the Chinese Population (2021) (《中国人群身体活动指南（2021）》) (under the guidance of the Disease Control and Prevention Bureau of the National Health Commission; led by the Chinese CDC and the China Institute of Sport Science of the General Administration of Sport): published in Chinese Journal of Public Health (《中国公共卫生》), 2022, Vol. 38, No. 2, pp. 129–130. Older people's section: the adult recommendation applies as well; keep up balance, flexibility and mobility exercises; if your body won't allow it, increase the activity you can manage as much as possible; people with chronic disease should consult a doctor before exercising. https://www.zgggws.com/cn/article/id/46482813-3205-4c34-a7b9-73bace965e59 checked 2026-10
  • Healthy China Initiative (2019–2030) (《健康中国行动（2019—2030 年）》), National Fitness Action and Older People's Health Promotion Action (Healthy China Initiative Promotion Committee, 2019-07-09): the definition of regularly taking part in physical exercise; moderate intensity equals 64%–76% of maximum heart rate (maximum heart rate = 220 minus age); the national physical fitness test target. https://www.nhc.gov.cn/guihuaxxs/c100133/201907/2a6ed52f1c264203b5351bdbbadd2da8.shtml checked 2026-10
  • National Physical Fitness Test Standards (2023 revision) (《国民体质测定标准（2023 年修订）》) (National Physical Fitness Monitoring Centre, 2023-08-10). https://www.sport.gov.cn/n315/n20001395/c25880704/content.html checked 2026-10
  • Clinical Practice Guidelines for Exercise Intervention to Prevent Disability in Older Adults (2023 edition) (《老年人失能预防运动干预临床实践指南（2023 版）》) (Nursing Group, Geriatrics Branch, Chinese Medical Association, et al.), Chinese General Practice (《中国全科医学》), 2023, Vol. 26, No. 22, pp. 2695–2710, DOI 10.12114/j.issn.1007-9572.2023.0223. https://www.chinagp.net/CN/10.12114/j.issn.1007-9572.2023.0223 checked 2026-10
  • Exercise contraindications for cancer patients: Chinese Society of Nutritional Oncology et al., Chinese Expert Consensus on Exercise Therapy for Patients with Malignant Tumors (《中国恶性肿瘤患者运动治疗专家共识》), Journal of Oncology Metabolism and Nutrition (electronic edition) (《肿瘤代谢与营养电子杂志》), 2022, Vol. 9, No. 3, pp. 298–311 (people with bone metastases plus pathological fracture or spinal cord compression are not suitable for exercise; those with bone metastases or suspected osteoporosis should not have routine strength assessment; with an acute systemic illness or fever, or in the acute phase of cerebral hemorrhage/cerebral thrombosis, don't move yet; its section on exercise contraindications cites the Chinese Expert Consensus on Exercise Therapy for Patients with Coronary Heart Disease (《冠心病患者运动治疗中国专家共识》)). https://www.ejmnc.com/CN/Y2022/V9/I3/298 checked 2026-10
  • Strength training and mortality risk: Momma H et al., British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2022, Vol. 56, No. 13, pp. 755 ff. https://bjsm.bmj.com/content/56/13/755 checked 2026-10
  • Muscle strength, aerobic exercise and all-cause death in older adults: JAMA Network Open, 2023 (US population aged 65 and over). https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2797402 checked 2026-10
  • Dose-response of breaking up sitting: Duran AT et al., Breaking Up Prolonged Sitting to Improve Cardiometabolic Risk: Dose-Response Analysis of a Randomized Crossover Trial, Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, May 2023 (11 middle-aged and older adults in an 8-hour crossover trial: getting up to walk for 5 minutes every 30 minutes clearly lowered the area under the post-meal blood glucose curve; the biggest drop in systolic pressure came from getting up to walk for 1 minute every 60 minutes). https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36728338/ checked 2026-10
  • Community square-dancing randomized controlled trial: Community-based square dancing is associated with improved physical and mental health in older adults: a 12-week randomized controlled trial in China, Frontiers in Public Health, 2026-07-14, DOI 10.3389/fpubh.2026.1758255 (150 people aged 60–79 in Zhengzhou, randomized into two groups of 75, 12 weeks, 3 times a week, 60 minutes a session; the paper's conclusion is "associated"; the sample was mostly women, about 78%, and it was not pre-registered on a clinical trial registry). https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/public-health/articles/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1758255/full checked 2026-10
  • Chest tightness during exercise and 120: Beijing Municipal Health Commission, Weekly First-Aid Topic: Watch for the Potential Risk of "Chest Tightness" After Exercise (《每周急救话题：警惕运动后"胸闷"潜在风险》) (2022-11-21). https://wjw.beijing.gov.cn/bmfw_20143/jkzs/jzjj/202211/t20221121_2863331.html checked 2026-10
  • "15-minute fitness circle" and 90.4%: General Administration of Sport, 2025 National Fitness Activity Survey Bulletin (《2025 年全民健身活动状况调查公报》) (Mass Sports Department, released 2025-12-28) — 90.4% of residents aged 19 and over report having sports facilities within 15 minutes' walk or cycle, 9.7 percentage points higher than 2020 (the "15-minute fitness circle" is basically in place). https://www.sport.gov.cn/n315/n20001395/c29322175/content.html ; release notice https://www.sport.gov.cn/n20001280/n20745751/c29327174/content.html checked 2026-10

docs.title: Chapter 14 · Vaccines, screening and checkup reports: only do what is worth doing
docs.text: Late in the year the phone rings: "Add two tumor markers, it's only a few hundred yuan." You spend close to two thousand. The report comes back with seven or eight arrows pointing up, and one small line at the end: "further examination recommended."

docs.title: 14.1 What this chapter settles
docs.text:
When it comes to checkups, many people carry a default formula in their heads: the more you test, the safer you feel; the more you spend, the more covered you are.

That formula is wrong. With a 2,800-yuan package, the more items get added, the more likely they are to be things you don't need; and a free national checkup is the one many people can't be bothered to go to.

Boiled down to one sentence: which vaccines, which screenings, which items on the report — that depends on your age and your risk, not on the price of the package. The old rule was "more testing can't hurt." At your age one word has to change: some testing does hurt.

docs.title: 14.2 Flu vaccine: one shot a year, given in September–October
docs.text:
• What it costs: a few dozen to one or two hundred yuan, once a year (money: next to nothing | time: once | effort: none | speaking up: not needed); in many cities it is free for people 60 and over.
  • In short: For a young person flu is a miserable week; for you it can be pneumonia and a hospital stay. This shot has to be given every year, and it is the cheapest shot there is.
  • What you can do: Get it every year (the virus changes every year); put it in September–October, before the season; if you miss that window don't give up — you can still get it at any point in the flu season.
  • Where this comes from: A | The Chinese CDC's Technical Guidelines for Influenza Vaccination in China (2026–2027) (《中国流感疫苗预防接种技术指南（2026—2027）》) lists people 60 and over as a priority group for vaccination official wording.
  • Who this is for: Almost everyone over 60; if you have a fever right now, or have had a severe allergic reaction to a vaccine ingredient, ask a doctor first.
  • What you get back: Independence + money — no longer afraid that "one bout of flu will knock my body down"
  • How this works in China: Go to a community health centre or a vaccination clinic; in Beijing it is free for Beijing-registered older people 60 and over (Beijing Municipal Health Commission, 2025-09-11) official wording.

docs.title: 14.3 Pneumococcal vaccine: the 23-valent one after 60
docs.text:
• What it costs: one or two hundred to three or four hundred yuan, usually once in a lifetime (money: next to nothing | time: once | effort: none | speaking up: not needed); in some cities it is free for people 65 and over.
  • In short: Streptococcus pneumoniae is one of the most common culprits in pneumonia in older people. This shot does not prevent an ordinary cold; it prevents the kind of pneumonia that puts you in a hospital bed.
  • What you can do: In China older people usually get the 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23), one primary dose; people with normal immune function usually do not repeat it; if you have high-risk factors and your last dose was more than 5 years ago, you can discuss one more dose with a doctor. The 13-valent conjugate vaccine (PCV13) also protects older people, and the 2024 consensus on pneumonia in older adults recommends the 23-valent and the 13-valent side by side; but in China the 13-valent label's approved population is still children, so use in older people is off-label and has to be assessed by a doctor.
  • Where this comes from: A | Chinese Expert Recommendations on Influenza and Pneumococcal Vaccination in Older Adults (《老年人流感和肺炎链球菌疫苗接种中国专家建议》) (Chinese Journal of Geriatrics, 2018) recommends PPSV23 for people 60 and over official wording; Expert Consensus on the Clinical Diagnosis and Treatment of Pneumonia in Older Adults (2024 Edition) (《老年肺炎临床诊断与治疗专家共识（2024 年版）》) recommends that older people receive PPV23 or PCV13, evidence level ⅠB third-party research.
  • Who this is for: People over 60, especially those with chronic heart or lung disease or diabetes. Which one to get and how many doses — ask the doctor at the vaccination clinic.
  • What you get back: Independence + money — no longer afraid that "one bout of pneumonia puts me in intensive care"
  • How this works in China: Go to the vaccination clinic at a community health centre; in Beijing, Beijing-registered older people 65 and over who have never had the 23-valent pneumococcal vaccine can book, be assessed, and get one dose free (Beijing Municipal Health Commission, 2025-09-11) official wording.

docs.title: 14.4 Shingles vaccine: worth it after 50, but ask about the price and local offers first
docs.text:
• What it costs: two doses, paid out of pocket, list price in the thousand-yuan range; many places are running a time-limited "get one dose free" scheme, with clear start and end dates (money: a fair amount | time: two doses, 2–6 months apart | effort: none | speaking up: easy).
  • In short: Shingles is nicknamed "the snake around the waist" in Chinese. The torment is not the string of blisters; it is the nerve pain that goes on for months after the blisters have healed. The older you are, the more likely you are to get it, and the worse it hurts.
  • What you can do: People over 50 with normal immune function can choose to get the recombinant shingles vaccine, 2 doses 2–6 months apart; people who have had chickenpox or shingles can still get it; it is a self-paid vaccine, so ask about the price and the local offer before you go.
  • Where this comes from: A | The eligible age and the dosing schedule for the two approved vaccines are given in Chinese CDC public information (2025-07-14) official wording.
  • Who this is for: People over 50 with normal immune function benefit most. If your immune function is deficient or you are on immunosuppressants, the live attenuated vaccine is not recommended, and whether you can have the recombinant one has to be weighed with a doctor.
  • What you get back: Independence — no longer afraid that "it burns like fire and stabs like needles, and hurts for months"
  • How this works in China: Go to your local vaccination clinic and pay for it yourself; Inner Mongolia, Shanxi, and some districts of Shanghai have run time-limited "get one dose free" schemes (Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region Disease Control and Prevention Administration, 2025-05-09) official wording. Take Inner Mongolia as an example: for people 50 and over who completed dose 1 between 2025-05-06 and 2025-08-31 and completed the full two-dose course before 2025-12-31, dose 2 was free (not including the per-dose vaccination service fee). Whether your area has such a scheme, and until when, depends on the latest local notice.

docs.title: 14.5 Before and after the shot: anything you are unsure about, ask the doctor at the vaccination clinic
docs.text:
• What it costs: a few extra questions (money: nothing | time: a few minutes | effort: none | speaking up: easy).
  • In short: A sore arm, a bit of fever and tiredness after the shot is mostly normal and passes in a day or two. What you actually need to ask about is what you are unsure of: can I have it with this condition of mine, do the medicines I take conflict with it.
  • What you can do: Before the shot, tell the doctor which medicines you are taking, which illnesses you have, and any past allergies; if you have a fever or an acute illness is flaring up, wait; after the shot, sit there a full 30 minutes before you leave; if you get a high fever that won't come down, a widespread rash, or can't catch your breath, go to hospital at once and say which vaccine you have just had.
  • Where this comes from: B | This is the standard way every vaccination is handled; the specific contraindications depend on that vaccine's label and on your own condition.
  • Who this is for: Everyone. Whether you can have it, and when, only the doctor assessing you on the spot can decide.
  • What you get back: Independence — no longer afraid that "the shot was wrong and something went wrong with me"
  • How this works in China: The doctor at the vaccination clinic assesses you on the spot and asks you to sign an informed-consent form; if you are unsure about anything, ask.

docs.title: 14.6 Colorectal cancer: from 40, scored by risk, stool test first
docs.text:
• What it costs: a stool test is a few dozen yuan, a colonoscopy several hundred to over a thousand (money: some money | time: once | effort: none | speaking up: you have to, and it's a bit embarrassing; a colonoscopy is a bit embarrassing).
  • In short: Polyps in the bowel take many years to turn into cancer, and that window — the time it leaves you — is the best value in all of screening. If you are afraid of a colonoscopy, you can do the stool test first, and have the colonoscopy if it comes back positive.
  • What you can do: The national plan scores you on age, sex, smoking, body-mass index and history among first-degree relatives; a cumulative score of 4 or more counts as high risk; for high-risk people who have never had the disease, screening is recommended from age 40 to 74; colonoscopy is first choice, and if you won't accept it you can choose alternatives such as an annual stool test; if no lesion is found, the next colonoscopy can be 5–10 years later.
  • Where this comes from: A | National Health Commission, Colorectal Cancer Screening and Early Diagnosis and Early Treatment Plan (2024 Edition) (《结直肠癌筛查与早诊早治方案（2024 年版）》) official wording.
  • Who this is for: People with a family history, long-term smokers and people carrying extra weight should be tested sooner. If you already have blood in the stool, a change in bowel habit, or unexplained weight loss, that is not screening — that is a doctor visit, straight to gastroenterology.
  • What you get back: Independence — no longer afraid that "by the time I feel something it is already advanced"
  • How this works in China: A community health centre can do the risk assessment and the fecal occult-blood test; for a colonoscopy you register with gastroenterology. Some cities have free places under the "urban cancer early diagnosis and early treatment programme" — ask at your community health centre.

docs.title: 14.7 Breast and cervical cancer: free screening in many places, ages 35 to 64
docs.text:
• What it costs: free within the government programme (money: next to nothing | time: half a day | effort: none | speaking up: you have to, and it's a bit embarrassing).
  • In short: These are two of the few cancers where screening really does bring the death rate down. The state has provided a free channel, with particular care for rural women and urban women on the minimum living guarantee.
  • What you can do: In many places the free screening is for women aged 35–64, with priority for rural women and urban women on dibao; cervical cancer screening means a gynecological examination plus a primary screen (cytology or HPV testing), and those with a positive result go on to colposcopy and a tissue sample; breast cancer screening means a breast examination plus breast ultrasound, with mammography added if needed.
  • Where this comes from: A | National Health Commission, official interpretation of the Cervical Cancer Screening Work Plan and the Breast Cancer Screening Work Plan (《宫颈癌筛查工作方案》《乳腺癌筛查工作方案》) (2022-01-18) official wording.
  • Who this is for: Women aged 35–64. Outside that age range, or if you already have symptoms (a lump you can feel, abnormal bleeding), book an appointment and get checked directly — don't wait for the free round.
  • What you get back: Independence + dignity — no longer afraid that "it is found too late and I suffer for nothing"
  • How this works in China: Go to a community health centre, a township health centre or the women's federation and ask how to sign up for the local free "two cancers" screening; the latest local wording governs.

docs.title: 14.8 Low-dose CT for lung cancer: for high-risk people only, not everyone
docs.text:
• What it costs: a few hundred yuan a time, generally once a year (money: some money | time: once | effort: none | speaking up: not needed).
  • In short: Low-dose CT is useful, but only for some people. If you don't smoke and have no other risk factors and you have one every year, most of what it finds is a false alarm, while the radiation is real.
  • What you can do: First match yourself against the state's definition of "high-risk": age 50 or over, and any one of the following: a smoking history of 20 pack-years (including people who have quit but for less than 15 years); living with a smoker or working in the same room as one for more than 20 years; COPD; occupational exposure to asbestos, radon or the like for more than 1 year; a parent, child or sibling who has had lung cancer. If you match, in principle one scan a year from 50 to 74.
  • Where this comes from: A | National Health Commission, Lung Cancer Screening and Early Diagnosis and Early Treatment Plan (2024 Edition) (《肺癌筛查与早诊早治方案（2024 年版）》) official wording.
  • Who this is for: Anyone who meets one of the five items above. If you are not high-risk, tumor markers, chest X-ray and PET-CT are not recommended for lung cancer screening — the plan says so in writing.
  • What you get back: Independence + money — no longer afraid that "I skip the scan I need and get one every year that I don't"
  • How this works in China: Most hospitals and checkup centres can do low-dose CT; whether you are high-risk and whether to scan every year is for a respiratory or thoracic-surgery doctor to decide.

docs.title: 14.9 Prostate and thyroid: not recommended as screening for everyone
docs.text:
• What it costs: one tube of blood for PSA is a few dozen yuan, an ultrasound a few dozen to just over a hundred (money: next to nothing | time: once | effort: none | speaking up: easy).
  • In short: These two are practically thrown into a package for free, but "it can be tested" is not the same as "it should be tested". You find a pile of nodules and one number slightly high, then come round after round of unnecessary tests and surgery, and the person is frightened to pieces first.
  • What you can do: Prostate (PSA) is not a matter of everyone getting a tube of blood drawn; domestic guidelines limit it to people with "a life expectancy of more than 10 years and high risk": age 60 or over, or over 45 with a family history of prostate cancer, or over 40 carrying a BRCA2 mutation — and the decision comes only after "fully understanding the pros and cons, together with the specialist's advice". Thyroid: the National Health Commission's diagnosis and treatment guideline states in writing that "screening the general population for thyroid tumors is not recommended"; only people with high-risk factors such as childhood radiation to the head and neck or a history of whole-body radiotherapy need earlier testing.
  • Where this comes from: A | National Cancer Center, Chinese Guidelines for Prostate Cancer Screening and Early Diagnosis and Early Treatment (2022, Beijing) (《中国前列腺癌筛查与早诊早治指南（2022，北京）》); National Health Commission, Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Thyroid Cancer (2022 Edition) (《甲状腺癌诊疗指南（2022 年版）》) official wording.
  • Who this is for: If you have no family history, no symptoms and no doctor's advice, you can skip both. An abnormal result (a high PSA, a thyroid nodule) does not mean cancer; have a specialist read it first, and don't rush into surgery.
  • What you get back: Dignity + money — no longer afraid of "being led along by a package into a pile of unnecessary tests"
  • How this works in China: Being "given" these two in a package doesn't mean you should have them tested; whether to test, register with urology or endocrinology and ask the doctor.

docs.title: 14.10 How to read a checkup report: what to manage, what to watch, and what you get pushed to investigate
docs.text:
• What it costs: one sheet of paper, read slowly (money: nothing | time: half an hour | effort: none | speaking up: not needed).
  • In short: Seven or eight arrows on one report does not mean you have seven or eight diseases. What a package sells is "lots of items", not "the right items".
  • How to do it (start by sorting into three groups): what you should manage is blood pressure, blood sugar, blood lipids, waist circumference and weight — the cardiovascular and metabolic problems you can actually act on, and the ones most likely to kill you; if they are abnormal, manage them the way the doctor says. What you can watch is mild fluctuation in liver and kidney function, a single thyroid nodule, a small cyst; many of these can be rechecked in six months or a year, and there is no need to rush off for a specialist appointment the same day. What you most easily get pushed to investigate further is a raised tumor marker added on along the way, an unexplained small shadow; these often lead to a long chain of "further examinations" that mostly end in nothing, with the money spent and the fright taken.
  • How to spot the pitch: when you hear "add two tumor markers for a few hundred yuan", "big discount on whole-body CT", "limited places, decide today" — slow down a step. Tumor markers are not cancer screening, and the national plan explicitly does not recommend them for lung cancer screening; a whole-body CT with no symptoms mostly finds false alarms, and the radiation is real.
  • Where this comes from: B | "Tumor markers are not used for general cancer screening" is in the national plan; the tiering of indicators and the package sales talk are put together from common practice and public warnings.
  • Who this is for: Anyone who has a checkup report in hand, or who often gets sales calls about checkups. An arrow is not a diagnosis; take the whole sheet to a general practitioner or your family doctor and have it read through, and don't look up single items online.
  • What you get back: Money + dignity — no longer afraid of "lying awake at night over an arrow, or being led along by a package"
  • How this works in China: The general-practice clinic at a community health centre, and your contracted family doctor, can both help you read a checkup report, and can help you judge which items in a package you don't need to add.

docs.title: 14.11 Free health management after 65: the one that costs you nothing
docs.text:
• What it costs: free, the state pays (money: nothing | time: half a day | effort: none | speaking up: not needed).
  • In short: This is the free annual checkup the state gives permanent residents 65 and over. Many people don't know about it, or can't be bothered to go. What you are entitled to, don't drop.
  • What you can do: Go to the community health centre or township health centre for your area, once a year: an assessment of lifestyle and health status; a physical examination including blood pressure and weight, with a rough check of the mouth, vision, hearing and movement; auxiliary tests including complete blood count, urinalysis, liver function, kidney function, fasting blood glucose, blood lipids, ECG and abdominal ultrasound; and health guidance. From 2025 it also adds a frontal chest DR and HbA1c testing, and continues the cognitive-function primary screen.
  • Where this comes from: A | National Basic Public Health Service Standards (Third Edition) (《国家基本公共卫生服务规范（第三版）》), older-adult health management service; the items added in 2025 are in the Notice on Doing the 2025 Basic Public Health Service Work Well (《关于做好 2025 年基本公共卫生服务工作的通知》) (Guowei Jicengfa [2025] No. 7) official wording.
  • Who this is for: Permanent residents 65 and over in the area (whether your household registration is local follows local rules). If you went once and haven't been back for years, you are throwing this state checkup away every year.
  • What you get back: Independence + money — no longer afraid that "I skip the free test I am entitled to and pay for a package instead"
  • How this works in China: Just go to your community health centre or township health centre and ask "how do I book the free checkup for older people, and when will you be in our neighbourhood". The results go into your electronic health record, and places are working on opening that record to you directly; the latest local wording governs.

docs.title: 14.12 If your body is already raising the alarm, don't wait for the next checkup
docs.text:
• What it costs: one doctor visit (money: the cost of one registration | time: half a day | effort: none | speaking up: easy).
  • In short: Screening is for people who feel nothing. If your body is already raising a clear alarm, this is not a screening matter — it is a matter of seeing a doctor as soon as possible.
  • What you can do: If any of the following appears, don't delay and don't wait for next year's checkup: unexplained weight loss — you haven't been starving yourself or dieting, and you have lost several jin over a few months; pain you can't explain, getting worse, worse at night; bleeding — blood in the stool, blood coughed up, blood in the urine, or bleeding again after menopause; a clear drop in weight over a short period, or not being able to eat or swallow; a change in bowel habit that shows no sign of settling.
  • Where this comes from: B | These are signals that recur across countries' "cancer alarm symptoms"; what they actually mean can only be judged by seeing a doctor.
  • Who this is for: Anyone with any one of the above. This is not a "watch it a while longer" situation — especially bleeding and short-term weight loss; register with the right department as soon as possible.
  • What you get back: Independence — no longer afraid that "my body is signalling and I am still waiting for the next package"
  • How this works in China: Register with the relevant specialty, and write on a sheet of paper when the symptom started and how it has changed, and take it to the doctor; if you have a contracted family doctor, call first and ask which department to register with.

docs.title: 14.13 In one sentence: what to test depends on your age and risk, not the price of the package
docs.text:
Keep just one line: whether a test is worth doing depends on your age + your risk factors + the guidelines, not on the price of the package.

Used the other way round it is also a ruler: if the same test is sold to everyone at the same price with the same reason, it was not calculated for you.

So work it out yourself: on your last checkup report, how many items can you say were aimed at which risk of yours? The ones you can't answer for, cross off the next one.

docs.title: 14.14 If you can only do one thing today
docs.text:
Open your phone, look up the number of your community health centre, call it, and ask three questions:

"How do I sign up for the free checkup for people over 65?" "When can I get this year's flu vaccine, and is it free?" "How do I take part in the local 'two cancers' screening and the urban cancer early diagnosis and early treatment programme?"

Three questions, one phone call. The benefits you are entitled to and the shots you should have start with this call.

docs.title: 14.15 If you are reading this for your parents
docs.text:
The hard part of this chapter for you is not not knowing; it is how to get your parents to agree to go.

How to say it out loud. Don't say "you should get the flu vaccine" — that is an order. Switch to a version that saves him trouble: "The community health centre is giving flu vaccines this week. I'll go with you, and we'll get the free checkup for people over 65 done at the same time — half a day and it's done." Turn "you should" into "it's convenient, it's free, and someone goes with you", and the chance he nods is much higher — and the flu shot and the free checkup can often be done in one trip.

What you can still do when he says no. Three things that don't need his agreement: go to the community health centre first and find out exactly how to sign up for the free checkup, the two-cancers screening and the urban cancer early diagnosis and early treatment programme, and write it out on one sheet of paper; collect the family vaccination booklet and all the past checkup reports in one place, and you keep an eye on when the next one is due; when the report comes, don't let him read it alone — sit with him and have a general practitioner read the whole sheet through. If he won't go, you lay the road first; on the day he softens, you won't have to start from zero.

docs.title: 14.16 What I am not sure about in this chapter
docs.text:
• The vaccine guidelines and plans cited in this chapter are written as of the version at the time of publication. The flu vaccine guideline is updated year by year (this chapter uses the 2026–2027 version), and the range of pneumococcal vaccine products is also changing; before you are vaccinated, the vaccination clinic's latest wording for that year governs.
  • The shingles "get one dose free" scheme, the free two-cancers screening and the urban cancer early diagnosis and early treatment programme all vary by place: start and end dates, participating clinics, ages and screening intervals are not identical everywhere. This chapter follows the national plan's 35–64 age range and its priority for rural women and urban women on dibao; locally, the latest notice governs.

docs.title: 14.17 Sources for this chapter
docs.text:
(Date checked: 2026-10-10)

  • Flu vaccine: Chinese CDC, Technical Guidelines for Influenza Vaccination in China (2026–2027) (《中国流感疫苗预防接种技术指南（2026—2027）》) (published 2026-09-02); priority group 2 for vaccination is people 60 and over, and vaccination is recommended in September–October (if you miss that period you can still be vaccinated at any point in the flu season). https://www.chinacdc.cn/jkyj/mygh02/jswj2026/202609/t20260902_1839739.html checked 2026-10
  • Example of free flu vaccination: Beijing Municipal Health Commission, Beijing Begins Flu Vaccination (《北京流感疫苗开始接种》) (2025-09-11), free for Beijing-registered older people 60 and over and others, with September–November the golden window; the same piece states that Beijing-registered older people 65 and over who have never had the 23-valent pneumococcal vaccine can get one dose free. https://wjw.beijing.gov.cn/xwzx_20031/mtjj/202509/t20250910_4198380.html
  • Pneumococcal vaccine: Chinese Expert Recommendations on Influenza and Pneumococcal Vaccination in Older Adults (《老年人流感和肺炎链球菌疫苗接种中国专家建议》), Chinese Journal of Geriatrics 2018, Vol. 37, No. 2, pp. 113-122; recommends the 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23) for people 60 and over. https://cmab.yiigle.com/uploads/guide_html/老年人流感和肺炎链球菌疫苗接种中国专家建议.html
  • Pneumococcal vaccine (updated product options): Respiratory Disease Branch of the Chinese Geriatrics Society, Expert Consensus on the Clinical Diagnosis and Treatment of Pneumonia in Older Adults (2024 Edition) (《老年肺炎临床诊断与治疗专家共识（2024 年版）》), Chinese Journal of Tuberculosis and Respiratory Diseases 2025, Vol. 48, No. 1, pp. 18–34, DOI 10.3760/cma.j.cn112147-20240611-00328: recommends that older people receive the 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPV23) or the 13-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13), evidence level ⅠB. https://rs.yiigle.com/cmaid/1526373 checked 2026-10

  • Example of a shingles subsidy scheme: Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region Disease Control and Prevention Administration, [Infographic] The "Get One Dose Free" Recombinant Shingles Vaccine Reduced-Fee Vaccination Scheme Has Started (《【图解】“打一针免一针”重组带状疱疹疫苗减免接种惠民活动开始啦》) (2025-05-09). https://wjw.nmg.gov.cn/hdjl/zcwdk/ymjz/202505/t20250509_2719906.html
  • Colorectal and lung cancer screening: General Office of the National Health Commission, Notice on Issuing the Lung Cancer Screening and Early Diagnosis and Early Treatment Plan (2024 Edition) and the Colorectal Cancer Screening and Early Diagnosis and Early Treatment Plan (2024 Edition) (《关于印发肺癌筛查与早诊早治方案（2024 年版）和结直肠癌筛查与早诊早治方案（2024 年版）的通知》) (Guoweiban Yijihan [2024] No. 281, 2024-08-27). https://www.nhc.gov.cn/ylyjs/gzdt/202408/42f43b5f0c4c4ebe90c78ee127959b92.shtml
  • Two-cancers screening: National Health Commission, Official Interpretation of the "Cervical Cancer Screening Work Plan" and the "Breast Cancer Screening Work Plan" (《〈宫颈癌筛查工作方案〉和〈乳腺癌筛查工作方案〉文件解读》) (2022-01-18); the target group is women aged 35–64, with priority for rural women and urban women on dibao. https://www.nhc.gov.cn/fys/c100077/202201/13c9867243e0447f88d0a5e33c394d89.shtml
  • Prostate cancer screening: National Cancer Center, Chinese Guidelines for Prostate Cancer Screening and Early Diagnosis and Early Treatment (2022, Beijing) (《中国前列腺癌筛查与早诊早治指南（2022，北京）》), Chinese Journal of Oncology 2022, Vol. 44, No. 1; the definition of the high-risk group, and a recommended screening start age of 60. https://urology.wiki/Guidelines/Cancers/Prostate/2022中国前列腺癌筛查与早诊早治指南.pdf

Diagnostic and treatment techniques and their application (1) Monitoring and screening of high-risk groups" says in the original text: "screening the general population for thyroid tumors is not recommended"; high-risk groups (a history of radiation to the head and neck in childhood, a history of whole-body radiotherapy, and so on) should be screened as early as possible. https://www.nhc.gov.cn/cms-search/downFiles/c19a52f5afca4b4a84d92f140fece9c7.pdf ; a journal reprint appears in Chinese Journal of Practical Surgery 2022, Vol. 42, No. 12, pp. 1343–1357, DOI 10.19538/j.cjps.issn1005-2208.2022.12.02 (https://www.zgsyz.com/zgsywk/CN/10.19538/j.cjps.issn1005-2208.2022.12.02) checked 2026-10

  • Urban cancer early diagnosis and early treatment programme: a major national public-health service programme, providing free high-risk assessment and screening for five cancers — lung, colorectal, upper gastrointestinal, breast and liver (Shenzhen Government Online, 2026 programme launch notice). https://www.sz.gov.cn/ztfw/ylws/wyk_183937/content/post_12882688.html
