docs.title: Chapter 15 · Where to live, and who to grow old with
docs.text:
You have lived in this flat for thirty years. You know where the light is with your eyes shut, and how high the step at the doorway is.

Two things have slowed you down lately. The stairs in the corridor — even holding the handrail, you take them more carefully now. Getting up in the night, you don't quite dare put the big light on. You haven't told anyone — saying it out loud would feel like frightening yourself.

When the time really comes to decide where to live, it usually isn't now. It's after a fall and a discharge from hospital, or after your other half goes first. By then, more often than not, someone else makes that decision for you. This chapter wants to move it forward a little.

docs.title: 15.1 What this chapter settles
docs.text:
Where you live, and who you grow old with, is the most expensive choice of your later life — expensive in money, and more expensive still in the time lost. It is almost always made passively, after something has gone wrong: you fall, and only on discharge do you find you can't get up the stairs; you sell the flat and move to your children's city, and only then find your medical insurance (yibao) is still registered back home and you can't follow what people say.

Each way of living is set out with four things made clear — who it suits, what it really costs (money / time / energy / face), how to try it once first, and when it doesn't hold.

docs.title: 15.2 Home: pass three gates first, then talk about moving the institution's bed into your house
docs.text:
• What it costs: a few hundred yuan for small changes, several thousand to tens of thousands for big ones, subsidy depending on where you live; the service fee for a family eldercare bed is billed monthly on top (money: a fair amount | time: days to weeks | effort: none | do you have to ask: easy)
  • In short: whether the old flat can still be lived in comes down to three things first — whether the building can take a lift; how many steps there are at the door and inside; and whether the toilet is a squat one or a seat.
  • What you can do: ① Lift: find out whether your building can have one added; for multi-storey old blocks there is now legal backing for adding lifts (Article 22 of the Law on Building a Barrier-Free Environment). ② Steps: for the height differences at the entrance, in the corridor and in the bathroom, add a ramp or a handrail. ③ Squat toilet: change it for a seated one, or add a commode chair. Where the money is best spent: the bathroom, the entryway, and the path from the bed to the toilet (see Chapter 5). Try it once first — start with the bathroom only.
  • Family eldercare beds: this isn't buying a bed, it's moving visiting care, age-friendly renovation and smart devices into your home. Do the ability assessment first (GB/T 42195-2022); you qualify only at mild disability or above. Then ask at the community how to apply and who pays.
  • Where this comes from: A + B | the World Health Organization lists home assessment and modification as one of the ways to prevent falls, and the direction of subsidies is in Minfa [2020] No. 86; family eldercare beds have a Ministry of Civil Affairs standard (MZ/T 234-2024), and by the end of 2024 the national program had supported 184 areas in setting up 358,000 of them. But which single change helps how much varies from home to home.
  • Who this is for: People who can still walk on their own and whose home is their own or a long lease; the beds are only for people at mild disability or above. A healthy 60-year-old should deal with steps and lighting first; at 75 with several conditions, start with bathroom handrails, non-slip surfaces and a night light; if you are already disabled, renovation alone isn't enough — you need a bed or home visits lined up.
  • What you get back: Independence + dignity — no longer afraid of "everywhere in the house is a trap" and "I want to stay home, but I'm afraid no one will be looking after me."
  • How this works in China: ask the community, the sub-district office, the district civil affairs bureau — how to apply for renovation and a family eldercare bed, and whether there's a subsidy. Go by the latest local wording.

docs.title: 15.3 Community care: which jobs day care and home visits can take off your hands
docs.text:
• What it costs: a few dozen yuan a time, or covered by government purchase or subsidy (money: barely any | time: per visit | effort: none | do you have to ask: easy)
  • In short: what the community can do for you is mostly the small things — somewhere to go in the daytime, someone to sit with, one meal taken care of; and at home, help with meals, bathing, cleaning, medical visits and getting about. It can't stand in for the night, or for a sudden acute illness.
  • What you can do: go to the community eldercare service station or the sub-district eldercare service centre and ask for a service list. Ask three things clearly: what they can do in your home, how they charge, and from what hour to what hour. A day-care centre is "checked in by day, home at night". Try it once first — book one home-delivered meal or one assisted bath, and see whether anyone actually turns up.
  • Where this comes from: B | home-visit eldercare services have a national standard (GB/T 43153-2023), and day-care centres have their own national standard for basic service requirements. But the density of stations and the quality of service differ a lot from place to place; having a station doesn't mean you can use it, or afford it.
  • Who this is for: People still living in their own home whose mobility isn't too bad. Most healthy 60-year-olds won't need it; at 75 with several conditions it's most useful, especially meals, medical visits and company in the daytime; if you are already disabled you need professional care, and the community usually can't take on the severe end.
  • What you get back: Independence + relationships — no longer afraid of "alone at home, no one in the daytime, and I can't be bothered to cook."
  • How this works in China: ask at the community eldercare service centre; for food, ask about the community canteen (see Chapter 12). Go by the latest local wording.

docs.title: 15.4 Institutions: when these signals appear, it is time to go and look
docs.text:
• What it costs: private ones start at several thousand yuan a month, and the higher the care grade the more you pay; public ones are cheaper but you queue (money: a lot | time: look first, decide later | effort: none | do you have to ask: yes, and it's a little embarrassing)
  • In short: the reason to consider an institution isn't the vague sentence "you're old". It's a few signals: living alone; a fall at night; no longer able to walk, and no longer going out; the person caring for you has given way first; needing professional nursing. Two of these together and you should go and look — don't wait for something to happen.
  • What you can do: look at it the way you'd look at a flat, and ask three things: ① is there a grade rating from the civil affairs department (GB/T 37276-2018)? ② how many residents does each care worker look after, is anyone on duty at night, how far is the nearest hospital? ③ the itemized fees, how leaving early is settled, and whether prepaid fees go into a bank-supervised account. Try it once first — ask whether you can stay a few days on trial. Public institutions mostly take people in extreme difficulty as a backstop: cheap, but you wait your turn; private ones admit you quickly, with wide differences in price and service.
  • Where this comes from: C | "try before you decide" is common practice, but there is no unified national rule on "trial stays / short stays"; policies and fees differ by area, so you can only ask your local civil affairs office or the institution itself. Public institutions have assessment and waiting-list rules (Shanghai, for example — see the sources); private ones have no common yardstick.
  • Who this is for: People whose family care can't hold, or who need professional nursing. For most healthy 60-year-olds it's early; at 75 with several conditions, first look at whether anyone at home can cover 24 hours; once disabled it is often a hard necessity. Some older people end up in an institution because a family member decided it for them.
  • What you get back: Relationships + dignity — no longer afraid of "the day I go down, no one at home can catch me."
  • How this works in China: ask the district civil affairs bureau or your city's eldercare service website; before signing a contract, look at the prepaid fees. Go by the latest local wording.

docs.title: 15.5 Group eldercare among friends: the villa in Hangzhou, and the lessons that came later
docs.text:
• What it costs: sharing the rent (one house split among several people) and splitting living costs (money: some money | time: long-term | effort: a bit tiring | do you have to ask: hard to bring up — this is where people most easily fall out over money)
  • In short: group eldercare (baotuan yanglao) is a few older people choosing to live together, looking out for each other and splitting the costs. In Hangzhou, 13 older people shared one villa, and for a while it was held up as a model. Behind the model there was a price — the first reason these arrangements break up is that people can't agree about money.
  • What you can do: try it once, don't sign up for a long stretch at the start, and above all don't sell your own house to fund it. Live together for a month first, or for one season, and test out three things: who buys the food and cooks, how the costs are split, and who looks after someone who falls ill — write it down before you move in.
  • Where this comes from: B | the Hangzhou house is real (2017, Yuhang, 13 older people, about 500 square metres), and both Xinhua Net and CCTV reported it in 2018. Why this kind of arrangement struggles to last was put more bluntly in a 2021 report (Beijing Evening News, reposted by CCTV.com): the people interviewed said "money is what stops this group holding together", and the report also points out that medical services on the outskirts can't keep up; Wu Danxing, a member of the expert committee on eldercare services at the Ministry of Civil Affairs, said self-organized groups have "nothing binding".
  • Who this is for: People who can still manage on their own, whose temperaments get along, and whose means are roughly similar. Fairly feasible for a healthy 60-year-old; at 75 with several conditions, be careful — a group on the outskirts has no professional medical care and the risk is higher; once disabled, it essentially doesn't hold.
  • What you get back: Relationships + money — no longer afraid of "being too lonely on my own" and of "falling out in the end".
  • How this works in China: there is no official protection for these arrangements, so disputes are yours to guard against — money put in, cost sharing, how someone leaves, who cares for the sick: all written down in black and white. Cizhou Nursing Home in Jiading, Shanghai, ran as a crowdfunded group arrangement for more than ten years before its members moved away one after another; that is one example.

docs.title: 15.6 Mutual-aid eldercare and time banks: Nanjing's ledger, and why it can't carry the weight
docs.text:
• What it costs: volunteering costs nothing; what you trade is future service hours (money: barely any | time: per session | effort: a bit tiring | do you have to ask: easy)
  • In short: a time bank is "today I help you and the hours go into the book; later someone helps me for the same number of hours". The difficulty isn't the bookkeeping. It's whether the hours you deposit can actually be withdrawn later.
  • What you can do: ask at the community whether there is a mutual-aid eldercare site locally, how to register, and how service is recorded and redeemed. Try it once first — do one short session and see whether the platform records it, and whether it pays out. Nanjing can serve as a reference: the civil affairs figures for June 2026 were more than 1,300 sites, covering over 99% of urban and rural communities, 94,000 registered volunteers, 1.47 million orders in total and 920,000 hours of service time stored; in mid-2024 it was 61,000 volunteers and 132,000 service recipients.
  • Where this comes from: A + B | Nanjing's is a citywide platform led by the government (piloted in 2019, renamed in 2023); Shanghai also rolled out an eldercare service time bank citywide in 2021 (Hu Min Yanglao Fa [2021] No. 28). In 2026 the Ministry of Civil Affairs and 10 other departments issued the Opinions on Advancing the Development of Mutual-Aid Eldercare Services (Minfa [2026] No. 11), the first national-level definition of mutual-aid eldercare, setting coverage of urban and rural community eldercare facilities with mutual-aid functions at no less than 70% by 2030. But research generally points to two reasons it can't carry the weight — weak law and supervision, and low participation (see the note at the end of this chapter).
  • Who this is for: The younger old (in their sixties) who are in good health and have time to spare are the best providers; at 75 with several conditions you can do light service and are also most in need of it; if you are already disabled you are a recipient. Don't stake acute nursing care on it.
  • What you get back: Relationships + dignity — no longer afraid of "being useless now that I'm old" and "having no one at hand".
  • How this works in China: ask at the community or the civil affairs office whether there is a mutual-aid eldercare pilot platform locally. Go by the latest local wording.

docs.title: 15.7 Seasonal migration: first work out whether this is eldercare or an investment
docs.text:
• What it costs: ordinary sojourn living means rent or a bed fee by the month or by the season; if someone asks you to "pay a large sum up front and promises to return the principal with interest", that isn't eldercare (money: a fair amount | time: by the season | effort: a bit tiring | do you have to ask: easy)
  • In short: for an older person in reasonable health, wintering in the south and summering in the north is fine — sojourn eldercare (lüju, living somewhere for a season), and what people here call migratory-bird retirement (houniao, the bird that follows the seasons). What you need to guard against is something else — people using the labels "sojourn eldercare" and "migratory-bird retirement" to get older people to put in a large sum of money up front.
  • What you can do: hold three bottom lines. ① Pay only by the month or the season; no large prepayment, no membership fee, VIP card or deposit. ② Don't sign a contract that promises to return your principal with interest. ③ Before any large outlay, leave it a day, and ask your children, the community, the civil affairs office. Try it once first — stay a season at the walk-up price; don't buy a card the moment you arrive.
  • Where this comes from: A | in 2023 the Ministry of Civil Affairs issued a specific risk notice on illegal fundraising in the eldercare sector; in 2025 a Supreme People's Procuratorate "eldercare finance" case, using the offer of retirement flats and sojourn bases as the hook, took in more than 5 billion yuan in illegal fundraising. But legitimate sojourn and health-retreat services do exist; the difference is exactly whether you have to hand over a large sum first.
  • Who this is for: People still in good health, with spare money, who can arrange their own travel. Fairly feasible for a healthy 60-year-old; at 75 with several conditions, be careful, because treatment away from home is the weak point; if already disabled, long-distance sojourns don't suit. If someone wants a large sum from you first, it doesn't hold at any age.
  • What you get back: Money — no longer afraid of "having money taken off me in the name of a sojourn".
  • How this works in China: for treatment away from home, file the out-of-area treatment record first; if you meet "pay a lot up front, get returns", call 110 or 12315 first. Go by the latest local wording.

docs.title: 15.8 The drifting old: following your children, and the bills to settle first
docs.text:
• What it costs: no extra money, but medical insurance, familiar faces and your own place in things all have to be built again from scratch (money: barely any | time: long-term | effort: a bit tiring, more so if you're minding grandchildren | do you have to ask: yes, and it's a little embarrassing — you feel like a guest in your child's home)
  • In short: the drifting old (laopiao zu) are older people who leave their hometown to live in the city where their children are, most of them to look after grandchildren. The difficulties are reimbursing medical costs away from home, not understanding the local speech, losing every old friend, and local benefits not reaching you.
  • What you can do: do three things first. ① File the out-of-area treatment record; do it properly, so that outpatient and inpatient costs can be settled directly. ② Ask the local community eldercare service station what you can use without local household registration (hukou). ③ Find one person or one circle you can talk to; don't tie your whole life to the grandchildren. Try it once first — live there a quarter first, and don't rush to deal with the old family house.
  • Where this comes from: B | there is no single official wording for the scale: the National Health Commission's Report on China's Migrant Population Development 2018 (《中国流动人口发展报告 2018》) said nearly 18 million older people had moved to be with family, 7.2% of the 247 million migrants at the time; after the seventh national census in 2020, media calculations based on census data put the migrant population aged 60 and over at about 33.27 million. The years and the definitions differ, and this book doesn't merge them into one number; read it as "tens of millions".
  • Who this is for: People in reasonable health who are willing to go, and whose relationship with their children is workable. Feasible for a healthy 60-year-old; at 75 with several conditions, be careful, since long-term treatment away from home is the hard part; if already disabled and moving with them, the care all lands on the children.
  • What you get back: Relationships — no longer afraid of "still drifting at my age" and "never at ease in my child's home".
  • How this works in China: file the out-of-area treatment record first (the National Healthcare Security Administration app, or the medical insurance office where you're enrolled); whether community services are open to you, ask the community. Go by the latest local wording.

docs.title: 15.9 Moving house, and living alone: arrange two things first
docs.text:
• Moving house (money: some money | time: a few weeks | effort: quite tiring, especially for the very old | do you have to ask: yes, and it's a little embarrassing)
  • In short: for a very old person, moving isn't changing address; it's pulling the person out of a place they know. The older you are, the more likely something goes wrong in the six months after the move.
  • What you can do: if you really are moving, go in steps. ① Separate what can be separated — don't cut off all your old ties on the same day. ② Keep the layout of the new place as familiar as you can. ③ For someone who already can't find their way, ask the doctor before the move.
  • Where this comes from: B | research suggests moving is linked to health outcomes, and to how well the new home fits old habits (see the sources). But the findings don't agree.
  • Who this is for: Everyone, with higher risk for people over 75, with several conditions, or who already can't find their way. For a healthy 60-year-old the risk of moving is small.
  • What you get back: Independence — no longer afraid of "moving somewhere else and coming apart, or getting confused".
  • Living alone: agree a check-in (money: nothing | time: ten minutes to agree | effort: none | do you have to ask: easy)
  • In short: the worst thing about living alone isn't that no one looks after you; it's that if something happens, no one knows. Fixing that is small: agree a way of making contact with your children, a neighbour or a friend.
  • What you can do: ① check in at a fixed time every day — one phone call or one message, either will do. ② agree how long with no word before someone phones you, and how much longer before someone comes to the door. Try it once first — agree a morning check starting today, and keep it up for a week.
  • Where this comes from: C | common practice. Localities have visiting arrangements for older people living alone, in empty nests, or left behind (Minfa [2022] No. 73). But visits can't cover an emergency.
  • Who this is for: People living alone, in an empty nest, or left behind, especially the very old and those with several conditions. For a healthy 60-year-old keep the arrangement light; at 75 with several conditions, make it tighter; disabled and living alone is the highest risk.
  • How this works in China: register as living alone or in an empty nest with the community or sub-district so you are on the visiting list; a one-button call device or fall-detection equipment can be installed.

docs.title: 15.10 How this works in China: four places that can give you an answer
docs.text:
• Sub-district and community eldercare service centres (stations): family eldercare beds, day care, home visits, mutual-aid sites, visits to those living alone — start by asking here.
  • Civil affairs departments (district civil affairs bureau, city eldercare service website): the list of institutions and their grade ratings, waiting-list rules for public institutions, subsidies for age-friendly renovation.
  • Long-term care insurance (LTCI, zhanghuxian): in March 2026 the General Office of the CPC Central Committee and the General Office of the State Council issued the Opinions on Accelerating the Establishment of the Long-Term Care Insurance System, to reach near-universal coverage nationwide by the end of 2028 over about 3 years, at a contribution rate of about 0.3%. This is a social insurance scheme that contributors pay into, not a private policy you take out for yourself. How to apply for the disability assessment, and how much your local scheme pays: ask the local medical insurance department or the body that administers it.
  • Meals for older people: under Minfa [2023] No. 58, local areas are rolling out meal points, and many subsidize by category — the very old, the disabled, those living alone. Ask the community whether there is a meal point in your area and whether they will bring it up to your door.

Projects, subsidies and thresholds differ from place to place. Go by the latest local wording.

docs.title: The one thing you can do today
docs.text:
Stand at your front door, or out in the corridor, and count: from the door to your chair, from the bed to the toilet, how many steps are there.

Then, for those steps, put up — or borrow — something to hold on to: a handrail on the wall, a post by the door, either will do. Today. Just this one place.

Steps are the thing many older people walk every day and have never once counted. Once you've counted them, you'll know whether this flat can still be lived in.

docs.title: If you are reading this for your parents
docs.text:
There is one thing you have to bring up first. He almost certainly won't say "it's not easy living here" on his own; you have to hand him that sentence — but not in the tone of "you should move somewhere else". The moves you can make for him are these:

  • Walk through the flat for him first: next time you're home, look at three places — how many steps in the corridor, whether the toilet is squat or seated, whether there is a light on the path from bed to toilet at night. Don't lecture once you've seen it; fix one of them yourself first, and you pay for it.
  • Ask at the community once: whether there is a meal point in the area, home-visit services, visits for people living alone, and how to apply for age-friendly renovation. Once you know, put the options in front of him — he chooses, you don't decide.
  • Arrange one thing that can be tried: whether the institution does short stays, whether the community has a taster, whether a family eldercare bed can begin with an ability assessment. Try first; make no decision yet.
  • If he is moving to your city, do these first: if he is going to drift along with you, file the out-of-area treatment record first; then tape the community's phone number beside his bed.
  • Leave one channel open for a check-in: agree a fixed time each day when he checks in, and say plainly that it is "I want to know you're all right", not "I'm watching you".

Do the one thing you can actually do first; it works better than waiting for him to agree.

docs.title: What I am not sure about in this chapter
docs.text:
• Trial stays and short stays at eldercare institutions: there is no unified national rule, policies and fees differ by area, and this chapter only says "ask whether you can stay on trial" — it has not checked specific standards place by place.
  • There is no single official figure for the size of the drifting-old population: the National Health Commission's 2018 report said nearly 18 million older people had moved to be with family, while media calculations from the 2020 census put the migrant population aged 60 and over at about 33.27 million. The years and the definitions differ, so this chapter gives a range and does not merge them into one number.
  • Claims about the "break-up rate" of group eldercare (the "over 60%", "90%", "34.2%" that circulate online) can't be traced to an authoritative source, and none of them is used.
  • "How moving affects the health of very old people" is treated here only as a direction; the studies I read don't agree with one another, and I haven't checked page numbers and data tables in each.
  • "Weak law and supervision, low participation" in time banks is the common ground of several research abstracts; this chapter hasn't checked the page numbers and data tables of any single full text.
  • This chapter gives no doses, makes no diagnoses, and doesn't decide for anyone where to live. These choices have no standard answer: the same way of living can hold for one family and not for another.

  • third-party research Zhang Ziqi and Wei Qin, Residential Migration and Health of Older People: An Inquiry from the Perspective of Residential Environment Fit (《老年人的居住迁移与健康：居住环境契合性视角下的探究》), Population and Development (《人口与发展》) 2025, No. 3, pp. 132–144 (journal of the Institute of Population Research, Peking University; reposted on the PKU journal site): migration status and the fit between the new home and old habits are associated with health outcomes. http://ccj.pku.edu.cn/article/info?aid=387635459
  • official wording General Office of the CPC Central Committee and General Office of the State Council, Opinions on Accelerating the Establishment of the Long-Term Care Insurance System (《关于加快建立长期护理保险制度的意见》) (2026-03-25): to be advanced over about 3 years; according to Xinhua, by the end of 2028 the long-term care insurance system will have achieved near-universal coverage nationwide. https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/202603/content_7063790.htm
  • official wording National Healthcare Security Administration and 7 other departments, Implementation Plan for Accelerating the Establishment of the Long-Term Care Insurance System (《加快建立长期护理保险制度实施方案》) (2026-03-26): benchmark contribution rate about 0.3%. https://www.nhsa.gov.cn/art/2026/3/26/art_104_20039.html
  • official wording Ministry of Civil Affairs and 10 other departments, Action Plan for Actively Developing Meal Services for Older People (《积极发展老年助餐服务行动方案》) (Minfa [2023] No. 58, 2023-10) and its policy interpretation: subsidies by category for older people who are very old, disabled or living alone. Policy interpretation (Ministry of Civil Affairs, reposted by the Baingoin County Government website, 2024-05-08): http://www.nqbgx.gov.cn/nqbgx/zcjd/202405/eb7fe1b1321543019c1390933ad40069.shtml

docs.title: Chapter 16 · Where the Money Comes From: How the System Pays Your Bills
docs.text:
Once you retire you find that the bills don't stop just because you stopped working. Utilities, food, medicine — small bills that arrive every day. What actually turns a household over is the other kind: one hospital stay, one serious illness, one person who goes down and never gets up again.

Chapter 4 said the money account has to be built early. This chapter asks a different question: on the day the bill actually arrives, which of these bills will the state's system pay for you, and which ones do you carry yourself. These bills have edges, and they come in an order.

docs.title: 16.1 What this chapter settles
docs.text:
The old saying is that you save for old age to guard against old age. In money terms it comes down to three different pots: the pension pays the cost of living while you're alive, medical insurance pays the doctor's bill, and long-term care insurance pays for care once you can no longer manage.

Each pot covers one stretch. The trouble is that a lot of people treat the three as one — "I have a pension, surely that covers seeing a doctor" — and only find out, on the day someone has to be turned and washed, that the earlier pot does not stretch to the later need.

This chapter sets out where each pot ends, how reimbursement is calculated, where to go, and what fills the gap. If you remember one thing, remember this: which pot pays for which thing, and where to ask when something happens. For an English reader, the three pots are roughly the shape of Social Security, Medicare and long-term care insurance — but these are mainland China's own contributory public schemes, with their own rules, and the differences matter more than the resemblance.

docs.title: 16.2 Three pots pay for three different things — don't merge them into one
docs.text:
This pot What it covers What it does not cover Basic pension Cash paid into your account every month; covers food and living while you're alive Not doctor's bills, not the carer's wages Basic medical insurance The medical cost of being ill: hospital, outpatient, medicines Not food, not day-to-day care after you become disabled Long-term care insurance Care services after you become disabled Pays out no cash, and covers no doctor's bills

Medical insurance does not put money in your hand; it pays the doctor's bill for you. Long-term care insurance doesn't hand out money either; it buys care services for you. Once you separate "paying out cash" from "paying the bill", you know which account to watch.

Between what the system will pay and what you actually take out of your pocket there is always a stretch, and the household fills that stretch itself.

docs.title: 16.3 Medical insurance reimbursement: learn the three catalogs and the three lines first
docs.text:
• What it costs: work it out once, and it keeps paying off (Money: none | Time: half an hour | Effort: none | Do you have to ask: no)
  • In short: medical insurance does not reimburse whatever you spent. It looks first at whether the medicine or the test you used is on the reimbursement list, then at how much you spent: what's off the list isn't covered, and neither is too little or too much. In mainland China this scheme is yibao, a contributory public scheme — the rough counterpart of Medicare. Medicare pays a defined share of covered services, with a deductible and coinsurance. yibao passes the same bill through a fixed list of what it will pay for, plus three limits of its own.
  • What you can do:
  • ① Learn the three catalogs: medicines, medical services, medical consumables. Only what is inside them is reimbursed; what is outside you pay in full.
  • ② Learn the three lines: the deductible (below it, you pay yourself), the reimbursement rate (at community level usually higher than at a big hospital), and the annual cap (above it, nothing more is paid).
  • ③ yibao only reimburses costs "within the policy scope". It also leaves alone the "self-paid" and "own-share" lines on the bill.
  • Where this comes from: A | National averages are only a reference: within policy scope the employee scheme's fund pays about 80% and the resident scheme about 70% (National Healthcare Security Administration reading of Guobanfa [2021] No. 42). Deductible, reimbursement rate and cap all vary with where you are enrolled, which scheme you are in, and the tier of hospital — the place you are enrolled governs. Ask the medical insurance bureau there, or look it up in the "National Medical Insurance Service Platform" app.
  • Who this is for: Who it applies to: everyone who is insured; first work out whether you pay employee medical insurance or resident medical insurance.
  • What you get back: money — no longer afraid that "one serious illness and the household collapses, and I have no idea how much medical insurance will actually pay"
  • How this works in China: the medicine catalog is the latest edition (Yibaofa [2025] No. 33, in force from 2026-01-01). Look up the details in the "National Medical Insurance Service Platform" app, or ask the medical insurance bureau where you are enrolled. The latest local wording prevails.

docs.title: 16.4 Before you travel for treatment, do the out-of-area filing on your phone
docs.text:
• What it costs: a few taps on the phone, a few minutes (Money: none | Time: a few minutes | Effort: none | Do you have to ask: no)
  • In short: if you go to the city where your children live for treatment without filing, you may be reimbursed less and may have to pay the hospital first and claim the money back by hand. With the filing done, you can settle on the spot by scanning your code. The reason a filing is needed at all is that in mainland China medical insurance is run city by city, not as one national plan: the city where you are enrolled is the one that holds the money, and the hospital in the other city has to be told in advance.
  • What you can do:
  • ① Pick the right category: long-term residence outside your province (moving somewhere else to live, moving to be near children, being posted there for work); temporary treatment away from home (referral, emergency rescue, seeing a doctor while visiting family or traveling).
  • ② Two entrances: the "National Medical Insurance Service Platform" app, or the "out-of-area treatment filing" service in the National Healthcare Security Administration's official account.
  • ③ After identity verification, choose the filing type and the place you will be treated, and upload the documents; some places accept a personal declaration in place of proof.
  • ④ Before you leave, check the progress of the filing and confirm that the hospital where you will be treated is set up for direct settlement.
  • Where this comes from: A | The rules come from Yibaofa [2022] No. 22 and Yibaofa [2024] No. 21; but the documents, the time limits and the size of the reduction differ from place to place — one place may cut reimbursement by 10 points, another by 20. The place you are enrolled governs: ask the medical insurance bureau there.
  • Who this is for: Who it applies to: people who live outside their home city long-term, or who go to a big hospital in another province. If you only ever see doctors in your own city, you don't need this.
  • What you get back: money + relationships — no longer afraid that "taking Mom and Dad to a big-city hospital means laying out tens of thousands first and then not getting it back"
  • How this works in China: the National Medical Insurance Service Platform app; the medical insurance bureau window where you are enrolled. For the filing type, the time limits and any reduction, ask that bureau. The latest local wording prevails.

docs.title: 16.5 On long-term medication for a chronic disease, get the outpatient chronic-and-special-disease designation first
docs.text:
• What it costs: one trip to a hospital or a medical insurance window (Money: none, or the cost of one registration fee | Time: one visit | Effort: none | Do you have to ask: no)
  • In short: with illnesses like high blood pressure and diabetes you take medicine every day, and the money goes out at the outpatient window. Get the condition designated an "outpatient chronic and special disease" and outpatient medicine is reimbursed at a higher rate; without the designation it is reimbursed against the ordinary outpatient quota.
  • What you can do:
  • ① First ask the medical insurance bureau where you are enrolled, or your designated hospital: is my condition on the local list of outpatient chronic and special diseases?
  • ② If it is, apply for the designation: take your medical records, the diagnosis certificate and the test results to the medical insurance agency or the designated hospital.
  • ③ Once it is approved, prescriptions and follow-up visits are settled at the chronic-and-special-disease rate, and a long-term prescription can be written to cover a longer period at one time.
  • ④ If you need treatment across provinces, first confirm that this condition can be settled directly across provinces both where you are enrolled and where you will be treated.
  • Where this comes from: A | The conditions that can be settled directly across provinces have gone from 5 to 10: high blood pressure, diabetes, outpatient radiotherapy and chemotherapy for malignant tumors, dialysis for uremia, and anti-rejection treatment after organ transplant, with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, rheumatoid arthritis, coronary heart disease, viral hepatitis and ankylosing spondylitis added in 2024 (Yibaobanfa [2024] No. 19). But the list of conditions that qualify for the outpatient chronic-and-special-disease benefit, and the reimbursement rates, are set by each pooling area; there is no national standard. The place you are enrolled governs — ask its medical insurance bureau or the insurance office of your designated hospital.
  • Who this is for: Who it applies to: people on long-term medication with high outpatient costs get the most out of it; if you only see an ordinary outpatient clinic now and then, you don't need it.
  • What you get back: money — no longer afraid that "the money for medicine every day all disappears into the outpatient quota"
  • How this works in China: the medical insurance bureau where you are enrolled, the insurance office of your designated hospital, the "National Medical Insurance Service Platform" app (which shows whether the chronic-and-special-disease designation is held). The latest local wording prevails.

docs.title: 16.6 Critical illness insurance is automatic; medical assistance you have to apply for yourself
docs.text:
• What it costs: applying for assistance means one trip to a civil affairs or medical insurance window (Money: none | Time: one visit | Effort: none | Do you have to ask: yes — and it is a little embarrassing)
  • In short: one hospital stay runs to hundreds of thousands. After basic medical insurance has paid, a second layer — critical illness insurance — pays on top; if you are on the resident scheme you pay nothing extra for it, it comes automatically. If that still isn't enough and the household is genuinely in difficulty, medical assistance is the floor underneath, but you have to go and apply for it.
  • What you can do:
  • ① Critical illness insurance: it is generally calculated together with the discharge settlement, with no separate application. If you are unsure, ask the bureau where you are enrolled: "Did this stay go through critical illness insurance?"
  • ② Medical assistance: first see whether you fall into one of these groups — dibao recipients, people in extreme difficulty, members of households on the edge of dibao, rural populations at risk of falling back into poverty, and people pushed into poverty by serious illness.
  • ③ Where to apply: start at the village committee, the residents' committee, or the civil affairs window of the township (sub-district) office; many places already handle it as a one-stop application.
  • ④ Bring the diagnosis, the hospital receipts and the household's income situation; if you are already registered as dibao or in extreme difficulty, the assistance is granted directly.
  • Where this comes from: A | From Guobanfa [2021] No. 42: critical illness insurance pays automatically after basic medical insurance; on medical assistance, for dibao and extreme-difficulty households the assistance deductible is in principle abolished and the assistance rate is no less than 70%, while for households on the edge of dibao and for people pushed into poverty by serious illness the deductible is about 10% and 25% of the previous year's per-capita disposable income of residents. The place you are enrolled governs; ask the civil affairs or medical insurance window.
  • Who this is for: Who it applies to: households genuinely in difficulty, where the out-of-pocket cost of a serious illness is heavy. Applying is not a loss of face.
  • What you get back: money + dignity — no longer afraid that "one serious illness drags the whole family down, and I am too ashamed to ask for help"
  • How this works in China: the village committee, the residents' committee, the civil affairs window of the township (sub-district) office, the medical insurance bureau where you are enrolled. Ask three things: which group we fall into, what the deductible and the rate are, and how to apply. The latest local wording prevails.

docs.title: 16.7 Supplementary policies like huiminbao: small money against a big bill — check three things first
docs.text:
• What it costs: a few dozen to just over a hundred yuan a year (Money: hardly anything | Time: one enrollment | Effort: none | Do you have to ask: no)
  • In short: huiminbao is supplementary medical insurance that is "guided by the government, sold by insurers, bought by you voluntarily": a few dozen to just over a hundred yuan a year, cover of several million yuan, mainly filling in costs outside the medical insurance catalogs, your own share, and specialty drugs. The deductible is usually not low, so minor illness never reaches it; what it guards against is serious illness.
  • Whether it is worth it comes down to three things:
  • ① Who runs it: is it an official product guided by the local government and underwritten by a licensed insurer, or a look-alike with a similar name?
  • ② How high the deductible is: the higher the deductible, the less it does for minor illness, and the more its whole point concentrates on serious illness.
  • ③ What it pays and how: are costs outside the catalogs covered, how are pre-existing conditions handled, and can it be settled directly?
  • Where this comes from: B | In July 2025 the National Financial Regulatory Administration issued a notice regulating it. The controversy is that enrollment is low nationwide: healthy people drop out, sick people buy in, and it can slide into a "death spiral".
  • Who this is for: Who it applies to: people who are older, have pre-existing conditions, and cannot buy ordinary commercial health insurance — for them "no health gate" may be the only policy still open; for people who already have good cover, it is mostly a top-up for specialty drugs and off-catalog costs.
  • What you get back: money — no longer afraid that "the off-catalog costs and the astronomically priced drugs are beyond what medical insurance can do"
  • How this works in China: the official enrollment entrance guided by the local government (in some places the premium can be paid from the balance in your medical insurance personal account). Before you enroll, ask clearly about the deductible and what is covered. The latest local wording prevails.

docs.title: 16.8 Long-term care insurance: the third pot, not yet in every city
docs.text:
• What it costs: one look-up, one question (Money: none | Time: one trip to a window or one phone call | Effort: none | Do you have to ask: no)
  • In short: long-term care insurance covers the care bill after you lose the ability to manage. It is the youngest of the three pots, and it generally does not pay you cash — it uses the money to buy care services for you. In mainland China this is a public social-insurance scheme rather than a policy you buy from an insurer; the rough counterpart is long-term care insurance in the US, except that there the cover is mostly a private policy you buy and pass medical underwriting for, and Medicare does not pay for custodial care.
  • Where it has got to: 15 cities piloted it in 2016, and in 2020 it expanded to 49. In September 2025 the National Healthcare Security Administration reported coverage of 190 million people and spending of more than 85 billion yuan. By the end of 2025 the number insured had reached 308.54 million (Ministry of Civil Affairs and National Office on Aging, "2025 National Bulletin on the Development of Aging-Related Undertakings") — the two figures are counted differently: the first is coverage by the system, the second is people actually insured. In March 2026 the General Office of the CPC Central Committee and the General Office of the State Council issued "Opinions on Accelerating the Establishment of the Long-Term Care Insurance System", with the goal of "about 3 years, near-universal coverage nationwide by the end of 2028", and the contribution rate held at about 0.3%.
  • What you can do: ① first check whether your city runs long-term care insurance; ② if it does, the disabled state has to last more than 6 months and be assessed and confirmed before you can receive benefits; ③ benefits mainly pay service fees, with no deductible.
  • Where this comes from: A | The timeline, the coverage figures, the contribution rate and the goal come from official documents (National Healthcare Security Administration, 2025-09-25; General Office of the CPC Central Committee and General Office of the State Council, 2026-03-25); but benefits differ widely from place to place, and the pilot cities still need about 3 years to align with the national catalog.
  • Who this is for: Who it applies to: people already in a city that runs long-term care insurance. Another city's standards do not necessarily apply — check locally first.
  • What you get back: money + relationships — no longer afraid that "one person becomes disabled, the whole family loses its balance, and the carer's bills drag the household under"
  • How this works in China: the medical insurance bureau where you are enrolled, a medical insurance service window, or the "National Medical Insurance Service Platform" app. Ask three things: "Does our place run long-term care insurance? How do I apply for the disability assessment? Which services are covered, and how much is paid?" The latest local wording prevails.

docs.title: 16.9 When one person goes down, these are the three bills the household actually pays
docs.text:
• What it costs: one careful pass through the accounts (Money: none | Time: half an hour | Effort: none | Do you have to ask: easy to bring up)
  • In short: what long-term care insurance pays out is services, not cash. What really flows out of the household's wallet is the carer's wages, the income your children lose, and care supplies and transport.
  • What you can do: list these separately and you can see how big the gap is.
  • ① The carer's wages: a live-in carer, an hourly carer, a bed in an institution — add it up monthly. This is the largest fixed cost after disability.
  • ② The income your children lose: if one child quits or takes long leave to provide care, that is tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of yuan a year in lost income — a bill with no receipt and no one to reimburse it.
  • Where this comes from: C | These are the ordinary costs of family care, and there is no nationwide statistic. How much is reimbursed depends on the local catalog and the assessment grade.
  • Who this is for: Who it applies to: households with a disabled older person who is already being cared for by someone. Ask about local long-term care insurance early in the disability rather than after they are bedbound — it is simpler.
  • What you get back: money + relationships — no longer afraid that "the carer's wages and the lost income drag the family's savings under"
  • How this works in China: for which services local long-term care insurance covers, and what a carer costs, ask the medical insurance bureau where you are enrolled and the elder-care service providers. Agree with the family in advance "who provides the care, and for how long" (see Chapter 21).

docs.title: 16.10 The order to build it in: fill the foundation first, then the gaps
docs.text:
Money is limited, so there is an order to what you protect first and what you leave for later. Buying something fancy before the foundation is paid up is putting the cart before the horse. Work down this order:

  1. Get basic medical insurance in place and paid up: the employee scheme or the resident scheme, never a year lapsed. This is the foundation under every reimbursement.
  2. Confirm whether critical illness insurance is there: the resident scheme includes it; on the employee scheme it depends on local arrangements. While you are at it, find out how to apply for local medical assistance.
  3. Check long-term care insurance: if your place has it, learn how the assessment works and which services are covered; if it doesn't, register that this risk is yours to carry.

  4. Fill the gaps: supplementary policies like huiminbao for the people they suit; enterprise annuities and the private pension (see Chapter 4) come later still.

  5. Where this comes from: C | This order is the book's own, sorted on "protect the frequent first, the extreme later": first the likely cost of seeing a doctor, then the low-probability, high-cost serious illness, and only then the long account that is care after disability.

  6. Who this is for: Who it applies to: people with spare money who want one more layer for later life; if your basic medical insurance is still lapsed and you are borrowing to see a doctor, reconnect the foundation first.
  7. How this works in China: for lapsed payments, back payments and enrollment, call 12333 or ask the social insurance agency where you are enrolled; for medical insurance, assistance and long-term care insurance, ask the medical insurance bureau there. The latest local wording prevails.

docs.title: 16.11 These "retirement products" — don't hand over money yet
docs.text:
• What it costs: a few minutes of judgment, and a lifetime's savings spared (Money: none | Time: a few minutes | Effort: none | Do you have to ask: easy to bring up)
  • In short: these categories go after people in later life specifically, and the tricks are always the same few.
  • How to tell, three ways:
  • ① The "house-for-pension" scam: the real thing is a reverse-mortgage pension insurance policy — an insurance product, not an investment. The scam borrows the name, has you mortgage your home and put the money into its "high-interest investment", and you end up with neither the money nor the house.
  • ② "High-interest wealth management": anyone promising "capital guaranteed, high interest, money back" and pressing you to sign on the spot should be treated as a scam. Regulated investment products are not allowed to promise your capital back.
  • ③ Prepaid elder-care schemes: cards that pay rebates, membership cards, prepaid cards, large membership fees — in substance they are using the money you paid in to keep their cash flow turning. The Ministry of Civil Affairs has issued a risk warning, and there is also a document regulating prepaid fees at elder-care institutions.
  • Three brakes: for a large transfer, wait 24 hours before you do it; if someone wants you to mortgage property or move savings into "a certain account", stop; if you are not sure, ask your children, the community office, or the bank counter.
  • Where this comes from: A | The scam types and methods come from warnings by the consumer protection bureau of the China Banking and Insurance Regulatory Commission and the Ministry of Civil Affairs' "Risk Warning on Illegal Fundraising in the Elder-Care Service Sector" (2023-06). Nothing here is investment advice.
  • Who this is for: Who it applies to: older people who own a home or hold a lump sum. If you have already put money in, don't be ashamed — call the police first and keep the evidence.
  • What you get back: money + dignity — no longer afraid that "a lifetime's savings get taken and I don't dare let anyone know"
  • How this works in China: if you think you have been scammed, call 110; for the rules on prepaid fees at elder-care institutions, ask the local civil affairs bureau; to check whether a financial product is real, ask the bank counter or the financial regulator. The latest local wording prevails.

docs.title: 16.12 If you can only do one thing today
docs.text:
Open the "National Medical Insurance Service Platform" app, claim your personal enrollment record and your electronic medical insurance credential, and while you are in there glance at whether you pay employee medical insurance or resident medical insurance.

This step doesn't cost a single yuan and takes ten minutes. But every question you have later — how much is covered, where to claim — begins its answer here.

docs.title: 16.13 If you are reading this for your parents
docs.text:
In our parents' generation there are a lot of things they would rather carry alone than bring up, "money" and "illness" most of all. If you are reading this chapter for them, the most useful help you can give is to turn "ask them" into "look it up".

How to say it out loud: don't ask "will your medical insurance cover this", say "let me put your electronic medical insurance credential on your phone, so you can just scan the code when you see a doctor". You are installing a tool for them, not auditing their finances.

Three things you can do without their agreement: ① use the "National Medical Insurance Service Platform" app to look up their enrollment status and whether they hold the outpatient chronic-and-special-disease designation; ② if they live outside their home city long-term, or are going to another province for treatment, do the out-of-area filing in advance; ③ go to the medical insurance bureau where they are enrolled, or to the community office, and ask whether there is long-term care insurance locally, how the chronic-and-special-disease designation is granted, and how to apply for assistance when things are hard. None of the three costs much.

What you can still do if they won't agree: get the paperwork together first — diagnosis, hospital receipts, medicine list — into one bag. When the day comes, one bag of documents is worth more than ten conversations.

docs.title: 16.14 Where I am not sure
docs.text:
• Outpatient chronic and special disease: the 10 conditions that can be settled directly across provinces are nationally uniform, but the list of conditions that get the benefit, and the reimbursement rates, are set by each pooling area. This chapter cannot give one rate that works everywhere, only how to apply and where to ask.
  • The documents, the time limits and the reimbursement reductions for out-of-area filing differ from place to place; the range given in this chapter is a summary and was not traced back place by place. The place you are enrolled governs.
  • There is no single official national publication of huiminbao's payout ratio or enrollment rate ("payout ratio above 90%" comes from a media report quoting a local regulator; "overall enrollment about 5%" comes from an industry research article). Use the local product terms and official notices.
  • Long-term care insurance benefits differ widely from place to place; this chapter gives the national timeline and targets. For what a particular city pays and how it assesses, go back and ask the local medical insurance bureau.
  • There is no nationwide statistic for the income family carers lose or for the price of a carer; this chapter only sets out which bills to count.

docs.title: 16.15 Sources for this chapter
docs.text:
Date checked: 2026-10-10. All links were tested and open (some pages on the financial regulator's site are dynamic and need to be opened in a browser).

  • Basic medical insurance reimbursement, critical illness insurance, medical assistance: General Office of the State Council, Opinions on Improving the Medical Insurance and Assistance System for Major and Critical Illnesses (Guobanfa [2021] No. 42, signed 2021-10-28, issued 2021-11-19): the scope of assistance recipients, the deductible standards, and an assistance rate for dibao and extreme-difficulty households of no less than 70%. https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/content/2021-11/19/content_5651446.htm checked 2026-10-10
  • Policy reading of that document: National Healthcare Security Administration, Policy Reading of the "Opinions on Improving the Medical Insurance and Assistance System for Major and Critical Illnesses" (2021-11-19): within policy scope the funds of the resident and employee schemes pay about 70% and 80% respectively. https://www.nhsa.gov.cn/art/2021/11/19/art_38_7354.html checked 2026-10-10
  • Out-of-area treatment filing: National Healthcare Security Administration and Ministry of Finance, Notice on Further Improving Direct Settlement of Basic Medical Insurance for Cross-Province Out-of-Area Treatment (Yibaofa [2022] No. 22, 2022-06-30). https://www.nhsa.gov.cn/art/2022/7/26/art_104_8629.html checked 2026-10-10
  • Steps for out-of-area treatment: National Healthcare Security Administration, How Do You Get Direct Reimbursement for Cross-Province Out-of-Area Treatment? (2025-03-16): filing types, the steps for filing on a phone, and how to look up chronic-and-special-disease status. https://www.nhsa.gov.cn/art/2025/3/16/art_14_16010.html checked 2026-10-10
  • Stronger management of out-of-area treatment: National Healthcare Security Administration and Ministry of Finance, Notice on Further Strengthening the Management and Service of Direct Settlement for Out-of-Area Treatment (Yibaofa [2024] No. 21, 2024-09-13). https://www.nhsa.gov.cn/art/2024/9/13/art_104_13857.html checked 2026-10-10
  • Cross-province direct settlement for outpatient chronic and special diseases: Office of the National Healthcare Security Administration and General Office of the Ministry of Finance, Notice on Steadily and Orderly Expanding the Range of Outpatient Chronic and Special Disease Types Covered by Cross-Province Direct Settlement (Yibaobanfa [2024] No. 19), policy reading dated 2024-09-13: the number of conditions rose from 5 to 10 — the original five being high blood pressure, diabetes, outpatient radiotherapy and chemotherapy for malignant tumors, dialysis for uremia and anti-rejection treatment after organ transplant, with five added: chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, rheumatoid arthritis, coronary heart disease, viral hepatitis and ankylosing spondylitis. https://www.nhsa.gov.cn/art/2024/9/13/art_105_13860.html checked 2026-10-10
