Also: Ministry of Civil Affairs and National Office on Aging, 2025 National Bulletin on the Development of Aging-Related Undertakings (issued by the Ministry of Civil Affairs and the National Office on Aging on 2026-07-31; full-text PDF): https://www.cncaprc.gov.cn/u/cms/www/202608/01013057jmzq.pdf (308.54 million insured as of the end of 2025; 2025 fund spending 18.644 billion yuan) https://www.nhsa.gov.cn/art/2025/9/25/art_105_18022.html checked 2026-10-10
  • Long-term care insurance (catalog of service items): National Healthcare Security Administration, Notice on Issuing the "Catalog of National Long-Term Care Insurance Service Items (Trial)" (Yibaofa [2025] No. 24, 2025-09-25): 36 items in total, 20 for daily living care and 16 for medical nursing; medical nursing items included in the catalog are paid by the long-term care insurance fund, and the medical insurance fund does not pay for them. https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/zhengceku/202509/content_7042325.htm checked 2026-10-10
  • Long-term care insurance (what the system is aiming at): General Office of the CPC Central Committee and General Office of the State Council, Opinions on Accelerating the Establishment of the Long-Term Care Insurance System (2026-03-25): about 3 years, near-universal coverage nationwide by the end of 2028; the contribution rate held at about 0.3%; for employed workers, shared in equal proportion by the employer and the employee. https://www.gov.cn/yaowen/liebiao/202603/content_7063789.htm checked 2026-10-10
  • Long-term care insurance (report on where it stands): Xinhua, Covering Everyone! China Speeds Up the Establishment of the Long-Term Care Insurance System (2026-03-26). https://www.gov.cn/yaowen/liebiao/202603/content_7063795.htm checked 2026-10-10
  • Huiminbao (regulation): General Office of the National Financial Regulatory Administration, Notice on Promoting the High-Quality Development of City-Level Commercial Medical Insurance (2025-07-31): an inclusive positioning, pricing graded by age and health status, a ban on disorderly low-price competition. https://www.nfra.gov.cn/cn/view/pages/ItemDetail.html?docId=1253070&generaltype=1&itemId=4216 (the page is dynamic and needs to be opened in a browser; checked 2026-10-10)
  • Huiminbao (background and the bind it is in): Ma Fengjiao, Promoting the High-Quality Development of City-Level Commercial Medical Insurance, originally in China Banking and Insurance News, "PKU Insurance Review" No. 892, reposted by the Center for China Insurance and Social Security Research, Peking University (2025-08-20): national enrollment about 5%, and the risk of a "death spiral". https://econ.pku.edu.cn/ccissr/bdbxpl/50161zgbxy390801.htm checked 2026-10-10
  • Huiminbao (what it is, payout ratio): CCTV.com, What Is Huiminbao? How Is It Different from Basic Medical Insurance and Commercial Insurance? A One-Article Explainer (2024-01-28): premiums from a few dozen to just over a hundred yuan, no age or health-status restrictions, an overall payout ratio expected to exceed 90% (this is a media report quoting a person at the Zhejiang office of the National Financial Regulatory Administration, not a nationwide official release). https://news.cctv.com/2024/01/28/ARTIZf6SbE7AQe6gVlDS1u1q240128.shtml checked 2026-10-10
  • The house-for-pension scam: Consumer Protection Bureau of the China Banking and Insurance Regulatory Commission, Risk Warning on Financial Fraud in "Investing for Retirement" and "House-for-Pension" (third issue of 2021, published on the website of the National Financial Regulatory Administration). https://www.nfra.gov.cn/cn/view/pages/ItemDetail.html?docId=992168&itemId=4100&generaltype=0 checked 2026-10-10
  • Retirement fraud: Consumer Protection Bureau of the China Banking and Insurance Regulatory Commission, Risk Warning on Preventing Retirement Fraud (2023 No. 1): three kinds of trap — agency surrender of policies, house-for-pension, and investment. https://www.nfra.gov.cn/cn/view/pages/ItemDetail.html?docId=1103021&itemId=915 checked 2026-10-10
  • Illegal fundraising in the elder-care service sector: Ministry of Civil Affairs, Risk Warning on Illegal Fundraising in the Elder-Care Service Sector (2023-06-15): the forms it takes, including card rebates, membership cards and investing in elder-care projects. https://www.gov.cn/lianbo/bumen/202306/content_6886556.htm checked 2026-10-10
  • Prepaid fees at elder-care institutions: seven departments including the Ministry of Civil Affairs, Guiding Opinions on Strengthening the Supervision of Prepaid Fees at Elder-Care Institutions (Minfa [2024] No. 19). https://www.gov.cn/gongbao/2024/issue_11386/202406/content_6955752.html checked 2026-10-10
  • Where to look things up: the "National Medical Insurance Service Platform" app (National Healthcare Security Administration); for social insurance questions, 12333.

docs.title: Chapter 17 · Care lands on particular people, and the people giving it should not fall first
docs.text:
Three in the morning. Movement beside you wakes you. Your spouse needs the toilet again. You take their arm and shuffle with them to the bathroom, then shuffle back. Once they are lying down again, you lie with your eyes open until daylight.

That is roughly how these years have gone. While you look after them, you quietly think: if I go down first, what happens to them?

This chapter is written for you as you grow old, and also for you as you look after someone. It says two things: when something happens, where your people come from; and the person giving the care needs to keep some breath for themselves too.

docs.title: 17.1 What this chapter is for
docs.text:
The chapters before this one dealt with the body, money, and medical care. This one deals with people.

"Someone to look after me" is useless as five words. It has to land on particular people and particular hours: who steadies you, who runs to the hospital, who signs, who pays. Those people and those arrangements all have to be assembled before anything happens.

The second half of the chapter turns around and is written for the person doing the caring. Care, in the end, always lands on one particular person — most often a spouse, or one particular adult child. That person can be worn out too.

docs.title: 17.2 Seven kinds of people you can lean on, each with its own limits
docs.text:
There is an old saying: raise sons to guard your old age. On the day disability actually arrives, you find there is more than one kind of person to lean on, and each kind can catch different things.

According to a 2021 sample survey by the Ministry of Civil Affairs, the National Working Commission on Aging and others, among older people who do have someone caring for them, a spouse is the main carer in 45.5% of cases, children (including daughters-in-law and sons-in-law) in 47.6%, and professional care workers only 3.4%. Those two or three people in the household carry more than ninety percent of the care.

Who you can lean on What they can catch What they cannot catch A partner Closest at hand, there all day, knows your habits best They are getting old too; the two of you going down together is the most dangerous case Children Hospital runs, signing, paying, paperwork, making the decisions Mostly not nearby, and they have jobs; the year-after-year work of turning and washing is more than they can carry Relatives and close friends Come in for a day or two at the critical moment, lend money, show up and lend weight Each has their own household; they can only help for a stretch Neighbors Can knock on the door within minutes, notice that something is wrong, run a small errand If the relationship is not that close it is awkward to ask; weaker still in new developments Volunteers Visits, company and conversation, small errands, volunteer hospital accompaniment Inconsistent, limited slots, no substitute for professional care The community (residents' committee, eldercare service station, family doctor, eldercare adviser) The entry point to policy: help applying for subsidies, signing up, being introduced to services Not a carer on call; they cannot do the daily feeding and turning Professional carers (hospital attendants, care workers, nurses, LTCI services) Know the professional handling, can take the physical load, can cover a night shift Costs money, high turnover, the good ones are hard to book

The people who can spend every day at the bedside are either a spouse who no longer has the strength, or children who cannot take that much leave. The gap in between is what this chapter is trying to fill.

docs.title: 17.3 Do not wait for the day it happens to scroll through your contacts
docs.text:
• What it costs: one afternoon and a pen (Money: none | Time: half a day | Effort: none | Do you have to speak up: easy to ask)
  • In short: Scrolling your phone for a number on the day something happens is the worst possible delay. Write down now, on one sheet of paper, the people who can come.
  • What you can do: Write it in three columns — can be there at once, can put in money, can handle paperwork and make decisions — with at least one name and phone number in each. Then agree one "signal" with the key person: curtains open, light on, all is well. This sheet is folded into the family index table in Chapter 19.
  • Where this comes from: B | Social support networks are associated with health and survival in older people, with cohort studies behind that. But there is no randomized trial showing that "a written list means fewer crises"; what the list protects is not being in a scramble on the day.
  • Who this is for: Who it holds for — at 60 and still sturdy, this list is something you are storing up for your future self; at 75 with a few chronic conditions, the list needs to be checked once a week; already disabled, the list has to be maintained by the children, and cannot wait for the older person to think of it.
  • What you get back: relationships — no longer afraid of "something happening at night and no one knowing"
  • How this works in China: Ask at the residents' committee or the community eldercare service station whether your area has visits to people living alone, "knock on the door" rounds, contracted family doctors, and registration of emergency contacts. The latest local wording governs.

docs.title: 17.4 Hospital accompaniment: paying someone to run the hospital for you
docs.text:
• What it costs: 100 to 300 yuan a time (Money: some money | Time: half a day to a full day | Effort: none | Do you have to speak up: yes, and it is a little embarrassing — you have to be willing to admit you cannot work it out yourself)
  • In short: The bigger the hospital, the more it is a maze — registering, paying, collecting medicine, finding the department, walking back and forth. What a hospital companion does is run the errands and do the talking for an older person.
  • What you can do: (1) Is it worth it: most worth it if you live alone, have trouble walking, cannot follow the process, or your children cannot get leave. (2) What counts as reasonable (Shanghai's published figures, updated 2026-10): in Pudong, "Pu Laohui" sets half a day (4 hours) at 198 to 280 yuan; across the city the market rate is mostly 50 to 80 yuan an hour, usually with a 2-hour minimum, an ordinary accompaniment is 100 to 200 yuan, and packages are mostly 200 to 300 yuan for about 4 hours. Each agency sets its own fees, but has to post them clearly at the place of service. (3) How to choose: use a proper agency, check the companion's ID badge, sign a contract, ask clearly whether pickup and help with wheelchairs and stairs are included, and ask for an invoice. (4) Do not count on them to add an appointment slot or grab a number for you: using accompaniment as cover to add slots and sell appointment numbers is explicitly banned. (5) Hand over the medical record and ID card only for that visit's use; do not leave the whole file with them.
  • Where this comes from: A | Shanghai piloted it from January 2025 in nine districts including Pudong, and extended it citywide on 1 July 2026, for people aged 60 and over regardless of household registration; agencies must have at least 5 companions, and companions' ID badges can be checked. But there is still no unified national occupational qualification for hospital companions; the "companion certificate" is mostly a local or industry assessment and is not necessarily recognized in another city.
  • Who this is for: Who it holds for — at 60 and in reasonable health you will mostly not need it; at 75 with chronic conditions or already disabled it is most useful, especially for follow-up visits, collecting medicine, and tests. Two things to guard against: privacy leaks (medical records, ID) and disputes (sign the contract first; if something goes wrong, go to the agency and to the consumer protection committee).
  • What you get back: independence + dignity — no longer afraid of "going to the doctor with no one with me, unable to explain myself, and treated as a nuisance"
  • How this works in China: In mainland China, in Shanghai you can order through the district platform (such as "Pu Laohui" in Pudong), or ask at a comprehensive eldercare service center or the service station at the end of your street; older people on the minimum living guarantee or low incomes can be brought into the eldercare service subsidy. In other cities, start by asking the district civil affairs bureau whether there is a "medical assistance and hospital accompaniment service." At national level, 民发〔2024〕52 号 has already written medical assistance and hospital accompaniment into home-based eldercare services. The latest local wording governs.

docs.title: 17.5 Respite care: a day off for the person who watches every day
docs.text:
• What it costs: depends on the place; sometimes the government pays, sometimes you pay part (Money: some money | Time: a few days a month | Effort: none | Do you have to speak up: yes, and it is a little embarrassing — you have to be willing to admit you cannot hold out)
  • In short: One person watching another sick person every day, 365 days a year with no break — the one who breaks first is the watcher. Respite care means either moving the older person into a facility for a few days, or having a professional come to your home and take over for half a day.
  • What you can do: (1) First ask whether your area has it; (2) it comes in two shapes — short-term residential care (the older person goes into a facility for a few days) and home care (a professional comes to your home and covers a few hours to a day); (3) do not buy a month at the start; try one day a month first; (4) keep that day for yourself: your own appointments, errands, or sleeping for a whole day.
  • Where this comes from: A (mechanism) | At national level there is only the word "explore": The 14th Five-Year Plan for National Aging Programs and the Elderly Care Service System (《"十四五"国家老龄事业发展和养老服务体系规划》, 国发〔2021〕35 号) says to "explore respite services for family carers of disabled older people." As of 2026 there is still no unified national respite care system; it exists as separate pilots in places such as Fengtai in Beijing, Qingyang in Chengdu, and Guanghan in Sichuan: where the money comes from (sometimes the government pays, sometimes you pay part), who is covered (mostly only severe disability), and how to apply all differ by place and by year.
  • Who this is for: Who it holds for — at 60 and in decent health you will not need it yet, but it is worth knowing such a thing exists; at 75 with someone in the household caring every day, it is worth asking about; if the older person is already disabled, this is the thing most worth asking about, because the family carer is often the one who goes down first.
  • What you get back: relationships — no longer afraid of "the carer collapsing first and the whole family going down with them"
  • How this works in China: In mainland China, ask at the sub-district or community eldercare service center, or the district civil affairs bureau: "respite services for family carers, short-term residential care, family eldercare beds — does this area have them, and how do I apply?" Fengtai in Beijing, Qingyang in Chengdu, and Guanghan in Sichuan have all run pilots. The latest local wording governs.

docs.title: 17.6 If you are the carer, count yourself in first
docs.text:
• What it costs: one self-check and one phone call (Money: none | Time: a few minutes | Effort: none | Do you have to speak up: yes, and it is a little embarrassing — you have to admit you might not hold out either)
  • In short: Caregiving is not a cold; it is a chronic drain that hollows a person out bit by bit. One meta-analysis pooled 13 studies and 4,970 people and put the detection rate of depressive symptoms among family carers of disabled older people in China at 41.81% (95% confidence interval about 37.6%–46.1%). Look closely at the words "detection rate": this is a proportion pooled from several studies, not a prevalence rate, and it certainly does not mean "one in every two carers has depression." What it says is that emotional problems are very common in this group, that they have never been treated as an illness, and that they should not be written off as "not being able to let things go."
  • What you can do: Check yourself against these; the more of them fit, the more seriously to take it — (1) you sleep badly and wake still tired; (2) things you used to enjoy, you do not want to do any of them; (3) you flare up for no reason, shout at the older person, and then feel guilty; (4) you cannot eat, or you eat enormously; (5) you keep saying "I can't hold out," "better if I went first"; (6) headaches, stomach pain, a racing heart, and nothing shows up on examination. If several of these fit, make one appointment at a psychiatry or mental health clinic, or make one phone call.
  • Where this comes from: B | The high detection rate of depression among carers has meta-analytic support pooling several studies; but the scales, samples, and regions differ between studies, and the pooled interval itself is wide (95% CI about 37.6%–46.1%, with subgroups from about 33% to nearly 50%), so treat 41.81% as a reminder, not a diagnosis, and certainly not as a "national prevalence."
  • Who this is for: Who it holds for — at 60 and in decent health, you can run into this the moment you start caring for your parents; at 75, ill yourself and also caring for someone, it is heaviest; if the older person is already disabled, the carer is often an even older spouse, and the risk is highest. If you hear "there's no point in living" or "I'd be better off dead," take it seriously and do only two things: stay with the person, and call for help. National psychological assistance hotline 12356 (set up by the National Health Commission in 2024, with each line required to provide at least 18 hours of service a day); the Hope 24 hotline 400-161-9995 (24/7). If someone is in immediate danger, call 120 or 110.
  • What you get back: relationships + independence — no longer afraid of "the person doing the caring collapsing first"
  • How this works in China: Call 12356; ask at the community whether there is an older-adult mental health care point or a community mental health doctor (more places to turn are in 17.10). The latest local wording governs.

There is no version of caregiving that is not tiring.

docs.title: 17.7 The four hurdles caregiving has to get over: body, money, work, feelings
docs.text:
Whether you are caring for a parent or a spouse, the wearing-down comes in just four forms.

Hurdle What it looks like One thing you can do first Body Turning, lifting, bathing, night trips to the toilet — by the end of the day your back goes first Stop carrying it alone and set a rota: schedule shifts at home, or use short-term residential care or home care to cover a few days Money Attendant fees, care supplies, the self-pay part of a hospital stay — one payment after another First check whether local long-term care insurance covers it and whether there is a disability subsidy; see Chapter 4 Work A job plus caregiving; take too much leave and you fear losing the job Check whether your province has one-child carer leave — there is no national rule, each province sets its own days (from 5 to 20, and in some provinces non-only children can take it too), your province's population and family planning regulations govern; take it if you can Feelings Irritability, guilt, grievance; you lose your temper at the patient and then regret it Find one person you can talk to and talk to them regularly; if you cannot hold out, call a hotline and go to a psychiatry or mental health clinic

The hardest one to say out loud is feelings: you can say you are tired, but being fed up is often something you do not dare say.

docs.title: 17.8 "It is time for a facility" is about capacity, not filial devotion
docs.text:
• What it costs: one assessment or one conversation (Money: assessments usually go through LTCI, or are free | Time: half a day | Effort: none | Do you have to speak up: hard to say — this is the hardest step to take)
  • In short: Whether the older person should move to a facility is not settled by "am I a good son or daughter," but by a few very concrete questions: can they go on safely at home, can the carer still hold out, is there enough money.
  • What you can do: The more of these fit, the more "a facility" or "paying a professional to come in" belongs among the options — (1) safety: repeated falls, wandering off, an emergency at night, forgetting to turn off the stove or the gas; (2) the care tasks: turning, lifting, feeding, changing a urinary catheter, managing pressure sores — can the household do them; (3) the carer's state: the carer's body or mind has already given way; (4) money and skill: round-the-clock care is unaffordable, or the nursing the older person needs simply cannot be done at home. If you want an objective reference point, you can have an assessment under the national standard Specification for Older Adults' Capacity Assessment (《老年人能力评估规范》, GB/T 42195-2022), which grades capacity in five levels, from "capacity intact" to "completely disabled."
  • Where this comes from: B | Capacity assessment for older adults has a national standard, so who assesses and how they assess has a basis. But no cut-off line makes the decision for you; "when is the time" has no single answer, and in the end you and the older person decide together.
  • Who this is for: Who it holds for — at 60 and in decent health, what you are thinking about now is "whether, later on"; at 75 with several chronic conditions, have the assessment done once and know where you stand; if the older person is already disabled, the question becomes "can this household still hold up where it is."
  • What you get back: relationships + dignity — no longer afraid of "am I unfilial," "the old person being sent away"
  • How this works in China: For the disability assessment, LTCI benefits, and whether a facility offers a trial stay, ask at the community or sub-district eldercare service center, the district civil affairs bureau, or the medical insurance bureau where the person is insured. If you are unsure, start by having the older person stay in a facility for a few days on trial. The latest local wording governs.

docs.title: 17.9 Between siblings, count money and time separately
docs.text:
• What it costs: one family meeting (Money: none | Time: an hour or two, possibly several of them | Effort: none | Do you have to speak up: hard to say — it means talking about money, and possibly opening old scores)
  • In short: The falling-out is usually not about who gives less, but about no one saying clearly who gave how much. Count the time given and the money given separately, write them on one sheet, and there is less to argue about.
  • What you can do: (1) Split it into two things: the people who give time and the people who give money; (2) set a conversion — whoever cannot give time gives money in proportion, or uses that money to buy services (hospital accompaniment, an attendant, respite) to cover that share of the work; (3) clock the work of "giving time": half a day for one hospital accompaniment, several days for one hospital stay, and record it on the sheet; (4) if you cannot agree, bring in someone to chair it: an elder, the residents' committee, a social worker. How to hold the meeting is in Chapter 21.
  • Where this comes from: C | Common practice and collected experience; there is no research on "how to divide it so that nobody argues." But no split satisfies everyone: the one who lives nearby gives more time, the one who earns more gives more money, and it is often called unfair; families in different cities, only children, and step-families get more tangled still.
  • Who this is for: Who it holds for — at 60, while your parents are still sturdy, set the rules first; at 75, with parents carrying chronic conditions, while their minds are still clear, lay the accounts out; if the older person is already disabled, do not wait for a collapse to talk.
  • What you get back: relationships — no longer afraid of "the family turning on each other over money and care"
  • How this works in China: The community mediation committee, the residents' committee, and social workers can all help get the family into one room to talk; if it really cannot be settled, go the legal route. The latest local wording governs.

docs.title: 17.10 For the carer: a few places you can call
docs.text:
When you are tired, fed up, or cannot hold out, these are places you can turn.

  • Respite care: have a professional cover for you for a few days (see 17.5).
  • The 12356 national psychological assistance hotline: set up by the National Health Commission in 2024; each line is required to provide at least 18 hours of service a day, and in many places it runs 24 hours. There is also the Hope 24 hotline, 400-161-9995 (24/7).
  • The community mental health doctor: if there is someone at home with a severe mental disorder (schizophrenia, for example), the community health center or township health center has a dedicated mental health doctor responsible for follow-up; it is part of the National Basic Public Health Service, with at least 4 follow-ups a year.
  • Older-adult mental health care points: under the action to care for older adults' mental health that the National Health Commission promoted from 2022 to 2025, in principle every county (city, district) has at least one such point in a community or village. Ask at your community whether there is one.
  • Eldercare advisers: the "eldercare adviser" role the state is promoting helps older people work out what to do among the pile of policies and institutions, and handles errands on their behalf (民发〔2024〕52 号).
  • A contracted family doctor: once signed up, an older person with limited mobility or disability can request home treatment, follow-up, nursing, and a home sickbed, and chronic conditions can be prescribed 4 to 12 weeks at a time.
  • Long-term care insurance: mainland China's LTCI scheme is the money for care after disability — whether it reimburses and how much, ask the medical insurance bureau where the person is insured (see Chapter 4). It is not the same product as the long-term care insurance policies sold in the US or UK; this book describes the mainland system only.

How far these have been built out differs from place to place; asking once is more accurate than guessing at home. The latest local wording governs.

docs.title: 17.11 If you can do only one thing today
docs.text:
Take one sheet of paper and write down three names and phone numbers: one who can be there at once if something happens, one who can put in money, one who can handle paperwork and make decisions. When you have written them, stick the sheet on the fridge.

If the second and third columns on that sheet are both empty, spend today on one phone call instead — to the person you have not been in touch with the longest, and who is most likely to help you.

docs.title: 17.12 If you are reading this for your parents
docs.text:
This chapter means two things for you: one is finding people for your parents; the other is a reminder that you are also one of the people who has to be counted in.

Assemble the people for your parents. Take the table in 17.2 and fill it in for your own family, see which kind is missing, and then go and look. Do not underrate neighbors: first help them get to know the people across the corridor and upstairs and downstairs, and leave each other phone numbers — when you are not there, the neighbor is the person closest to them. Ask at the community once whether your area has visits to people living alone, contracted family doctors, meal services, and respite care.

Do not use yourself up. Many people run everywhere for their parents, cast themselves as the substitute player, come whenever called, and do not dare get sick or get fed up. Once disability is long-term, one person cannot carry it for a year. While there is still time, do three things: settle how the siblings divide money and time (17.9); ask clearly about respite care and short-term residential care (17.5); and keep for yourself one person you can talk to and one hotline (17.10).

And one more layer. The way you care for your parents today is, most likely, the way your children will care for you later. Do you want your children to quit a job, or break down, for your sake? If not, then now — for yourself and for them — set the ground rules for the road that is "paying someone to help."

docs.title: 17.13 What I am not sure about in this chapter
docs.text:
• The qualifications and fees for hospital accompaniment: there is no unified national occupational qualification, the "companion certificate" is mostly a local or industry assessment, and whether another city recognizes it I have not checked city by city. Fees are set by each agency; the Shanghai figures in this chapter (198–280 yuan for half a day in Pudong, 200–300 yuan for citywide packages, and so on) represent only Shanghai's published figures in 2026, and other cities have to be asked separately.
  • Respite care, long-term care insurance, and one-child carer leave are almost one pattern per province, sometimes per city: at national level respite care is only at the "explore" stage (see 17.5), LTCI's disability assessment and benefits are still being rolled out, and the number of days of carer leave depends on your province's regulations — this chapter stops at "where to ask," and the specific terms have to come from your own locality.
  • Carer depression at 41.81%: this is a detection rate pooled from 13 studies; the scales differ between studies and the pooled interval is wide (about 34%–49%), so it can only serve as a reminder, not as the prevalence in your area or in any one person.

docs.title: Chapter 18 · Phones and scams: get the thing done, don't get taken
docs.text:
Seven in the morning. You want to book an appointment on your phone. You poke at the screen for a long while and can't find the place. The letters are too small, there are too many steps. You put the phone down and say, "I'll go early and queue tomorrow."

Put it down, and you have handed someone else a thing you could have done yourself.

docs.title: 18.1 What this chapter is for
docs.text:
This book works out four accounts, and the first is self-reliance. The old saying about managing for yourself meant being able to feed yourself and get to the toilet on your own. Today that sentence is only half of it — you have to add one more line: being able to pick up your own phone and get done the things that mean seeing a doctor, going out, paying money.

Appointments are on the phone, payments are on the phone, and to get into a hospital you first have to show a code. If you can't do the things on the phone, you have to ask for help everywhere. Not being able to use a phone already amounts to being half-disabled today.

This chapter has two halves. The first half is about getting things done on the phone; the second half is about scams — because what a scammer is after is exactly this screen you now depend on most.

docs.title: 18.2 First set the phone so you can see it and hear it
docs.text:
• What it costs: ten minutes, one setup (money: none | time: ten minutes | effort: none | do you have to ask: no)
  • In short: Every phone hides a switch that makes the letters bigger and the sound louder, and it goes by different names: on the phone itself it's "simple mode / large font", in WeChat it's "care mode", in Alipay it's "elder mode". Turn it on and you don't need a new phone.
  • What you can do: ① The phone itself: "Settings" → "Display" or "Accessibility" → "Simple mode / elder mode / large font". On an iPhone, "Settings → Accessibility → Display & Text Size"; on Huawei, "Settings → System & updates → Simple mode" (after a system upgrade this moved into "care mode", under "Settings → Care and accessibility → Care", as "simple layout"). ② WeChat: Me → Settings → Care Mode → turn on (in newer versions there is an extra "More" step inside "Settings"). ③ Alipay: Me → Settings (top right) → Elder Mode, or just search "elder mode" in the search box. ④ Sound: turn "media volume" and "call volume" up to the maximum.
  • Where this comes from: C | Button names and their positions change with the version; the direction doesn't — if you can't see it or can't hear it, look first for "care", "elder", "large font".
  • Who this is for: People whose sight and hearing are getting worse but who can still hold a phone themselves. If you can't see the screen at all, move to voice assistants and have your children operate it for you.
  • What you get back: self-reliance — no longer afraid that "I can't make out a single character on this phone"
  • How this works in China: If you can't get it right yourself, take the phone to a community eldercare service station, a university of the third age, or a phone brand's own shop, and have the staff set it up in front of you. The latest local wording prevails.

docs.title: 18.3 When your children help from far away, there is only one hard rule
docs.text:
• What it costs: one phone call, one video call (money: none | time: a few sessions | effort: none | do you have to ask: easy to ask)
  • In short: Your children aren't nearby — so how do they teach you to use the phone? The steadiest way is a video call: you hold the phone up facing the screen, and they watch and say "tap this next". Software that lets the other person take over your phone screen — don't use it if you can do without it.
  • What you can do: ① Have your children call by video and teach you one step at a time: you tap, they watch. ② If you really want remote assistance, use only the one that came with your phone brand; have your children install it for you face to face, and teach you how to agree and how to hang up. ③ In any remote session, never read a verification code out to the other person on the phone — not even to your own son.
  • Where this comes from: C | Common practice. Screen-sharing software helps people and is also often exploited; the rules have to be set in advance, see 18.6.
  • Who this is for: Households with children who can do a video call. If your children aren't comfortable with phones either, swap "the person who teaches you" for a young volunteer at the community office or the university of the third age.
  • What you get back: self-reliance + relationships — no longer afraid that "no one will teach me, and I daren't tap anything"
  • How this works in China: Communities, universities of the third age and libraries often run phone classes. Ask once at the community office: "Is there any activity that teaches older people to use a phone?" The latest local wording prevails.

docs.title: 18.4 Getting it done: six tasks, and where the first tap goes
docs.text:
• What it costs: about fifteen minutes per task, one task at a time (money: none | time: fifteen minutes each | effort: none | do you have to ask: easy to ask)
  • In short: There are only a few things you need to do on a phone: book an appointment, call a car, pay, pay bills, show your medical insurance code, and prove that you are you.
  • How to do it (each step starts from what to tap the first time): ① Book an appointment: WeChat → search box → type the hospital name → open the hospital's official account → "Book an appointment". ② Call a car: Amap or Baidu Maps → "Ride" → check "my location" → "Request". ③ Pay: WeChat "Me → Services → Pay and receive", which shows a code for the cashier to scan. ④ Pay bills: WeChat "Me → Services → Utilities", choose water, electricity or gas, and link the account number once. ⑤ Electronic medical insurance credential (the insurance code): install the "National Medical Insurance Service Platform" app, or search "medical insurance e-credential" in WeChat or Alipay, do the face verification, and show it when you see a doctor or buy medicine. ⑥ Prove that you are you: people drawing a pension do a liveness check once a year, using the "electronic social security card" or the "Zhangshen 12333" app — blink, open your mouth, and it's done.
  • Where this comes from: C | These are all features the various apps already have, and their position shifts slightly with each version; the direction is "search box + scan + payment code".
  • Who this is for: People who can read and can see the screen. If your eyes are poor or your fingers shake, turn on the large font and the voice first, then learn these steps.
  • What you get back: self-reliance — no longer afraid that "I can't even get through the hospital door, I have to ask someone for everything"
  • How this works in China: The insurance code is accepted only from the "National Medical Insurance Service Platform" app or the official entrances in WeChat and Alipay; the pension liveness check only from "Zhangshen 12333" and the "electronic social security card". Anything else — a mini-program that has you enter a bank card password or read out a verification code — is not official. The latest local wording prevails.

docs.title: 18.5 If you can't follow it, don't force it: the places and people who can do it for you
docs.text:
• What it costs: one conversation (money: some free, some paid | time: one trip | effort: none | do you have to ask: you do, and it's a little awkward)
  • In short: Not being able to learn it isn't shameful. Tapping around on your own is what's dangerous.
  • What you can do: ① The community: the residents' committee and the community eldercare service station can pay or register on your behalf, and the counter can handle things for you. ② Government service center: ask at the door "which window handles assisted service for older people" — there is usually a fast track. ③ Paid hospital accompaniment: if you live alone, your children are far away, or getting around is hard, you can pay someone to go with you to register, queue and collect medicine; Shanghai and some other places already run official pilots. ④ The bank counter: if you don't want to use mobile banking, do it at the counter. That is your right.
  • Where this comes from: C | Assisted handling and hospital accompaniment are practices being promoted in various places; coverage and charges vary a lot, and accompaniment still has no nationwide qualification standard.
  • Who this is for: People who live in the city and can get out of the house. If you live far out or can't get out, rely on the community's home visits and your children operating the phone for you.
  • What you get back: self-reliance + dignity — no longer afraid that "I can't understand it and daren't ask, so I just sit there fretting"
  • How this works in China: Government services have a reform called "get one thing done efficiently"; hospital accompaniment costs about 198–300 yuan for a half day (it differs from place to place). Who to ask: the community residents' committee, the guidance desk at the government service center, or the manager on the bank floor. The latest local wording prevails.

docs.title: 18.6 One family agreement, taped to the fridge
docs.text:
• What it costs: one sheet of paper, one signature from each person in the family (money: none | time: half an hour | effort: none | do you have to ask: easy to ask)
  • In short: One rule set by the whole family is worth more than an argument after something has happened. Just two lines: verification codes go only to your own family; if a stranger asks for a code, hang up, every time.
  • What you can do: ① Write it down and tape it to the fridge: verification codes, bank card passwords, payment passwords — you give them to no one. Not to someone claiming to be customer service, not to the police or the procuratorate, not to the bank, and not to someone claiming to be a colleague of your child. ② The moment the other person mentions "transfer money", "verification code" or "screen sharing", hang up. ③ Agree at home on one small thing that only the family knows; when the "grandson" on the video opens his mouth, ask him that first.
  • Where this comes from: C | Common practice. But "never give a verification code to anyone" is the first line of almost every anti-fraud leaflet.
  • Who this is for: Families that can still sit down and talk it over. If someone in the house has already lost judgement, the guardian has to enforce this rule for them.
  • What you get back: money + dignity — no longer afraid that "if I've been cheated I daren't say, for fear the family will blame me"
  • How this works in China: Photograph the agreement, send it to the family group chat, save it in the album; the National Anti-Fraud Center's own materials say the same sentence. The latest local wording prevails.

The scammer is younger than you, and knows the phone better than you do.

docs.title: 18.7 Fake relatives: the "grandson" on video may be assembled
docs.text:
• What it costs: hang up, call back (money: none | time: one minute | effort: none | do you have to ask: no)
  • In short: A scammer can take your grandson's photos and voice and stitch together a face-swapped video to call you, with the face and the voice both close. Don't judge it by "does it look like him" — judge it by "check it another way".
  • What you can do: ① The moment you hear "it's me, something's happened, send money quickly", hang up. ② Call the grandson back on the number you saved yourself, or call his parents; do not call back the number that showed on your screen. ③ Ask him about an old thing that only the family knows. ④ On the video, ask him to put a hand over his face for a moment — fake video often gives itself away there.
  • Where this comes from: A (case) | In Zhengzhou, an older woman known as Grandma Li was sent an AI face-swap and voice-clone video of her "grandson" asking for 50,000 yuan; at the bank the staff flagged the account as risky, and a call-back to verify stopped the transfer second-hand (People's Daily Overseas Edition, 2026-04-13). Another report, citing Ministry of Public Security data, says that in the first quarter of 2025 the number of AI face-swap and voice-clone fraud cases filed nationwide rose about 45% quarter on quarter, and people over 60 made up 38% of those cheated second-hand (same paper, 2026-04-13).
  • Who this is for: Everyone, especially older people who watch a lot of short video and often video-call their grandchildren. If cognition has already declined and they can't tell true from false, the family has to hold the "call the child before giving money" line for them.
  • What you get back: money — no longer afraid that "the person on the video is obviously him"
  • How this works in China: After hanging up, dial 96110 for advice; the Zhengzhou case was stopped only because bank staff flagged the account as abnormal, so doing a large transfer at the counter adds one more human check. The latest local wording prevails.

docs.title: 18.8 Fake customer service: if they say "automatic monthly charge", hang up first
docs.text:
• What it costs: one hang-up (money: none | time: one minute | effort: none | do you have to ask: no)
  • In short: "You've signed up for a membership / a livestream, and it charges automatically every month" — that sentence itself is the hook. Real customer service does not call to teach you how to cancel a charge, and certainly does not have you download software or give a password.
  • What you can do: ① The moment you hear "automatic charge" or "it affects your credit record", hang up. ② If you want to check, call the platform's official customer line yourself — for the short-video platform in this case, 95152 — not the number that called you. ③ Don't download any "meeting", "screen cast" or "security" app the other person names; that step is how they get to see your phone and operate it for you. ④ A bank card password, an SMS verification code, a face scan — if the person on the phone asks for any of them, it's a scammer.
  • Where this comes from: A (case) | In Shenzhen, a 70-year-old woman known as Aunt Yi was told by someone posing as platform customer service that "you've opened a livestream and will be charged"; she did as told and installed three unfamiliar video-meeting apps, and 147,000 yuan was transferred out within an hour (Shenzhen Municipal Public Security Bureau anti-fraud bulletin, 2025-07) second-hand.
  • Who this is for: People who often watch video or shop online on the phone. If someone is already disabled, the money and the phone should not both be in their hands alone.
  • What you get back: money — no longer afraid that "he sounded so plausible that I believed him"
  • How this works in China: If a suspicious call comes, hang up and dial 96110 or the platform's official hotline; install the National Anti-Fraud Center app and leave call warnings on. The latest local wording prevails.

docs.title: 18.9 "Housing for pension": the real one is insurance, the fake one has you mortgage the house
docs.text:
• What it costs: one more question, one more day (money: none | time: one trip | effort: none | do you have to ask: easy to ask)
  • In short: "Housing for pension" comes in a real version and a fake one. The real one is called "reverse mortgage pension insurance", a state-approved insurance product: you mortgage the house to the insurer, keep living in it, and draw a pension monthly. The fake one borrows the name, has you mortgage the house and hands the money to him to put into "high-interest wealth management" — the crux is "the mortgaged money has to be invested again".
  • What you can do: ① Tell the two apart: real — mortgaged to an insurer, you keep living there, money monthly, and it is insurance; fake — the house is mortgaged, the money goes to a "wealth management company" to invest, and high interest is promised. ② The moment someone says "mortgage the house → put it in our product → high interest every month", stop. ③ If you are genuinely interested, go only to an insurer's counter and to products filed with the financial regulator, and ask face to face; don't go by the leaflet.
  • Where this comes from: A | "Reverse mortgage pension insurance" is a state-approved pilot insurance product (Baojianfa [2014] No. 53, in force from 2014-07-01), run by insurers and not a wealth-management product; the volume of business has always been very small.
  • Who this is for: People over 60 who own their home outright. If the flat is your only place to live and your children still live with you, talk it through with the family before mortgaging.
  • What you get back: money + dignity — no longer afraid that "even a state policy gets used to cheat me"
  • How this works in China: For the real product, ask at a regular insurer's counter; if you meet "housing-for-pension wealth management", dial 96110 or report it to the financial regulator. The latest local wording prevails.

docs.title: 18.10 The free-eggs lecture isn't selling eggs
docs.text:
• What it costs: one trip, one time holding back (money: none | time: half a day | effort: none | do you have to ask: easy to ask)
  • In short: "Free eggs, free health lecture" is a way of pulling people in, not a kindness. First a small freebie, then you are led into a group chat, and slowly they sell you "miracle medicine" at thousands or tens of thousands of yuan. Most of those "medicines" are sugar pills, or food.
  • What you can do: ① If "free gift + lecture + expensive health product" come as a set, don't go. ② If you are already in the group, leave it; if they tell you "don't tell your children", that sentence itself is the alarm. ③ If you really want a supplement, ask your children first, or ask at a proper pharmacy or hospital; don't trust an "expert's live lecture". ④ Keep the receipts and the transfer records.
  • Where this comes from: B | CCTV Finance, China News Service and several other outlets have reported the "free eggs" routine; some cases have been found by the courts to be fraud and drawn prison sentences.
  • Who this is for: Older people who live alone, like company, are afraid of getting ill and have a bit of money are the easiest to catch. What the family should do is not scold them — it is to go with them once to ask at a proper channel.
  • What you get back: money + relationships — no longer afraid that "I'm scared of getting ill, so I want to buy some peace of mind"
  • How this works in China: Report false advertising to the market regulator on 12315; if illegal fundraising or fraud is involved, call the police. The latest local wording prevails.

docs.title: 18.11 The "roaming retirement" membership that costs hundreds of thousands up front — don't pay it yet
docs.text:
• What it costs: one check, one refusal to pay (money: none | time: one trip | effort: none | do you have to ask: you do, and it's a little awkward)
  • In short: "Pay a hundred-odd thousand, or several hundred thousand, once to become a member, and later you can stay at any of our retirement bases anywhere in the country" — with prepaid membership fees like this, the thing to fear is the day the company's money runs out and the people are gone.
  • What you can do: ① Remember the lines the state has drawn: a care home may collect service fees at most 12 months ahead; the deposit taken from a single older person may not exceed 12 times the monthly bed fee, and beyond that it is non-compliant. ② If someone wants several hundred thousand in "membership fees" or a "lifetime card" in one go, they have probably crossed the line already. ③ Before paying, check whether the institution is on file with the local civil affairs department. ④ If you want to spend a few winter months in the south, paying a year at a time, one month's deposit against one month's rent, is enough — don't stake your whole savings at once.
  • Where this comes from: A | The Guiding Opinions on Strengthening Supervision of Prepaid Fees at Elderly Care Institutions (《关于加强养老机构预收费监管的指导意见》), issued by the Ministry of Civil Affairs and six other departments (Minfa [2024] No. 19, effective from 2024-10), sets out the prepayment caps and the escrow of funds.
  • Who this is for: People who own a flat, have savings, are still in reasonable health and fancy "roaming retirement". If you are already disabled and need care, you are not a candidate for roaming — you are a candidate for care.
  • What you get back: money — no longer afraid that "I went looking for a dignified old age and put the principal in"
  • How this works in China: Before paying, go to the local civil affairs bureau and ask about the institution's filing and how its prepaid fees are supervised. Ask three things: Is it on file? How are prepayments supervised? How are refunds calculated? The latest local wording prevails.

docs.title: 18.12 Set yourself one rule: big money waits a day before it leaves
docs.text:
• What it costs: one day (money: none | time: one day | effort: none | do you have to ask: easy to ask)
  • In short: What a scammer fears most is that you wait. Almost every scam contains a "if you don't do it today it's too late", precisely so that you have no time to think. Put a "one day later" on big money and the scammer's words stop working.
  • What you can do: ① Agree with the family: above a certain amount (you set it — three or five thousand, say), nothing goes out that day; sleep on it and do it the next day. ② When transferring in mobile banking, choose "arrives in 24 hours", not "instant". ③ To be safer still, put the large sums into a fixed-term deposit, or open a separate account where getting money out means going to the bank.
  • Where this comes from: C | This is a house rule. Years ago a transfer from an ATM to an account not in your own name was required to arrive 24 hours later; that was later relaxed and instant transfer allowed, so this cooling-off period now has to be set by you.
  • Who this is for: Everyone. Even in a real emergency (a hospital deposit) there is usually another way; calling the family first often works better than transferring first.
  • What you get back: money — no longer afraid that "I transferred in a hurry, with no time to think"
  • How this works in China: Look for the "transfer arrival time" setting in your mobile banking app; if you're not sure, dial 96110. The latest local wording prevails.

docs.title: 18.13 If you really are cheated: stop the payment, keep the evidence, call the police — and don't hide it from the family
docs.text:
• What it costs: the first few hours (money: none | time: a few hours | effort: none | do you have to ask: hard to bring up)
  • In short: If you have been cheated, don't start by cursing yourself, and don't hide it. Whether the money can be recovered depends on these first few hours. The order is: stop the payment → keep the evidence → call the police.
  • What you can do: ① Stop the payment: call the bank's hotline or go to the counter at once, and ask them to freeze or stop that payment — whatever can be held back, is. ② Keep the evidence: don't delete the chat records, the transfer text message, the incoming call; take screenshots, record, the fuller the better. ③ Call the police: dial 110, or 96110 to explain the situation, the sooner the better. ④ Tell the family: hiding it only makes the hole bigger, and you may be cheated a second time.
  • Where this comes from: A | The Ministry of Public Security has introduced 96110, the National Anti-Fraud Center app and other measures; the Anti-Telecom and Online Fraud Law of the People's Republic of China took effect on 2022-12-01 and provides for stopping payments, freezing funds and recovering assets.
  • Who this is for: Everyone. If someone already has dementia and has been "played" for a long time, the family should go with them in person to the police and the bank.
  • What you get back: money + dignity — no longer afraid that "if I've been cheated no one will help me, and I daren't say it out loud"
  • How this works in China: 110, 96110, the bank counter; the National Anti-Fraud Center app has a one-tap report. The latest local wording prevails.

docs.title: 18.14 If you can only do one thing today
docs.text:
Today, set the phone's font size to the largest, and turn on WeChat's care mode. Just that one thing.

With bigger letters you can see everything in this chapter clearly — where the first tap goes for those six tasks, and the one place in a scam where something doesn't sit right.

docs.title: 18.15 If you are reading this for your parents
docs.text:
It is hard to say "be careful, don't get cheated" straight out. The moment you say it, it becomes distrust.

How to say it: turn the conversation onto yourself. Don't say "let me adjust your phone for you"; say "I want bigger text on mine too — let's do both together." While he watches you do it, he learns the method himself.

To guard the gate, start with three things that don't need his approval: ① install the National Anti-Fraud Center app on his phone and turn call warnings on; ② save your number, 96110 and the nearest bank branch's number into his phone, and teach him one sentence — "if they ask for a code, hang up"; ③ set large transfers to "arrives in 24 hours", and agree with him that above a certain amount he calls you first.

If he won't agree, what you can still do: ask at the community whether there are phone classes or assisted handling; get his insurance code and pension liveness check working smoothly on his phone; print out the family agreement in 18.6 and tape it to his fridge.

The hardest part: don't let him feel that you are investigating him or guarding against him. For someone who has been cheated, what they fear most is often not that the money is gone, but being scolded by the family. If he is willing to tell you first thing, the money can still be saved.

docs.title: 18.16 What I am not sure about in this chapter
docs.text:
• unverified Two figures on AI fraud — "up about 45% quarter on quarter" and "older people made up 38% of those cheated" — this chapter found only the People's Daily Overseas Edition (2026-04-13) and reprints by the Legal Daily site and Credit China saying they are cited from Ministry of Public Security data; I did not read the ministry's original bulletin, so they are still treated as second-hand. To check the original wording, go to the ministry's website or look up the transcript of a ministry press conference.
  • The entrances for elder mode and care mode have to be found again every time a version changes: the current paths for Apple, Huawei and WeChat can all be matched against their own official help pages (see 18.17); Huawei, for one, merged its earlier "simple mode" into "care mode", which shows that renaming really does happen. Alipay has no long-term stable official page, so go by what the app on your own phone actually shows.
  • There is no nationwide system for hospital accompaniment, and no nationwide qualification standard. Shanghai is furthest ahead (see Chapter 17 and 18.5): open to everyone over 60, with no household-registration requirement, so older people who have come to Shanghai from elsewhere can buy it too. A few cities (Xiamen, for instance) have also issued municipal accompaniment schemes through the civil affairs department in recent years, but most have not. Whether your city has one, and what it charges, you have to ask the local civil affairs bureau.
  • On how many disputes "roaming" and prepaid retirement membership fees have actually produced, there is no public authoritative statistic, and we did not find a number — what this chapter gives is the regulatory wording (Minfa [2024] No. 19) plus an official risk notice: on 2025-09-09 the National Office on Aging, the Ministry of Civil Affairs, the China Association of Aging and the China Consumers Association jointly issued an eldercare consumption notice, naming the problem of "membership-based eldercare" and "prepaid cards" charging large membership fees. To check whether a particular institution is compliant, go to the Ministry of Civil Affairs' National Elderly Care Service Information Platform (see 18.17), or ask the local civil affairs bureau.
  • The default for "arrives in 24 hours" in mobile banking differs from bank to bank, and there is no nationwide page explaining it: some default to instant, some make you choose "next-day arrival" under "arrival time" when you transfer. Open your own mobile banking and look for that option once on the transfer screen; if you're not sure, call the bank's hotline.
